📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida. (Photo by Donald Miralle/Getty Images for IRONMAN) (Photo: Getty Images for IRONMAN).

One month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back. His 7:19:17 took 1:47 off the previous men’s iron-distance world best that Sam Laidlow (FRA) set at Challenge Roth earlier this year.

Industry observers note that florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona. He’d taken the lead late on the bike and looked on course for the win until he abruptly came to a stop on the run with roughly 30 minutes of racing left.

However, ahead of Kona, Ditlev said he was putting up career-best numbers across the swim, bike, and run at his training camp in Colorado. In Florida, he finally got to reap the rewards of what fitness could produce all the way to the finish line.

According to recent reports, ditlev came out of the water in fifth, right on the heels of Ben Kanute (USA) and Rudy von Berg (USA). He took his time in T1 and started the bike nearly a minute down, but it didn’t take him long to ride back to the front. And then, just past mile 10, he made his move. No one could go with him, and they wouldn’t be able to stay remotely close to him either.

Sources indicate that by the time Ditlev came off the bike, he was 11 minutes clear of a chase group that included Sam Long (USA), von Berg, and Kanute. His 3:51:16 was the fastest bike split ever recorded at an Ironman, nearly two minutes quicker than the 3:53:12 Robert Kallin (SWE) rode at Ironman Kalmar in August.

Sources indicate that off the bike, he once again took his time in transition. But transitions were the only slow part of Ditlev’s day. Once through T2, he picked up another minute on the chasers over the opening 10 miles. He hit halfway in 1:15, on pace for a 2:30 marathon and well within reach of Laidlow’s 7:21:04. With such an unassailable lead, one can assume he must’ve known the record was within reach to keep such an aggressive pace.

Ditlev eventually closed with a 2:33:31 marathon, crossing the line in 7:19:17. Von Berg took second, 14 minutes back, securing the early Kona slot and podium he’d come for. Matt Hanson (USA), meanwhile, ran a remarkable 2:28:07 to beat Long to the final podium spot, but still finished 16 minutes behind Ditlev.

#115019. Want to Live Longer? Start Flossing Your Teeth

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Want to Live Longer? Start Flossing Your Teeth

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there’s no shortage of hacks, snacks, and habits that purportedly help you stay healthier for longer.
  • Recent findings suggest that one such staple is the humble roll of floss, which is probably collecting dust in your medicine cabinet.
  • Keep reading to see why skipping that single strand of string could have consequences that go far beyond tender gums.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there’s no shortage of hacks, snacks, and habits that purportedly help you stay healthier for longer. But while we’re busy chasing cutting-edge upgrades—from cold plunges and greens powders to living by the gospel of your Oura ring—we tend to miss out on less sexy yet still powerful tweaks that have been shown to meaningfully move the needle on long-term health.

Recent findings suggest that one such staple is the humble roll of floss, which is probably collecting dust in your medicine cabinet. However, you should probably break it out nightly not just for a brighter, cleaner smile, but to potentially benefit your heart and brain, too.

Keep reading to see why skipping that single strand of string could have consequences that go far beyond tender gums.

If you believe that brushing twice daily will suffice for oral health, you’re in for some sobering news. According to Kami Hoss, DDS, author of If Your Mouth Could Talk: An In-Depth Guide to Oral Health and Its Impact on Your Entire Life, your toothbrush cleans only 60 percent of the surface of your teeth. Read: If you don’t floss, nearly half of your mouth goes uncleaned day after day.

In a recent development, “Flossing is a simple but critical intervention because it disrupts bacterial biofilm between the teeth—areas a toothbrush cannot reach,” adds board-certified periodontist Richard Nejat, DDS. When you floss consistently, you reduce bacterial load, plaque buildup, and gum inflammation—all of which can help keep periodontal disease (a.k.a. gum disease) at bay. And there’s a decent chance you’ll be affected: Per the Cleveland Clinic, about half of adults in the U.S. have some form of gum disease.

The tissue surrounding these small crevices also warrants your full attention. “The sulcus—the shallow groove where your gum meets your tooth—is lined with some of the most permeable tissue in the human body,” Dr. Hoss tells SELF. “It’s richly vascularized, meaning bacteria and whatever compounds we introduce there have a remarkably direct pathway into the bloodstream.” And here’s where the longevity benefits of flossing come into play.

Industry observers note that on top of staving off periodontal disease, research demonstrates that regular flossing is associated with reduced risk of dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, and stroke. It can also be an important part of managing diabetes. Meanwhile, poor flossing habits have been associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD mortality. And according to one study of over 5,000 older adults, never flossing increased mortality risk by 30% compared to flossing daily.

So how can one tiny string make such a big difference in long-term health outcomes? For starters, you have some unfriendly bacteria to contend with. “Porphyromonas gingivalis, which occurs in the mouth, infects the gums and causes gum disease and periodontitis,” says Jennifer Timmons, MD, a longevity physician and the founder of Timmons Wellness. She says that this bacteria is present in atherosclerotic plaque that can plug arteries during a heart attack, while Dr. Hoss adds that it’s also been found in the brain tissue of Alzheimer’s patients. That’s why addressing it at the source matters. “If you don’t floss, [the bacteria] can enter the bloodstream and lead to blood vessel inflammation, damage, and tiny blood clots that could cause heart attacks or strokes in other areas,” Dr. Timmons warns. (She notes that these are correlations, not proven causations, though the associations are strong.).

It has been revealed that flossing also actively helps decrease inflammation in the gums, thereby preventing a cascade of vascular damage throughout the body, Dr. Timmons explains. After all, inflammation is a major driver of not only gum disease but also the chronic conditions listed above. When you don’t floss, inflammation proliferates in the mouth—and it doesn’t stay put. “Chronic gum disease creates a systemic inflammatory burden that touches almost every major disease category,” Dr. Hoss warns. That doesn’t mean flossing is a panacea, but it highlights how interconnected oral health and overall health really are.

Industry observers note that if you already floss daily, rest assured that you’re ahead of the game. For the rest of us who skimp here and there—or have yet to make flossing routine, despite the awkward biannual urges from our dentist—now’s a great time to pick up the habit.

It has been revealed that dr. Hoss advises flossing at night rather than in the morning. “You’re sealing your mouth for six to eight hours. Clearing that biofilm before bed matters far more than doing it after breakfast,” he states. He also recommends good old string floss above the likes of picks and water flossers, as neither can get into the nooks and crannies at and below the gumline as efficiently. (If traditional floss is tough to maneuver, these alternatives are still better than skipping it altogether.) As for the right way to floss? “Curve it into a ‘C’ shape around each tooth and use an up-and-down motion,” he shares.

According to recent reports, in short, flossing is crucial to maintain oral health, and good oral health has clear downstream effects on the rest of the body. Since heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States—and dementia significantly impacts both quality and length of life —anything that meaningfully reduces risk, even modestly, matters in the longevity conversation. “While flossing alone is not a cure-all for heart or brain health, it is one of the easiest daily habits that can support both oral and overall health,” notes Dr. Nejat. All said, flossing might not be revolutionary, but it has surprisingly far-reaching potential.

Whenever you’re taking CBD or THC, keep these factors in mind.

However, it’s key to note that CBD and THC can work one way in one person, but works a different way in the next person.

There is some research that suggests CBD may interact with the liver, potentially interfering with the metabolism of other medications. If you take any medications or supplements, talk with a healthcare professional before taking any CBD or THC products.

According to recent reports, research notes that THC can induce symptoms of psychosis in people who do not already have the condition, and THC at high doses can increase anxiety. Other research also cautions against THC use if you have cardiovascular or respiratory conditions.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA)Trusted Source warns that THC can pose health risks and causes adverse effects like hallucinations, tremors, anxiety, and more.

Industry observers note that stricter legislation is coming in, and it may affect access to CBD and THC products. The federal government is changing how they define “hemp” at the federal level. The new definition seeks to ban hemp-derived THC, the cannabis compound that causes a “high.”.

Sources indicate that the current law states that hemp is any part of the cannabis sativa plant that contains up to 0.3% of THC by dry weight. The change will restrict any hemp-derived products to a total of 0.4 milligrams (mg) of THC per container. This is much stricter than the current law and will impact access to products with a higher THC content.

It has been revealed that the newly introduced law also bans synthetic cannabinoids, affecting CBD manufacturing. Cannabinoids, like CBD or THC, occur naturally in the hemp plant. However, chemical synthesis is often necessary to make CBD available on a commercial level, and this is where we may see further restrictions.

States with established recreational and medical cannabis regulations may be less affected by the ban. Meanwhile, those without existing regulations, such as Texas and Kentucky, may see a bigger impact.

Full-spectrum and broad-spectrum CBD products are most likely to be affected as they contain trace amounts of THC.

The ban is at the moment due to take effect by mid-December. It’s unclear exactly how these changes will affect the industry, but until then, people can still purchase CBD THC gummies and other CBD products, like oils and topicals.

Gummies that contain THC, or tetrahydrocannabinol, do get you high. THC is the main psychoactive component of cannabis, so even a small amount could make you feel the effects strongly.

Industry observers note that if you decide to venture out, make sure you’re following the suggested dose on the packaging and remember that every person is different when it comes to how THC affects them. Take it slow and one step at a time to avoid any anxiety or adverse effects.

It has been revealed that gummies can typically take from 30 minutes to 2 hours to kick in. “They have to be digested and processed through the liver before entering your bloodstream,” says Alex Nguyen, PharmD, RPh, CPh.

It has been revealed that “CBD may help soften some of THC’s more intense effects while contributing its own calming and anti-inflammatory properties. Many individuals find the combination more balanced and effective than either one alone.

“Keep in mind that even small amounts of THC can affect people differently, so starting with a low dose is always the safest approach,” he indicates.

However, in November 2025, a newly introduced ruling was passed that allows no more than 0.4 mg total THC per container.

#115017. Industry News: Single Women Deserve Honeymoons Too—Here’s How to Plan One

📅 23 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1111 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Single Women Deserve Honeymoons Too—Here’s How to Plan One

📅 23 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m on a speedboat whizzing towards my latest vacation destination.
  • Sources indicate that so often we have our dream destinations on reserve for the day we can go with the person we’ve agreed to spend our life with.
  • Sources indicate that for my most recent we-moon, I was invited to the Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla and joined by two girlfriends.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m on a speedboat whizzing towards my latest vacation destination. As we bounce along, I attempt to take a selfie. The shot I want is the waves, the boats, the islands, but I can’t seem to get the kissing couples out the background. No matter which way I turn, there are honeymooners in my viewfinder. The boat operators and I are the only single people on this vessel. Technically I, too, am a part of a couple—actually, a throuple of single girlfriends heading for an Anguilla getaway. The trip is what I like to call a we-moon.

Sources indicate that so often we have our dream destinations on reserve for the day we can go with the person we’ve agreed to spend our life with. There’s the honeymoon and the babymoon, but when do single women get to celebrate life milestones and fulfill the desire for companionship and adventure? That’s the we-moon.

Sources indicate that for my most recent we-moon, I was invited to the Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla and joined by two girlfriends. Now, you are probably wondering: What is the difference between this and your average girls trip? Well, similar to a honeymoon or babymoon, a we-moon is taken to celebrate a significant life milestone. For me, it was my first book. Single women are so often traveling to celebrate others for their bachelorette or wedding or baby shower. Rarely do we get friends to travel and celebrate something that doesn’t fit into the typical timeline.

Sources indicate that that is the purpose of a we-moon. It’s making the phone call to ask your friends to travel and celebrate an achievement with you, just like you do for others. It could be a promotion, a fresh job, a masters degree, or a book deal.

When crafting the perfect we-moon, there are things to keep in mind to make sure that the trip goes smoothly. I spoke to Joy Harden Bradford, PhD, author of Sisterhood Heals about the best way to pull off a destination celebration with no drama.

It has been revealed that on a honeymoon or babymoon, the whole point is to spend more time together. On a we-moon, it’s a balance of time together and time alone. That’s why Dr. Bradford recommends separate rooms if your budget allows. For this Anguilla trip, we were staying in a villa rental, so we all had our own room and bathroom. It was perfect for the early risers who wanted to read a book on their balcony quietly, or late sleepers who wanted to lay in and order room service. This location was perfect for the we-moon because the Four Seasons Villa and Residence Rentals have the privacy of a personal home but you still can tap into hotel amenities and personalized services (more on that below). Whatever you decide, you should talk about it ahead of time.

“I think having a place where everybody can retreat and have alone time is really good if that is something that the group can do. So private sleeping quarters are key,” she indicates. “Also having conversations about budget ahead of time. Because some people [might say], ‘Oh, we don't need a five-star hotel. We’re just going to be there to sleep. We’re going to be out.’ And other people are like, ‘No, I like luxury.’ So you don’t want to wait until you get there to find out that there’s a difference in the group about that.”.

Another thing you should talk about ahead of time is how many group excursions everyone is down to do. “Because I think for a lot of us, there’s so much going on in our regular life that there’s a lot of expectations for what a vacation should be,” states Dr. Bradford. “‘It’s the one time I get to get away,’ and so people really put a lot on it.”.

Sources indicate that there are many different vacation styles. We’ve all been on a trip that is overplanned and leaves you more exhausted than when you left. Everyone should discuss what activities they want to do, and a good portion should be optional. For example, we worked on an itinerary with our villa concierge. When it came time to do the private yoga session poolside, some people wanted to rest. So I locked in for a one-on-one session, in which I was able to pay extra attention to modifications and my personal pain points. There were plenty of things that we did together, like an afternoon at the spa, where we all got Anguilla-themed massages, and an excursion across the island in a Jeep to see a different beach. Sometimes you just want to take a nap on vacation, and that is okay.

Me doing yoga with my instructor by the villa pool.

It has been revealed that one of the things we did as a group was a margarita-making class. The three of us lined up at the bar of the villa and learned how to properly shake and measure lime juice, orange liqueur, and tequila. Research states that picking up a new skill is good for your brain health. (Although I’m not sure they meant consuming three margaritas in an hour….) The new experience for you can be learning a new sport like pickleball, going to a cooking class, or even playing board games by the beach. This is even better when it becomes a social experiment because even if you fail, you can laugh it off with friends.

What is a girls trip without girl talk? You have to set the mood for conversations. It’s not always a good time to dive deep into your last breakup as you are sitting at a noisy restaurant or relaxing at a spa appointment. But when you are away from your regular routine, there is a great opportunity to open up. “If these are people that you’re actually hoping to grow closer to, then it is vital to continue to go deeper with those relationships. And that really requires a lot of vulnerability, which is really hard for people,” says Bradford. “Girls trips really provide a great opportunity and a great backdrop because you are away from your regular routine to maybe get into some of those things that you don’t have time to talk about later.” You have to set the mood for your friends to unravel. For me, I planned a night in the villa's private jacuzzi tub, watching the sunset, and drinking wine. That’s where we shared our work woes and dating troubles as a night cap.

My friends and I having girl talk by the fire.

#115015. Tech Report: What is the Ironman World Record? It’s Complicated

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (979 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What is the Ironman World Record? It’s Complicated

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Depending on who you ask, it's Magnus Ditlev and Anne Haug, who own the fastest iron-distance time.
  • After a dramatic DNF in the final miles of the run at the 2026 Ironman World Championship, Magnus Ditlev (DNK) raced at Ironman Florida just four weeks later to post the fastest Ironman finish time ever with a 7:19:17.
  • That time upended the previous best iron-distance set by Sam Laidlow just a few months prior at Challenge Roth, where the Frenchman finished in 7:21:04 on the course where the fastest women’s race ever is still held by Germany’s Anne Haug from 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Who holds the Ironman world record? Depending on who you ask, it's Magnus Ditlev and Anne Haug, who own the fastest iron-distance time. (Photo: Ironman (Donald Miralle), Challenge Family, FinisherPix).

After a dramatic DNF in the final miles of the run at the 2026 Ironman World Championship, Magnus Ditlev (DNK) raced at Ironman Florida just four weeks later to post the fastest Ironman finish time ever with a 7:19:17.

That time upended the previous best iron-distance set by Sam Laidlow just a few months prior at Challenge Roth, where the Frenchman finished in 7:21:04 on the course where the fastest women’s race ever is still held by Germany’s Anne Haug from 2024.

And yet, despite all these amazing feats, there are no world records in full-distance racing.

It has been revealed that confused? It’s understandable. Pour yourself a cup of coffee and get ready to learn why Ironman (and iron-distance) world records technically don’t exist.

Recent findings suggest that in the world of running, 26.2-mile marathons must adhere to rigorous certification standards set by World Athletics that include restrictions on things like point-to-point courses, elevation drop, and (recent) International measurement, but triathlon operates without such official oversight. Course configurations are notoriously inconsistent, often shifting from one season to the next, and triathletes don’t even think twice about point-to-point courses or elevation drops between start and finish.

Certainly course distances are confirmed in high-level World Triathlon races like the Olympics, but there is no course certification for long-course or for regular age-group races. Often, you’ll hear athletes remark that their GPS watch clocked an Ironman course as short or long – rarely does a race hit exactly 2.4 miles of swimming, 112 miles of cycling, and 26.2 miles of running. Those are ballpark figures that races would love to hit if they can, but permitting concerns might mean the host city can only close 110 miles of roads for the bike course – this occurred at Ironman Texas in 2018, when “Ironman record times” were clocked by Melissa Hauschildt and Matt Hanson.

Beyond the logistics, an athlete’s clock is at the mercy of Mother Nature; factors like local climate, hilly terrain, or even a current-assisted swim can skew the data (as was the case in 2021, when Blummenfelt floated downcurrent to a 39:41 swim en route to a then “Ironman record” of 7:21:12 in Cozumel).

Because of that, Ironman confirmed in 2026 that they do not keep track of “official” world records for that reason, with a spokesperson telling Triathlete, “Due to variance of courses (even from year-to-year the same race could have course alterations), combined with the fact that unlike marathons, triathlon does not have official course certification for records, we use world best, course best, race best, swim/bike/run course best, etc.”.

The same holds true for Ironman 70.3 races and non-branded half-iron triathlons; no course certification, no “official” record.

According to recent reports, for what it’s worth, the Guinness World Records recognizes the “fastest time to complete an Ironman triathlon,” but not fastest iron-distance time (which we’ll explain in the next section). This may be more a function of marketing, as Ironman has established its own “partner” page on the Guinness Book of World Records website. Guinness does recognize some other triathlon records, including “fastest lumberjack triathlon,” which raises many other questions we’ll save for a different article.

Then there’s the branding gymnastics of Ironman™ versus an iron-distance race like Challenge Roth.

Sources indicate that you see, even though Challenge Roth is a 140.6-mile triathlon, it’s not an Ironman. Ironman is a distinct brand of 140.6-mile races, though many use the name to designate the distance (similar to how most Americans say “pass me a Kleenex” for tissue, or “I need a Band-Aid,” instead of requesting an adhesive bandage).

Recent findings suggest that and though Challenge Roth has been around for decades, the course and race have evolved. In 2010, the Challenge Roth run course was adjusted to be more spectator-friendly, and the bike course has been altered several times for safety, most recently in 2024. In 2026, Roth expanded the pro bike drafting zone from 12 to 20 meters, creating entirely different race dynamics altogether.

Ultimately, establishing a definitive “record” is difficult even for a single event, given how much can change from one year to the next. And though iron-distance “records” are often broken at Challenge Roth, they’re technically not the site of “the fastest iron-distance times in history.”.

In 2022, Kristian Blummenfelt and Kat Matthews covered the 140.6-mile distance in what would have been record-setting times of 6:44:25 and 7:31:54 – except that they did it in a unique setup involving pacers, drafting, and extra equipment as part of the Sub7/Sub8 Project. The event allowed for advanced technological and athletic optimizations, featuring specialized gear like prototype bikes and pace teams on the swim and bike to provide slipstreams for Blummenfelt and Matthews to draft off of — all things you’d never be allowed to do in a legitimate race.

According to recent reports, this format drew considerable criticism and debate on social media, with the community questioning whether the Sub7/Sub8 times should be viewed as legitimate records. Many referenced Jan Frodeno’s 7:27:53 time for a similar iron-distance experiment known as Tri Battle Royle, which was held on a highly modified course featuring special ramps and a perfectly mapped swim line to remove tricky turns.

Because these events were so heavily optimized, no one regards these times as actual world records — just like the much-hyped 2017 Breaking2 Nike marketing event for the marathon record. Instead, they’re chalked up to fascinating experiments for fans to geek out over. (And for that, we’re thankful.).

So now that we’ve determined there is no official world record for Ironman, iron-distance triathlon, or otherwise, we can establish there are fastest-known times, with all the caveats above.

#115014. 13 Black Women Share How They Found the Strength to Survive—and Thrive—With Breast Cancer

📅 18 Oct 2021 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4448 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

13 Black Women Share How They Found the Strength to Survive—and Thrive—With Breast Cancer

📅 18 Oct 2021 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story.
  • It has been revealed that but here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight.
  • Industry observers note that the stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story. Black women are diagnosed with breast cancer at a younger median age (60, compared with 62 for white women) and are 38% more likely to die from the disease. They have the lowest survival rate for every known stage of breast cancer. And about one in five Black women with breast cancer are diagnosed with hard-to-treat triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), more than any other racial or ethnic group.

It has been revealed that but here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight. Black women have always been more than a data point, and perhaps nowhere is that truer than in the way they face, survive, and remake their lives after a breast cancer diagnosis.

Industry observers note that the stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic. They are individuals with careers, children, humor, faith, rage, and joy whose experiences with breast cancer changed them in ways both devastating and profound. In finding their own paths through treatment and beyond, they’ve built something the data can’t quantify: community, purpose, and a hard-won blueprint for survival they’re passing on to every woman who comes after them.

Sources indicate that monique Bass, 53, had always been proactive about her health. A single mother of twin sons and grandmother of four, she started getting annual mammograms at 40. But it was a self-exam at 47 while lying in bed one night that changed everything. She found a lump that didn’t feel right.

Sources indicate that what followed were three tissue biopsies of the lump over three years, each coming back benign. Doctors wanted to keep monitoring. Bass pushed back. The lump was growing, and she knew her body well enough to realize something was wrong. She insisted they remove the lump (a procedure called a lumpectomy) and test it. The diagnosis: stage 1 invasive ductal carcinoma that was aggressive enough to require immediate chemotherapy.

It has been revealed that bass got the call while sitting in a car wash. “I felt like I was in The Twilight Zone,” she notes. “Not in a million years did I think I would ever hear the words, ‘You have cancer.’” The timing made everything harder. It was 2020, the height of the pandemic, so she navigated much of her journey alone. Adding “another emotional layer,” she was also going through a divorce. Treatment included four rounds of doxorubicin, four rounds of paclitaxel, and 21 radiation treatments. Losing her hair hit the hardest. “But the silver lining is that it grew back even more beautifully after treatment,” Bass says.

It has been revealed that throughout it all her faith anchored her. “I’m not a deeply religious person, but I believe in God, and I knew he had me in the palm of his hand,” Bass states. On the other side of treatment, she founded What’s Behind the Bra?, a Newly introduced Jersey nonprofit that distributes comfort care packages to breast cancer patients year-round and hosts a weekly podcast of the same name every Sunday at 7:30 p.m. ET.

Sources indicate that jaqueline Beale, 64, comes from a family with a long history of cancer, including her mother, who had breast cancer. That’s why it wasn’t a huge surprise when, at 40, she found a lump during a breast self-exam. Even though a sonogram and mammogram came back clear, it was obvious that something wasn’t right, so Beale got a biopsy.

It has been revealed that when the radiologist called with her result—stage 1 breast cancer, which means the cancer hadn’t spread beyond where the abnormal cells had developed—she could hear a lot of noise in the background. He said, “I’m in New York trying to hail a cab, but you have breast cancer. You need to find a breast surgeon.” Despite the bluntness, Beale states she couldn’t help but find the humor in the situation, which is something she carried with her through treatment.

“I made sure that I surrounded myself with laughter and love,” she notes, “and I told my family that I knew they loved me, but I also needed a lot of laughter to get through it.”.

It has been revealed that she recalls one incident in an elevator after her sister had taken her to a chemo treatment. “I had been sick as a dog after, and a woman got in and asked if I was okay. My sister remarked, ‘Oh, she’s fine. She’s just got a little bit of cancer.’ The woman looked horrified, but I laughed. My family knew that their sense of humor is what I needed.”.

Sources indicate that annita White, 51, was five months late for her mammogram. As a single mother of two boys, a higher education administrator, and a first-year PhD student, she always had something more pressing. When she finally went, she expected the usual letter in the mail saying everything was fine. Instead, she got a call. There was a mass that hadn’t been there before.

In a recent development, by the time the biopsy came back, she already knew. A technician had commented on how hard the mass was, and White felt the diagnosis in her spirit before the words were ever spoken. The confirmation came the next day. “When I got the call, I fell to the floor and cried tears of desperation,” she says. “My first thought was, ‘Lord, I can’t do this.’”.

It has been revealed that what followed was hard in every way: chemotherapy, losing her breasts, losing her hair, which had always been full. “Being bald left me feeling vulnerable and insecure,” White claims. “Physically, losing my breasts and going through chemotherapy made me feel like my body was no longer my own.” Through it all the fear that drove her was running out of time—time to see her sons become men and to meet her grandchildren someday.

Industry observers note that her faith, which she’d been privately wrestling with for years, met her exactly where she was. She’d been asking God to truly show up in her life. “He did,” she states. “In the middle of one of the hardest seasons of my life, he carried me through.”.

Three years later White is cancer-free, her hair is back, and she recently finished her PhD. She now walks in her purpose as Dr. Nita, a member of the African American Breast Cancer Alliance survivor network, sharing her story and those of others facing the disease. “What once felt like the end became the beginning of something greater,” she says.

According to recent reports, marylande Regis, 38, had been in her new Georgia home for four months when everything changed. A registered nurse, realtor, wife, and mother of three, she had just stopped breastfeeding her nine-month-old when she found the lump. Her baby had never latched well on that side. When she messaged her provider, the on-call response was that it was probably a clogged milk duct and that she was too young to worry about it being something more serious. Regis didn’t accept that. She called back and left a message, insisting that something was wrong. “Another ob-gyn saw the message and encouraged me to make an office appointment immediately,” she indicates. Within two weeks she had a diagnosis: aggressive stage 2B, BRCA1-positive breast cancer. Within two more weeks what had been one tumor and one impacted lymph node had become three tumors and four impacted lymph nodes. Regis was 36.

“I was relieved that I advocated for myself,” she states. “I was proud that fear didn’t factor into my decision.”.

Sources indicate that what followed was relentless. Regis went through six months of chemotherapy, a bilateral mastectomy, six weeks of radiation, a total hysterectomy (to eliminate her body’s main source of estrogen), and breast reconstruction, all over a span of roughly 18 months. She lost friends to cancer along the way, as well as a cousin diagnosed around the same time. Her faith was, as Regis describes it, “shaken and stirred and flipped every way possible.” She wrote the key letters. She wrote her own obituary. She was practical about it. “I wanted to be positive, but I am also very realistic,” Regis says.

The hardest part wasn’t any single treatment—it was losing control. As her family’s go-to planner for everything from doctor’s appointments to vacations, she found it foreign to ask for help. But when she told her parents, her mother showed up and never left. “We joke, but my mom never went home,” Regis indicates. “This is her house now.” Her husband, Kory, came to every appointment and held steady even through both of them losing their jobs. “He deserves a trophy,” she says.

As the daughter of Haitian immigrants, raised to be everything her parents couldn’t be, Regis indicates the fight was never just medical. Today strength looks different than it did before cancer. It looks like making it to the bus stop with her son, who has autism. It looks like seeing her oldest finish nursing school and work toward becoming an ob-gyn. It looks like watching her youngest hit milestones like learning to talk. “I would have missed that if I didn’t fight,” she says. “The clouds are moving. The sun has decided to show itself. I can’t wait to soak it all in.”.

Illness had always been an afterthought for 75-year-old Judy Fambrough-Billingsley. Why would it cross her mind? She walked three miles every day, swam laps all summer, took Zumba classes, and played soccer for 30 years. Judy Fambrough-Billingsley had never smoked or drank, and she didn’t even need to take medication. Being healthy wasn’t something she worked at; it was just who she was. A naturalized American citizen born in Germany, she traveled back to her home country regularly to visit family. Her life was full and active.

Recent findings suggest that so when she felt a lump—and then another six months later—she ignored them. After all, she’d had a clean mammogram earlier that year. But when she noticed them growing and multiplying, she went back to her doctor. The results were not what she expected.

In a recent development, “I was shocked,” Fambrough-Billingsley says. She suddenly found herself navigating an entirely new set of experiences: prescription bottles, hospital procedures, lab processes—the whole medical system. “Being a part of a world where sickness exists had never been my world until now,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that what carried her through was far older than her diagnosis. She grew up during the Civil Rights Era, the daughter of a successful Black entrepreneur who built his business during tumultuous years in US history. Both her parents were lifetime members of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). She was president of the NAACP Youth Council and an active member of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Fambrough-Billingsley knows something about fighting for your life in systems that weren’t built for you.

“Growing up during the Civil Rights Era contributed to this era of fighting,” she says. “Never giving up.” That same spirit—the one her parents modeled, the one she fell into during her work as a community organizer and across decades of a life fully lived—is the one she’s bringing to this too. She may still be on her breast cancer journey, but this is not her first fight.

Taylor Johnson was nearly 30 when she found the lump on her left breast. A mom and content creator who loves trying fresh things and staying active, she went to her primary care doctor, who referred her for an ultrasound and a mammogram. Johnson was denied a mammogram—she was told she was too young. She pushed anyway, got a biopsy (in lieu of the mammogram), and days later, had a diagnosis: stage 2 triple-negative breast cancer.

According to recent reports, “My reaction was a very deep pause, trying to process what my doctor had told me,” Johnson says. “It then hit me, and all I could do was cry.”.

She’s in the middle of her treatment strategy, which includes six months of chemotherapy, followed by surgery and three weeks of radiation. After finishing chemo Johnson felt confident that would be the hardest part of her journey, both physically and emotionally. But her own health wasn’t her only concern: She knew her five-year-old was watching her every move, and she wanted to stay stable for her daughter. “I was so used to always being the strong one,” Johnson claims. “This definitely tested that.” She held it together not because it came easily, but because she understood what her daughter was absorbing.

She is grateful for the community that rallied around her while she waited. Weekly prayer calls, rotating visits from family and friends, and a medical team at Mayo Clinic in Arizona that went above and beyond carried her through.

Though Johnson hasn’t finished treatment yet, completing chemo clarified something for her. “It has reassured me how strong I truly am,” she claims. Strength, she’s learned, isn’t just physical. The emotional and mental muscle it takes to keep going counts just as much.

Sources indicate that jessica Ncube, 41, built her life around caring for others. A licensed clinical social worker, the co-owner of a mental health practice, and a mom, she was always in motion. Her life revolved around showing up for others and helping them navigate their hardest moments. “Looking back I do not know that I was always receiving,” she claims.

According to recent reports, her diagnosis came quietly. A routine mammogram caught it; nothing in her body had felt amiss. That silence, Ncube indicates, is exactly why early detection matters. When she got the news she went into survival mode. “You hear the words, but it takes time for them to land,” she says.

Ncube’s journey started with a lumpectomy. When her margins came back unclear, meaning the pathologist could not determine whether all the cancerous cells were removed, she made the decision to move forward with a double mastectomy with reconstructive surgery. “Losing a part of your body, even when it is lifesaving, is still a loss,” she claims. “The hardest part was learning how to sit in both gratitude and grief at the same time.”.

As someone professionally wired to be strong for others, letting that tendency go was its own kind of work. “Strength became less about holding everything in and more about being honest about what I needed,” Ncube notes. Her faith grounded her, and her community revealed up, but she also had to unlearn something deeply familiar. “As a Black woman there is a resilience that is almost ingrained in us,” she says. “I had to learn how to balance that resilience with softness.”.

Recent findings suggest that after completing treatment Ncube has become more present and deliberate. Her definition of strength has changed entirely. “Strength today is softness. It is honesty. It is allowing myself to receive, to rest, and to not have all the answers,” she claims.

Ameiko Newman, 40, didn’t learn of her diagnosis through a routine screening. She was rushed to the hospital for abdominal pain, and that’s when she learned she had breast cancer. Life before her diagnosis had been stressful, uncertain, a season of not quite knowing where she was headed. In a strange way, cancer gave her direction.

“For me, cancer saved me,” she says. “It made me a better person. It made me fight harder, push through the hard times and know what I want in life.”.

Newman is still in treatment, receiving chemotherapy and immunotherapy every week, and she is honest about what that looks like: There are good days and bad days. She goes to church faithfully, prays every day, and tries to stay positive through it all.

In a recent development, what has surprised her most is that in the middle of fighting for her own life, she found her purpose: helping others fight for theirs. Newman rebranded her business entirely around that mission and started designing scarves with chemo patients in mind. “I started making them mainly for my Black women because you know we love having style,” she claims. But a wide variety of women from all over have since bought them.

She wakes up every day, gets her kids ready, works out, and moves through life. Faith, she notes, is what makes that possible. Her message to any Black woman who’s just gotten diagnosed is both simple and hard-won: “Cancer doesn’t define you. You define you. Even though you’re fighting for your life, help someone else fight for theirs.”.

Industry observers note that charlotte Connor, 38, had just undergone a breast augmentation when she felt a lump in her breast. “When I saw my doctor, they weren’t concerned, in part because of my young age,” says Connor, who was 30 years old at the time. She had a mammogram and ultrasound to check for signs of cancer, but no MRI. “Looking back now I wish I would have asked for that MRI,” she says.

At the first checkup six months later, they told her she was fine. At the second—one year after the original lump was found—the lump had tripled in size. Her doctor ordered a biopsy, and her diagnosis was confirmed: stage 2A ductal carcinoma, which means the cancer was growing but contained to the breast and surrounding lymph nodes.

In a recent development, “When they told me I had cancer, I was calm,” she says. Her mindset immediately shifted from a sinking feeling to being optimistic about the future. “I focused on getting healthy again,” says Connor, who started fantasizing about what she would do after treatment.

In a recent development, she remembers thinking, I may be feeling sick and throwing up from chemotherapy, but what restaurants am I going to go to after all this is over? It’s an outlook that didn’t necessarily come naturally to her, either. “I’m not even overly optimistic in life—I think I’m a realist—but in this situation, I shifted to being overly optimistic.”.

Recent findings suggest that part of that mindset shift was for her young daughter. “I couldn’t be pessimistic; I had to be strong for her,” she indicates. “And I knew that how I acted in this situation was how she was going to mirror things and react to stressful situations when she got older.”.

Connor’s other pillar of support came from a tight-knit circle of friends and family, who threw her a head-shaving party before she lost her hair due to chemo. “Making things fun and lighthearted like that got me through my darkest, saddest moments,” she claims.

According to recent reports, it was 1999, and Donna Culmer had just received a clean mammogram. A few months later she felt a stone-size bump on her right side, so she went back to her ob-gyn to get it checked out. They redid the mammogram on both breasts, and while what she’d felt was actually a fibrocystic lump, the imaging found a small, not palpable spot on her left side that turned out to be a stage 1 cancer. “I was stunned,” Culmer says. “I didn’t even know what questions to ask.” She drove back to work in a daze and told her boss what had happened.

Sources indicate that at 46 she was serving in the Navy as an instructor and trainer to personnel who were working alongside the Marines. She was married to a Marine and raising three children. There was no good moment for this. There never is.

Recent findings suggest that four months of chemotherapy followed, with nausea and exhaustion that never quite let up. Her doctors were concerned that the chemo might not work, so she had a mastectomy. Through it all her community refused to let her go through it alone. Her father drove her to every session and sat with her. Her church came to her, literally; services were held at her house.

Recent findings suggest that twenty-seven years later, Culmer, now 73, has had time to reflect. “As Black women, we have been through challenges our whole lives,” she claims. “This is just one more.” Her advice is practical and clear. “Don’t panic and ask questions, even if you have to write them down,” Culmer says. “The treatments available now are so much better than what I had.”.

Industry observers note that one morning, Patricia Fox, 38, woke up with a lump in her right breast that wasn’t there the night before—she was just 26 years old at the time. Fox scheduled an appointment with her ob-gyn that day. “They told me that I was a young Black woman and had dense breasts, and it was likely a cyst,” she says. “They were ready to turn me away.”.

Sources indicate that the lump, which was a little smaller than a golf ball, seemed strange to Fox. Thankfully, she listened to her intuition. “There was something telling me to get it checked out,” she indicates, so her doctor did a biopsy just to be sure.

Recent findings suggest that her results came back as estrogen receptor-positive stage 2A breast cancer, meaning her cancer had estrogen receptors that would respond to hormone therapy drugs. Fox claims she’ll never forget her doctor’s words: “Patricia, you’ll be a breast cancer survivor.” That sentiment set the tone for her mindset as a fighter. “It made me think that I could face this and survive this,” she says.

Still, cancer treatments quickly overwhelmed Fox, and soon she faced her lowest point: crying on the floor for hours, feeling like having cancer at such a young age was a punishment for being a “bad person.” But she pulled herself out of it with hard work in therapy.

Sources indicate that “I found that talking to a therapist helped me process my diagnosis and examine the areas of my life—certain people and my own behavior patterns—that were cancerous for me that I needed to do something about,” she notes. “While therapy didn’t make the pain go away, it did make how I coped with it much better.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the Black community, therapy is often taboo, says Fox, but it’s become her mission to dispel that belief. “Therapy fortified me to get through cancer,” she says, “and I tell everyone that they don’t have to suffer in silence.”.

Annette Colden, 63, was sitting at her sister’s bedside during the last days of her final battle with breast cancer when the conversation turned to screenings. Her sister had been through cervical cancer and two bouts of breast cancer before passing away from the disease. “She made me promise I’d get my mammograms,” Colden claims.

According to recent reports, colden’s first two yearly mammograms were clear. On the third there was a spot, but she was told by her doctor that things looked okay and it wasn’t cancer—she just had lumpy breasts.

“There’s this inner feeling you have,” she says. “Something was inside me saying, That’s not right.” Her sister’s doctor had told her the exact same thing, but Colden was so happy to hear she didn’t have cancer that she didn’t follow up.

A year later she went back for a mammogram, and that’s when her doctors found it: stage 0 breast cancer, meaning only abnormal cells had been found. She was 42. “Now, looking back, I always tell women that if something doesn’t feel right, get a second opinion.”.

According to recent reports, despite the diagnosis Colden remained calm. “I’m a religious person,” she indicates. “In my prayer I remarked, ‘Lord, if you will be my pilot on this journey, I’ll be your copilot.’” She immediately felt a sense of peace.

Sources indicate that after her recovery she decided to share that calming presence with other women going through breast cancer at a support group through Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, where she had treatment. “I say, ‘It’s going to be a long road. If you don’t want to travel it alone, I’m right there with you.’”.

And she means it. Sometimes that involves talking with someone at 3 a.m. when the pain from chemotherapy hits. Other times it means sending food delivery boxes to the homes of people with breast cancer who can’t muster the strength to leave. “My sister did a lot of support work before she got really sick,” she notes. “This is her vision.”.

Industry observers note that ricki Fairley, 69, was in the security line at the airport for a work trip when she got a call from her doctor. They’d found a peanut-like lump under her nipple that turned out to be cancer.

It has been revealed that fairley, who was 55 at the time, mentioned, “I don’t have time for this right now. I’ll call you when I get to my destination.” A couple days later she found out she had stage 3A TNBC, and it was really aggressive. Compared with other breast cancers, TNBC has fewer targeted-therapy treatment options, often spreads beyond the breasts, and is more likely to recur. Black women have nearly three times the risk of developing triple-negative breast cancer.

According to recent reports, her diagnosis woke her up. “It made me realize that I needed to get all of the ‘cancers’ out of my life,” Fairley says. During treatment that first year which involved a double mastectomy, aggressive chemotherapy, and radiation, she quit her job and started her own manufacturer. Then she filed for divorce and later sold her house. “I quit my life and started a new one, and changed everything,” she says. “I had to learn that my peace is nonnegotiable. I really think that stress caused my breast cancer.”.

Industry observers note that A year later her life changed again. Fairley was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer and told she had two years to live. After finding out her current doctor had only treated two previous cases of TNBC and both women had died in eight months, she found a newly introduced doctor, who was well-versed in current research and treatments for the disease. She beat cancer a second time. “I remember sitting at my daughter’s graduation thinking, Okay, I made it. What’s next for me?” Fairley notes. The answer: helping others. In the years that followed, Fairley cofounded The Black Breast Cancer Alliance, which works to reduce the mortality rate for Black women.

Tech Report: What Is a Timeshare? Why Financial Experts Say Avoid Them

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • According to recent reports, A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property.
  • The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

According to recent reports, A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that at the moment average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

According to recent reports, right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Industry observers note that ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

Side hustlers! With the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card you can earn free travel from your business expenses.

Industry observers note that chooseFI has partnered with CardRatings for our coverage of credit card products. ChooseFI and CardRatings may receive a commission from card issuers.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:.

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most vital financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Consumers Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:.

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare People Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

According to recent reports, timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:.

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

It has been revealed that choose a card that matches your spending patterns and offers flexible points or transferable miles. Sign-up bonuses alone often cover 1-2 free flights or hotel stays in the first year.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Pay the balance in full every month. Travel rewards only work financially if you never carry a balance and pay interest.

According to recent reports, instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

Research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

According to recent reports, if you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

No. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

Recent findings suggest that the average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Sources indicate that technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

It has been revealed that the resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

Industry observers note that in very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

A timeshare is a prepaid vacation proposal with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.
