Skratch Labs Unsweetened Hydration Sport Drink Mix.

Raw Nutrition Bum Hydration Fruit Punch.

Thorne Daily Electrolytes Blood Orange.

Sources indicate that when it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid. But these drinks also contain a lot of sugar, and though that’s exactly what your body needs during a workout, that’s not the case for the hours of your day not occupied by swim-bike-run.

According to recent reports, but the effects of those workouts linger, especially during the summer months, during peak training periods, or even when we’re ill. The more we sweat, the more water and electrolytes we lose, and we can feel it in a lot of ways: brain fog, headache, muscle cramps, and fatigue.

Recent findings suggest that water, along with electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, is quite easy to replenish through whole-food sources, but to fill the gaps (or to rehydrate quickly), many endurance athletes also turn to sugar-free electrolyte drinks, which deliver all of the rehydration without the added sugar. These beverages provide a tasty alternative to drinking plain water all day, which may lead to increased consumption.

To be clear, sugar-free electrolyte drinks shouldn’t automatically be touted as a “healthier” option than traditional sports drinks. They often contain artificial sweeteners, which some studies suggest can negatively impact gut health and potentially lead to other health problems (for more on this, read sports dietitian Matthew Kadey’s deep dive on sugar-free formulations). Many also list “natural flavors” in their ingredient list, which could be just about anything: LMNT, an electrolyte drink that markets itself as having “no sugar” and “no dodgy ingredients,” has recently come under fire for hiding maltodextrin, a sugar with a high glycemic index, as a “natural flavor.”.

But sugar-free electrolytes aren’t going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, many popular sports drink manufacturers, including Gatorade, now offer low- and no-sugar versions of their flagship beverages to avoid penalties in countries with sugar taxes and to meet growing consumer demand for sugar-free options.

Whether you’re looking for an electrolyte complement to your high-carb fueling strategy on race day or a hydration boost at the office after a sweaty lunchtime run, sugar-free electrolyte drinks may have a place in your daily nutrition blueprint. Triathlete editors shook up eight no-sugar electrolyte blends in search of the best – here are their picks.

Industry observers note that you might pucker slightly while drinking this sugar-free electrolyte mix. With no sweeteners and real lemon and lime juice in the ingredients, it’s a delightfully tangy way to get in some electrolytes when you don’t need a hefty dose of carbs during or after exercise.

Sources indicate that the salted margarita flavor is certainly reminiscent of its namesake, so sip it on the patio as a little end-of-the-day treat to yourself in the summer, or heat up your water before adding it for a great way to warm up in the winter. While you can get these as individual serving packs for about $1 each, the resealable bag offers a slightly more eco-friendly option that saves you 10 cents per serving.

If you detest the taste of stevia but want a palatable everyday electrolyte that supports super light training or days off, Quince offers an affordable option at 67 cents per serving.

With no sweeteners, this mix mostly delivers a salty flavor with a little fruity flair. The citrus flavor is crisp while the watermelon gives off summer vibes, even if you’re using it to recover from a long day of skiing or ice skating with the fam in the winter. But the raspberry was our favorite as the most balanced flavor in the mix. The multi-pack is great if you proposal to drink it frequently and don’t want to get burnt out on any one flavor.

If you like lemon-lime Gatorade, you’ll love this formulation from LMNT. The flavor is oddly reminiscent of the neon-green drink served at the soccer games and track meets of your youth, but without the eyebrow-raising ingredients. (As mentioned above, however, LMNT is presently facing accusations of using maltodextrin as a “natural flavor,” which may negate the halo effect for some customers.).

With 1,000mg of sodium, this is a super-salty blend that takes some getting used to at first; we recommend diluting it in more water or trying only half a packet until your taste buds adjust. But after a long ride in the summer sun, the salt and citrus combo hit the spot much like a margarita at your favorite Mexican joint for post-ride burritos.

Instead of loading up on sodium, Just Ingredients follows a 3:1 ratio of potassium to sodium, along with multiple other electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, and chloride. All of this is derived from real-fruit sources: the first three ingredients listed on the package are guava, peach, and mango. This makes for a pleasant flavor, though the formulation is very clumpy, no matter what method is used to shake or stir the powder into water. Try blending into a smoothie for a cool, tropical treat instead.

Cure’s Hydrating Electrolyte Mixes follow the World Health Organization’s Oral Rehydration Solution formula recommendations for the ideal ratio of water, glucose, sodium and potassium to facilitate rapid rehydration.

It has been revealed that despite the presence of stevia and monk fruit as sweeteners, no chemical taste is present, and the watermelon flavor actually tastes like watermelon, not an artificial dupe of it. For best results, shake vigorously and serve ice-cold (paper umbrella optional).

Led by top triathlon coach Natasha Van Der Merwe, Raw Nutrition’s endurance line has gained a steady following with athletes looking for a comprehensive approach to nutrition and fueling. They’ll find it in this formulation, which contains not only the essential electrolytes but also vitamins C, B6, B12, and taurine.

The mix dissolves well and goes down smooth – best of all, the fruit punch flavor is reminiscent of Hawaiian Punch, making it a nostalgic delight to drink both in and out of workouts.

Sources indicate that made with five real fruits (raspberry, coconut, lemon, lime, banana), a sprinkling of beet powder for nitrates, and a blend of unique ingredients not typically seen in electrolyte powders (bamboo silica, anyone?), DryWater claims to give athletes “complete cellular hydration.” Indeed, many of the ingredients are backed by scientific research. However, some feel a bit of a stretch – the sweetener derived from katamfe fruit extract, for example, provides natural sweetness without spiking blood sugar. However, there is limited evidence of DryWater’s claims that the ingredient “supports balanced energy levels [and] promotes better digestion.”.

According to recent reports, the flavor is strong and lingers, leaving a film on the tongue and inside the mouth. To avoid this effect, consider using only half a packet or diluting the mix with more water.

In a recent development, as a trusted supplement manufacturer, Thorne is a go-to for many athletes looking for tested and certified products by NSF, or the National Sanitation Foundation, which conducts independent testing to ensure ingredient lists are accurate and free of ingredients banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. That peace of mind pairs well with Thorne’s blood orange flavor – the mix hits the salty-sweet balance perfectly, with a flavor profile that never gets old. Add to your water bottle at work or while running errands to top off electrolytes throughout the day.

#114984. Trek’s New Domane Trades IsoSpeed for Wider Tires. I Think It Works

Trek’s New Domane Trades IsoSpeed for Wider Tires. I Think It Works

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • This Review Continues for MembersMy full test and verdict are here.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you want a comfortable, relatively upright road bike for rough pavement, long rides, and some light gravel, the upcoming Domane belongs on your list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

This Review Continues for MembersMy full test and verdict are here. Next, I want to hear what you think. Bicycling members can continue the discussion with me on Discord, where I’ll answer questions and hear how the Domane works for riders beyond my test. The invitation appears after the review.

Recent findings suggest that if you want a comfortable, relatively upright road bike for rough pavement, long rides, and some light gravel, the upcoming Domane belongs on your list. It feels more eager under power than previous versions, while keeping the stability and confidence that have always made the bike good at everyday riding.

The version I’d point most people toward is the $4,200 SL 6 AXS. It gets the same geometry, tire clearance, and basic frame features as the expensive SLR models, along with electronic shifting and carbon wheels. The SLR saves weight and opens the door to Trek’s Project One customization. Those are real advantages, but they don’t make it a fundamentally different bike.

I tested the $11,499 SLR 9 AXS 2x. It weighed 16.3 pounds in size M. The bike I’d recommend first costs less than half as much.

BIKE TESTED: Trek Gen. 5 Domane SLR 9 AXS 2xACTUAL WEIGHT 16.3 pounds (Size M, as tested) USE Road, light gravel PRICE AS TESTED $11,499 MODEL PRICE RANGE $2,400 to $11,499; $14,999 limited edition ICON No. 76FRAME ONLY OPTION: Yes. $3,700 (SLR) $2,000 (SL)CUSTOMIZABLE BUILDS Yes, SLR models through Project One SIZES OFFERED XS, S, M, ML, L, XL WEIGHT LIMIT 125 kg/275 lb (bicycle, rider, and cargo) TIRE CLEARANCE 40mm BB STANDARD T47 threaded BRAKE HOSE ROUTING Internal, RCS headset; under bar/stem on most buildsDRIVETRAIN COMPATIBILITY 1x and 2x, electronic shifting only DERAILLEUR HANGER UDH WARRANTY Lifetime, frame and rigid fork, original owner CRASH REPLACEMENT Yes, Trek Carbon Care discounted replacement.

It has been revealed that I’ve ridden every generation of the Domane, including several of the more aggressive RSL versions. Over the years, Trek added adjustable IsoSpeed, front IsoSpeed, internal storage, aero shaping, and hidden cables. The fifth-generation bike pulls back on much of that.

In a recent development, the Gen 5 feels more solid and reactive underfoot than its predecessors. It’s stiffer when I get on the pedals, accelerates with more snap, and climbs with a crispness that used to elude the Domane. In that way, it feels more like a Madone than any previous version.

Sources indicate that it hasn’t lost the stability and confidence that make the Domane a good everyday road bike. I can push it hard down a descent without feeling like I’m taking a test of nerves. The fit is excellent, too. The taller front end should help more riders find a position that’s comfortable and aerodynamic.

Industry observers note that and no, it doesn’t feel slow on 35mm tires. The bike feels quick and responsive. The wider tires are part of what makes it work, not an anchor holding it back.

According to recent reports, the original Domane’s signature feature was IsoSpeed, a mechanism that let the seat tube flex to add comfort. Trek developed it over several generations, then removed it from the bike that introduced it.

It has been revealed that the new Domane gets much of its comfort from wider tires at lower pressures, along with frame and seatpost tuning. Most models come with 35mm tires, and the frame clears up to 40mm. Trek notes that combination provides enough comfort that IsoSpeed’s remaining benefit isn’t worth its weight and complexity.

Industry observers note that isoSpeed still works. Trek told me that with the same 35mm tires, the Gen 4 transmits slightly less vibrational energy than the Gen 5. Trek also indicates the Gen 5 on 35mm tires comes within 5 percent of the Gen 4 on its stock 32mm tires at the rear. At the front, Trek says the two generations perform similarly.

Those are Trek’s test results, not measurements I made. But the decision makes sense to me. Wider tires add traction and capability that IsoSpeed couldn’t provide. Trek decided the system’s remaining comfort advantage wasn’t enough to justify keeping it.

If you own an older Domane, what did IsoSpeed do for you? Did you notice a difference when you moved to wider tires, or do you miss the old system? I’d like to hear what you’ve felt on real roads.

Industry observers note that according to Trek’s white paper, the Gen 5 frame is about 292 grams lighter than Gen 4. It also eliminates IsoSpeed and its associated maintenance.

According to recent reports, the frame uses a threaded T47 bottom bracket, a round fork steerer, a Universal Derailleur Hanger, and a standard 27.2mm seatpost. For a modern performance bike, there’s not much proprietary weirdness here. That’s a feature.

Recent findings suggest that the internal storage compartment is gone, too. I’ll miss it. It was useful. Trek says its research indicated that many Domane owners weren’t using it. The new frame retains fender mounts, top-tube mounts, and frame-bag mounts. I like the trade: less hardware and complexity, with straightforward ways to carry gear when you need to.

Recent findings suggest that the cable routing is another smart compromise. On most models, brake hoses run beneath the two-piece bar and stem before entering the frame at the headset. It looks clean, but changing a bar or stem doesn’t become a major repair job. Fit changes and service matter more to me than hiding every cable at any cost.

Sources indicate that the SL and SLR share the same geometry, tire clearance, seatpost size, bottom bracket, UDH, and general feature set. The SL uses Trek’s 500 Series carbon; the SLR uses lighter 900 Series carbon. Trek claims both frames are designed to the same stiffness requirements. The SL supports mechanical drivetrains; the SLR is electronic-shifting only.

The SLR primarily buys lower weight, access to Trek’s highest-end builds, and the ability to customize components through Project One. Buyers can specify details such as crank length, handlebar width, and stem length. If you’re spending this much on a bike, getting those dimensions right from the factory is a meaningful advantage.

According to recent reports, but the SLR doesn’t change the core experience enough to be the obvious choice for most riders. I’d look closely at the $4,200 SL 6 AXS first. It has a carbon frame, electronic shifting, carbon wheels, 40mm tire clearance, and the same accessible fit. The carbon range starts at $2,400 with the Tiagra SL 4. The SLR 9 AXS 2x I tested costs $11,499.

Trek also offers an ultralight SLR 9 AXS 1x with 28mm tires. Trek describes it as the racier interpretation of the Domane, but it did not vibration-test that configuration. If comfort is a big reason you’re considering the bike, pay attention to the tire setup, not just the frame name.

If you’re shopping for a Domane, which versions are you weighing? Would you spend more for the SLR’s lower weight and Project One options, or put that money toward another bike or gear?

Sources indicate that trek indicates it applied aero lessons from the Gen 8 Madone, but aerodynamics weren’t a major priority. In a pedaling-mannequin test, Trek claims the Gen 5 improved by 0.6 watts over Gen 4.

In other words, essentially the same.

It has been revealed that that seems appropriate. Trek prioritized weight, simplicity, and ride quality instead of chasing another aero headline.

Recent findings suggest that the fifth-generation Domane is an excellent road bike. It’s light, comfortable, stable, and lively. It’s easier to adjust and service than many integrated performance bikes, retains useful mounts, and drops features that added weight and complexity without improving the bike enough to justify them.

Sources indicate that the old Domanes were more technically adventurous. I miss that part of the story more than I miss riding them.

For most riders, I think Gen 5 is the right Trek road bike. The SL 6 AXS is the model I’d point people toward first. The SLR makes sense if you want the lighter frame and factory customization, but the expensive build doesn’t change the core experience. Taken as a whole, the upcoming Domane is my favorite drop-bar bike Trek makes.

Sources indicate that that’s my take after riding the bike. Now I want to hear from people who own a Domane, have ridden an earlier version, or are considering the Gen 5. What questions do you still have? What would you like me to investigate or compare? I’ll continue the conversation on Discord and bring the most useful questions and experiences back here.

Industry observers note that what do you think of the newly introduced Trek Domane? What questions do you still have? What did I screw up? If you own or have ridden the Gen 5 Domane, share your impressions.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Can’t get back into working out? It’s not a motivation problem.

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdfitness

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?
  • Industry observers note that hundreds of you wrote back.
  • One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, remarked it this way:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

Industry observers note that hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

I’m working my way through all of them.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, remarked it this way:.

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

Industry observers note that I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

You were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Of course that’s going to feel rough!

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:.

Sources indicate that that’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

After multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

And it’s vital to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

Recent findings suggest that you know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

Maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

Try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌.

And if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

It has been revealed that if you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

Your on-ramp doesn’t have to be forever.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.

#114980. Clipless Pedals Can Feel Intimidating—Here Are Some Tips to Make Those First Clipless Rides Feel Smoother

Clipless Pedals Can Feel Intimidating—Here Are Some Tips to Make Those First Clipless Rides Feel Smoother

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when a rider switches from flat pedals to clipless pedals, they typically aren’t thinking about the differences of pedals like Shimano SPD or SPD-SL, Wahoo Speedplays, or egg-beater pedals.
  • Industry observers note that not all people considering the switch realize this—as contradictory as it sounds, clipless pedals refer to a pedal system where you are clipped into the pedal.
  • Here we’ll dig into what clipless pedals are, how they can benefit you on your ride, tips for setting up your pedals and cleats, and tips for those daunting first few rides with your newly introduced pedals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when a rider switches from flat pedals to clipless pedals, they typically aren’t thinking about the differences of pedals like Shimano SPD or SPD-SL, Wahoo Speedplays, or egg-beater pedals. Many times, they haven’t heard of Time pedals or the different Assioma or Garmin models. The first thought many have is, “How do I get out of the pedal once I’m clipped in?”.

Industry observers note that not all people considering the switch realize this—as contradictory as it sounds, clipless pedals refer to a pedal system where you are clipped into the pedal. If you aren’t familiar with the system, think about being clipped into a ski binding. Some pedal options offer different release settings—similar to how a DIN setting on a ski binding can be adjusted to offer different levels of force needed to release the ski boot from the binding.

Here we’ll dig into what clipless pedals are, how they can benefit you on your ride, tips for setting up your pedals and cleats, and tips for those daunting first few rides with your newly introduced pedals.

Industry observers note that I have plenty of friends who swear by the saying, “flat pedals win medals.” However, there is a reason you’ll only see clipless pedals at world tour road races or on the majority of gravel bikes at your local gravel grinder. When you ride clipped in you end up using more of your leg musculature during each revolution of your pedal stroke.

In short, this means you’re typically more efficient when using clipless pedals compared to flat pedals. For clarity, you don’t need to ride clipless pedals to be a cyclist. But for those riders looking to take their riding to the next level, it’s worth giving them a try.

According to recent reports, because you’re literally attached to the pedal, you use not only your quads in the downstroke part of the revolution, but you also work your hamstrings, hip flexors, and glutes as you pull up. All of those muscles at work translate to more power while you’re riding, especially as you refine your pedaling technique. To get started, here’s your expert-backed guide to pedaling with clipless pedals—without falling over.

“Cleat placement is paramount,” states Issac Denham, owner of bike fitting studio Befitting Bicycles in Wayne, Pennsylvania. “Since incorrect cleat placement can lead to injuries, we suggest booking time with a bike fitter to place your cleats. Having a professional install your cleats also ensures that they won’t be installed improperly or even upside down.”.

Industry observers note that for those riders that want to try clipless pedals, but don’t want to jump into a precision fit, start with cleats in a neutral position. This means setting the cleats up in the middle of the slots in the shoe with the cleats relatively straight. Just make sure the left and right cleats are in roughly the same position—this will give you a good baseline moving forward.

It will take time doing the guess and check method for cleat placement, but this method gives you the chance to play around going clipless before you invest hundreds into a bike fit. If you start to develop pain after using clipless pedals, stop pedaling. This is likely due to cleat position and that is when it is time to see a local trusted shop for direction.

“Many clipless pedals have adjustable pedal tension. This is basically how hard the built-in spring holds the cleat in the pedal,” claims Dan Chabonov, Bicycling test editor. “Setting this tension as low as possible means you need less force to clip in and out of the pedals and can make the learning process a little easier.”.

While most clipless pedals already come set at the lowest tension setting from the manufacturer, you can also easily make the adjustment.

According to recent reports, “Typically out of the box, pedals are set up with the least amount of release tension,” claims Becky Quinn, former pro and bike fitter. “The pedal tensioner is on the rear of the pedal. There is a small 3mm bolt that requires a 3mm Allen wrench to adjust the tension. It can be turned counterclockwise to loosen the tension or clockwise to tighten it. There is a small window on the back of the pedal that has a small horizontal pin that moves up or down depending on which way you turn the tensioner.”.

If you adjust the tension on your pedals, make sure you confirm that the pins are in the same place on both the left and right pedal, so the release tension is the same on both sides.

Practice does indeed make perfect when it comes to learning how to pedal with clipless pedals. The goal is to become so comfortable with the movements that they become part of your muscle memory, so you don’t have to look down at your foot or pedal for longer than a quick glance.

It has been revealed that when you’re just starting out pedaling with clipless pedals, do it inside first. “Practicing indoors either on a trainer, or even leaned up against a wall, can be a great place to start where you don’t have to worry about falling down or looking silly,” says Denham.

In a recent development, when I ran a shop and was getting people set up on clipless pedals, I would suggest they get on the bike inside, ideally on a trainer or next to a wall to stabilize themselves, then put on a show or a movie. It sounds monotonous (and the people you live with might give you an odd look or two), but simply clip in, clip out, clip in, clip out, over and over. Do it looking down at your shoe, then when that’s comfortable practice doing it without looking down. Feel it out inside and you’ll be much better off when you head out the door.

To clip into your pedal, start with the pedal positioned at the bottom of the pedal stroke.

Recent findings suggest that “Softly lift the front of the pedal with your toe to flip it over so that you can engage. Your toe will be slightly pointed downward. Slide your foot forward until the tongue of the cleat stops on the lip of the pedal,” Quinn explains. “Once you can’t slide your foot any further forward, continue to pedal forward and add pressure to the pedal. It will click in. Sometimes you will need to rotate your heel inward or outward at the 6 o’clock position to engage securely.”.

Then it’s time to clip out: “In order to practice clipping out of your pedals, place one leg all the way down to the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock). Then, firmly rotate your heel outward. Be sure to not roll your ankle,” Quinn advises. “The motion should be similar to that of smashing a bug under the ball of your foot.”.

If there is a single gem of advice we would love to pass on to every cyclist who has ever learned how to ride with clipless pedals, this would be it: Unclip the foot you intend to put down when you come to a stop before you come to a stop. “This is the most vital piece of the puzzle,” claims Quinn.

Recent findings suggest that once you unclip, “here is the most critical piece: Keep the unclipped foot on the pedal but continue to pedal a half stroke,” Quinn adds. “Once the foot that is still clipped in gets to the 6 o’clock position, coast and stand up. Your butt needs to get off the saddle. Continue to apply your rear brakes until you are almost at a stop. When you are about to come to a complete stop, apply your front brake and step down with the unclipped foot.”.

Many cleat and pedal systems will follow a similar process with the general idea being: line up the cleat on the pedal and add downward force to clip in once the cleat is aligned.

Sources indicate that remember how we stated switching to clipless pedals is a cycling rite of passage of sorts? Well, so is falling over as you’re learning. Practicing while riding on grass can make the falls a little easier, and falling with the proper technique (yes, there’s a technique for falling, too!) will lower your chances of serious injury.

According to recent reports, “You will fall. We all have done it and it’s okay,” says Quinn. “Just remember that if you start to fall over, turn your buttocks so you land on it. It is the most padding we have on our bodies. Putting out an arm can break a wrist. You most likely will only get a bruise on your butt.”.

According to recent reports, the most key thing is not to get in your head, beat yourself up, or give up. Falling over at least a few times has happened to every single cyclist who rides with clipless pedals.

According to recent reports, I’ll never forget one of my first rides with clipless pedals. I rolled over to the group in the parking lot overly confident, forgot I had to unclip my foot from the pedal, and slowly tipped over—still attached to the bike. It happens to everyone when you’re first making the switch, but some practice at home can make the transition a little less painful.

In a recent development, natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman).

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

Thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a newly introduced fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my big shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

According to recent reports, after finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

It has been revealed that “I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev remarked, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”.

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

“Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he said. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”.

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

Sources indicate that “There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the plans because of those doubts.”.

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

Industry observers note that “That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that plan. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”.

Sticking to the plan slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

In a recent development, “It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”.

It has been revealed that and for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

Physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

Industry observers note that “To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

“It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’.

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

“You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”.

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

It worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

According to recent reports, “I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before massive races.”.

The day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

Sources indicate that “When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”.

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

“I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”.

Sources indicate that that feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

“It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”.

In a recent development, thankfully for him, time went by swiftly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

After that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”.

It has been revealed that recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”.

In a recent development, starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a latest world’s best time, the specter of the Massive Island tempered his elation.

“It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his new, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev rapidly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a big difference in how hot I feel.”.

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of latest cooling strategy.

“It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”.

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

“So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”.

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”.

In a recent development, when you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

“We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”.

Recent findings suggest that A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

Sources indicate that “Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he mentioned, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”.

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev rapidly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

“I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”.

The bike offered another potential saving.

Industry observers note that “My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”.

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”.

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”.

In a recent development, for now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev says he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

“Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”.

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

In a recent development, “He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”.

The Benefits of Biking for Seniors, Including the Mental and Physical Payoffs

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, we know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what?
  • In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

In a recent development, we know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what? According to a 2023 scoping review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, studies show that when older adults cycle regularly, their happiness improves and they are better able to maintain their quality of life.

In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.

Read More of Ride Strong at 50+.

In a recent development, “Regular physical activity helps seniors maintain good health, improve their quality of life, and increase their overall well-being,” Mary Sabat, MS, RDN, a personal trainer and dietitian in Georgia tells Bicycling. “It can enhance physical strength, flexibility, and endurance, making it easier to perform daily activities and maintain independence.”.

Those are just few reasons why biking for seniors is so great—but here are all the advantages you gain when you start pedaling regularly.

It has been revealed that while almost forms of physical activity improve physical and mental health, cycling is particularly well-suited for those in their golden years due to its accessibility. After all, cycling is easy on the joints, even for those with joint pain or injuries. “It can be tailored to individual fitness levels and adjusted to accommodate different abilities and physical limitations, too,” says Sabat. “Recumbent bikes, trikes, or electric-assist bicycles can be used to make cycling more accessible for those with mobility challenges or balance complications.”.

Robert Patterson, a cyclist and lawyer, has been cycling for more than 40 years. He points out all the obvious aerobic and strength-building gains he’s enjoyed over the years, but also the psychological benefits. “Cycling also benefits my mental health. My attitude and overall focus are always improved by being on the bike,” he claims.

Here are nine reasons, according to the experts, for you to saddle up and hit the road (or the gym) for a ride.

Sources indicate that aerobic exercise is the key to managing heart health. Because the heart is a muscle, it needs to be exercised on a regular basis to maintain its strength and optimal function. And because the heart and lungs work together with the venous system to deliver oxygenated blood to your muscles, any exercise that increases your heart rate and breath rate for an extended period of time will help improve your heart health and overall cardiovascular function.

Recent findings suggest that plus, as anyone who has ever pushed the pedals and pumped through a 20- or 30-minute bike ride knows, cycling will definitely get your heart rate up. The repetitive cycling motion qualifies as a moderate to intense form of aerobic exercise that you can easily adapt to your personal fitness level. This means that even if you haven’t exercised in years, by starting at a lower intensity and making adjustments to your workouts based on your heart rate, you can safely and effectively add cycling to your weekly routine.

In a recent development, “As individuals age, the risk of heart disease increases,” claims Sabat. “Cycling is a low-impact aerobic exercise that helps improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthens the heart muscle, and enhances blood circulation. It can lower the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and high blood pressure, thereby promoting a healthy heart.”.

In fact, a series of two 2019 review studies (part 1 and part 2) published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that all forms of cycling reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and also reduced the risk factor profile for poor heart health—meaning that cyclists had better body composition stats, blood lipid profiles, cardiorespiratory fitness levels, and more time spent exercising. All of these together help mitigate the risk for developing heart disease.

According to recent reports, you can combat practically any chronic condition, including heart disease, along with type 2 diabetes, arthritis, and cancer with a regular ride. Exercise helps keep the blood flowing, systems moving, and cells turning over in a way that promotes overall health. For instance, high-intensity exercise (and high-intensity cycling, specifically) helps improve blood glucose response, according to research, which may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.

It has been revealed that even in the case of cancer, participating in a regular cycling routine has been shown to reduce the risk. For example, May 2020 study published in The Lancet found an association between participating in a daily bike commute and a 16 percent decrease in cancer mortality and an 11 percent decrease in cancer incidence.

In a recent development, “By incorporating a ride here and there into their routine, seniors can reduce the risk of chronic conditions. These conditions can be debilitating, but with regular exercise, seniors can take proactive steps toward prevention and management,” Josh Weight, a certified sports physiotherapist and the director of Gravity Physio in Australia tells Bicycling.

It has been revealed that it’s not unusual for seniors to experience regular joint pain associated with arthritis or previous injuries. In fact, according to the National Poll on Healthy Aging, about 70 percent of older adults report current joint pain. This can be exacerbated by extended periods spent sitting, or simply not moving around much, as sedentary behavior is directly associated with increased incidences of knee and other joint pain.

It has been revealed that while on the surface this may not seem like a big deal, it can lead to a cascading series of events where joint pain or arthritis contributes to a reduced range of motion. This reduced range of motion can influence balance, coordination, and even the ability to perform everyday tasks. These complications can also contribute to a reduced quality of life and even an increased risk of falls. As such, any activity that can be done without contributing to joint pain while protecting and strengthening the structures that help stabilize the joints (muscles, tendons, and ligaments) is an important undertaking for older adults’ overall health and well-being.

In a recent development, “Cycling is a low-impact activity that puts minimal stress on the joints, making it an excellent option for individuals with joint-related concerns. It provides a cardiovascular workout without placing excessive strain on the knees, hips, or ankles,” Sabat says.

According to recent reports, whether done on an indoor bike or a more traditional road or mountain bike, one thing’s for sure: Cycling works the legs. It takes muscular strength, power, and endurance to keep the pedals moving, especially when climbing a hill or ramping up the resistance. But it’s not just the legs and glutes that benefit—cycling can help build strength in the shoulders, upper back, and core, as well.

Of course, you may not be looking to build massive quads as one of your long-term fitness goals, but developing muscular strength isn’t just about looking strong—it’s about maintaining your quality of life.

Research estimates muscle mass begins to decline by 3 to 8 percent every decade following your 30th birthday, with those rates increasing further once you hit 60. This age-related muscular decline over time makes it more challenging to continue doing everyday activities like climbing stairs or carrying groceries. It’s important to participate in exercises, like cycling, that will help maintain or build muscle mass over time to safeguard your ability to perform these daily activities.

According to recent reports, in fact, according to a 2015 review study published in the European Review of Aging and Physical Activity, adults over 70 years of age experienced increased muscular strength and power when participating in a cycling exercise program at least three times a week for 12 to 16 weeks. This data flies in the face of anyone who believes they can’t develop muscle or strength as they age—it’s not only possible, it’s critical to overall health and functional ability.

In a recent development, one area in which cycling can be particularly beneficial is balance and coordination. This has ties to muscular strength, as strong, trained muscles tend to perform and react more promptly to stimuli than those that aren’t worked regularly. However, it also has to do with the unique requirements of cycling itself.

“Cycling requires balance and coordination to stay upright and navigate,” states Andrew White, a personal trainer and owner of Garage Gym Pro. “This can be especially beneficial for seniors as these abilities tend to decline with age, increasing the risk of falls and injuries.”.

It has been revealed that this isn’t just conjecture—a 2018 prospective study published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity found that older adults (between the ages of 65 and 85) who cycled daily had better balance, a faster pace while walking, and better self-reported lower-extremity function compared to those who didn’t bike regularly. Based on this study, it appears that cycling helps preserve balance and coordination which contributes to lower-body function that can help prevent falls.

Sources indicate that just as muscle mass tends to decline with age, an associated change in body composition takes place, which often leads to increased weight gain. And as weight creeps up, so do the risks for heart disease and chronic illness, particularly in populations considered obese.

According to recent reports, cycling and other forms of exercise can help keep weight and other disease risk factors in check. This is partly due to the muscle-protective benefits exercise offers, but also due to the increased calorie burn that occurs during moderate- to high-intensity exercise like cycling.

“Cycling can help seniors maintain a healthy body weight, reduce excess body fat, and prevent obesity-related health problems,” Sabat emphasizes.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience social isolation that can contribute to physical and mental health decline. Changes in health, mobility, or driving status can keep seniors alone at home. This is unfortunate because strong social connections are positively associated with longevity.

According to recent reports, cycling can provide seniors with an accessible way to get out and about, and to also engage with other people of all ages. “Cycling can be an enjoyable and social activity for seniors. Exploring outdoor trails, participating in group rides, or engaging in community cycling events can foster a sense of camaraderie and connection with others,” says Weight.

And for seniors who want to start cycling, but don’t know how, community cycling clubs offer a great way to learn and connect at the same time.

In addition to the benefits of social interaction, cycling can boost mental health in a number of ways, especially if you’re riding your bike outside. “Cycling outdoors provides an opportunity to connect with nature, which can be therapeutic and stress-relieving,” says White.

In a recent development, in fact, according to a 2022 study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, individuals who participated in outdoor cycling (or other outdoor activities like walking, jogging, or team sports), were less likely to experience depression than those who were inactive. Likewise, there’s evidence that even a single outdoor exercise session (like cycling) can impact mood, more than indoor exercise equivalents.

Even in the absence of an outdoor setting, physical activity as a whole is good for mental health. “Regular exercise releases endorphins which can elevate mood and reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression,” Sabat explains.

It has been revealed that one final benefit of cycling for seniors: It can support cognitive function. “Studies have shown that physical activity can have positive effects on cognition and may help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults. Exercise promotes better blood flow to the brain, stimulates the release of hormones that support brain health, and improves memory and attention,” Sabat shares.

In a recent development, laura Williams, M.S., ACSM EP-C holds a master's degree in exercise and sport science and is a certified exercise physiologist through the American College of Sports Medicine. She also holds sports nutritionist, youth fitness, sports conditioning, and behavioral change specialist certifications through the American Council on Exercise. She has been writing on health, fitness, and wellness for 12 years, with bylines appearing online and in print for Men's Health, Healthline, Verywell Fit, The Healthy, Giddy, Thrillist, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and Runner's World. After losing her first husband to cancer in 2018, she moved to Costa Rica to use surfing, beach running, and horseback riding as part of her healing process. There, she met her current husband, had her son, and now splits time between Texas and Costa Rica.

Your Weekly Horoscope, November 22-28, 2026: Letting Go of the Old

Think of it as a need for productivity that asks to be intentionally and consciously channeled into physical expression. The pairing of this planet and sign brings endurance to the way we move, create, build, and exist.

According to recent reports, this requires adaptation. Mars, and therefore we, are not just moving for the sake of movement. We are taking conscious, precise, efficient, and discerning actions guided by our most aligned desires.

On the same day Mars enters Virgo, the Sun in Sagittarius comes into direct opposition with Uranus retrograde in Gemini on November 25, 2026.

There is an expansive nature to these planetary bodies coming together. And it invites us to expand with it.

Sources indicate that the astrological alignments and transits in the days ahead speak to potential. Can your inner voice narrate your experience from a more expensive perspective of what is possible for you? You get to choose. Your weekly horoscope explains. Read for your rising sign.

This week asks you to see and think differently. To consider possibilities and desires from a new perspective. To bring intention to the way you move through your days, your routines, your habits, your self-talk, and your way of connecting with your body’s rhythm. Consider it the highest form of self-love.

Sources indicate that empowerment sings your name this week. As you encounter fears around safety, self-trust, and inner strength, approach them with self-compassion and confidence. There is more of you waiting to be met, more layers of your truth, parts of you hidden or shamed by outside minds. May you reclaim all of you.

Think of this week as a space to meet yourself as if anew. A space to observe the narratives and identities, the past that shapes and motivates you, and to bring them into non-critical questioning. Do these still fit? Do they still sing with truth? Who am I becoming? What is this asking of me?

What would a daily rhythm that serves you look like? One built on respect for your pace, awareness of your intuition, and true care for yourself. As you create space for this, what results is an unconscious clearing from your mind, your body, your emotions, and your patterned thinking. As a result, your intuition becomes heightened and your inner desires aligned with who you are.

According to recent reports, reclaim your creativity, vitality, and whatever brings you pleasure. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, as a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a newly introduced helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

When shopping for new road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Industry observers note that helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

Recent findings suggest that so, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? At the moment, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Sources indicate that virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

Industry observers note that “The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

Recent findings suggest that virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a upcoming helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

According to recent reports, editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

In a recent development, “Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

It has been revealed that all of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

In a recent development, the Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

For a newly introduced brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the company grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically major lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

In a recent development, the Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

Sources indicate that in our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina said it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

It has been revealed that P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on said it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

It has been revealed that ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Recent findings suggest that of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.
