#114946. Industry News: The 7 Best Garmin Watches for Cyclists: Editor-Tested Picks for Training, Recovery, and Everyday Wear

📅 25 Mar 2022 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2144 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The 7 Best Garmin Watches for Cyclists: Editor-Tested Picks for Training, Recovery, and Everyday Wear

📅 25 Mar 2022 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that cyclists, myself included, are often data driven.
  • Many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that cyclists, myself included, are often data driven. Even for cyclists that aren’t particularly motivated to optimize their performance there’s a belief that if a ride, run, hike, or any activity isn’t on Strava, it didn’t happen. Tracking your rides is easy to do with a head unit, but the tracking is limited to just the time spent on your bike.

Many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years. Smartwatches offer many of the same features that you find on bike computers, but smartwatches can also track sleep, heart rate, and activities you do off the bike. I have a few friends who even track mowing their lawn to make sure they don’t lose out on the activity for the day. With so many smartwatches out there, it can be hard to pick which one to choose, but time and again we go back to Garmin as the benchmark for tracking tech.

Sources indicate that tracking three back-to-back activities can be an annoyance for data-hungry triathletes. However, the Forerunner 970’s “Triathlon” mode gives multisport athletes the freedom to change between workouts without ending their activity. You only need to tap the lap button at the start and end of each transition. However, the 970 is a great option for folks who aren’t also swimming and running on their bike rides.

Sources indicate that while I’m not a triathlete, I’ve been testing the 970 for a couple of weeks during road rides, commutes, and my daily routine; my overall impression is quite positive. This is a performance-optimized smartwatch for performance-minded athletes. It can track and measure seemingly every data point across an enormous range of sports and activities. Specifically related to cycling, the Forerunner 970 has preset profiles for: Road, mountain biking, gravel, commuting, touring, e-biking, eMTB riding, indoor, cyclocross, and BMX. If none of those options meet your niche, you can also create your own.

According to recent reports, the variety and specificity of data you can track with the Forerunner 970 is mind-boggling. If you want to measure or see something related to riding, you probably can—although finding it in the array of options is sometimes the hardest part. And like Garmin’s head units, that’s the watch’s biggest downside. Garmin packs so many options into its devices that it can be difficult to navigate within the screens. Luckily, the Garmin Connect app is (mostly) easy to use, and changes made in the app instantly push to the phone.

According to recent reports, A feature I like on the 970 is the ability to “Lap by Location”. With this turned on, your watch will automatically start a upcoming lap each time you pass through that GPS location again. That means no more forgetting to tap “Lap” when you’re deep in the red zone with one lap to go in an event. This makes the 970 perfect for cyclocross, criterium, and XC mountain bike racers seeking to track in-race performance data at a granular level.

Sources indicate that the Venu 4’s sleek, not-too-techy profile allows you to maximize your smartwatch mileage, both during workouts and in daily life. It prioritizes general smartwatch functionality, but there’s still plenty of processing power. That makes the Venu great for all-day wear, both on and off the bike.

Senior Art Director, Colin McSherry, has tested the Venu 4 against his trusty Forerunner. He notes the Venu‘s solid 12-day battery life is closer to 8 to 10 days when heavily using route navigation for cycling, running, and hiking. He also remarked, “I found the navigation a bit simpler and easier to use compared to the Garmin Forerunner 970 due to fewer physical buttons.”.

Industry observers note that on the bike, starting and tracking a workout is easy. McSherry noted that, “GPS does take a few seconds to register, but usually picks up as you are taking your first few pedal strokes.” Compared to his Wahoo Elemnt, he found the GPS data was very close. “So if I forgot my computer or wanted to get away from staring at a screen while on a ride, it’s a great way to track basic metrics,” he mentioned.

Garmin released the Fēnix 9 this fall, but we still love the Fēnix 8—and there are some great deals on the watch right now. The 8 Pro is Garmin’s flagship model in its class-leading Fēnix lineup. This watch is packed with virtually every feature you could want to measure and manage your outdoor adventures. The Fēnix 8 Pro includes it all in a rugged design featuring dive-rated buttons, a crisp AMOLED display (or MicroLED for an extra $400), and a titanium bezel. The device connects via ANT+ or Bluetooth to third-party sensors and supports a wide range of activity profiles.

Sources indicate that however, the Fēnix 8 Pro’s biggest upgrade is the included inReach satellite/LTE connectivity. (You previously needed a separate Garmin inReach device for that.) For backcountry adventurers, the ability to message, call, share location, or trigger SOS from your wrist is a must-have feature. All that capability comes at a cost—in both price and battery life. Garmin claims up to 15 days of battery life (in smartwatch mode) for the 47mm model and 27 days for the 51mm version. However, those numbers drop when LTE or satellite features are active.

Jason Griffin, Senior Health and Fitness Editor, is currently testing the 8 Pro. He said, “It’s smarter than I expected a watch could be,” and notes that “answering calls through the watch is super easy, and tracking both rides and runs is intuitive.” He added, “The flashlight was great to find things in the middle of the night while I was holding my sleeping toddler.”.

In a recent development, while the Forerunner 265 is an older model, we find it strikes a good balance between Garmin’s budget-minded watches and its thousand-dollar devices. The 265’s accuracy is top-tier for its price, and this model has a far more readable display than its predecessor, thanks to a bright OLED screen—a near-critical feature if you don’t want to take your hands off your grips for too long to check your mileage.

If you have smaller wrists (or prefer a more compact watch), the Forerunner 265S is a great choice. It’s lighter, slimmer, and even offers longer battery life.

Industry observers note that garmin’s new Forerunner 70 isn’t really an revision of its long-running Forerunner 55 entry-level model: the 70 is an entirely new device. The new model has a larger display, tons more features, and (most importantly for cyclists) many more bicycle profile options.

Industry observers note that the Forerunner 70 is designed to be a great running watch, and its features and data logging abilities are best for off-bike activities. However, the 70 is still a good option for fitness-minded riders or cyclists needing to log their rides and basic training data. So, while the 70 cannot connect to your power meter or smart trainer, it still features solid GPS tracking, a heart rate monitor, and it can follow pre-planned courses.

Buying Tip: If you need to track power, spend the extra $50 and upgrade to the Forerunner 170 model.

Garmin released the Enduro 4 this fall and we are right now testing it to see how it compares to the Enduro 3. The Enduro 3 is still a great option from Garmin and is on sale right now. The Enduro 3 is what happens when you take the top-shelf performance of the Fēnix and optimize it for maximum battery life. It’s a high-caliber solar watch that can last a staggering 36 days in smartwatch mode and up to 150 hours in GPS mode. It’s perfect for long bikepacking outings to places lacking spots to recharge.

Sources indicate that at 51mm, the watch face is large but surprisingly unobtrusive. It feels light (63 grams) and comfortable on the wrist, even during long rides. The Enduro also has a sleeker profile than many premium smartwatches, with fewer sharp edges and oversized buttons. A feature our tester didn’t know they needed is the built-in flashlight. It works very well and is unexpectedly useful in everyday situations.

While the Velcro strap may not win style points off the bike, it’s incredibly functional. It allows for a perfectly snug fit, unlike traditional watch bands (frequently, one loop is too tight and the next is too loose).

Garmin markets the Forerunner 170 Music as a running watch, but that label doesn’t do it justice. It’s a true multi-sport smartwatch, built to support a wide range of activities—including multiple cycling disciplines—and it connects to ANT+ and Bluetooth sensors for more detailed ride data and notifications.

As the name suggests, it includes 4GB of onboard storage for music. This means you can leave your phone behind and still have your playlist. It also features an altimeter, barometer, compass (ABC sensors), a pulse oximeter, and advanced tracking tools, making it capable in almost any scenario.

If you participate in various outdoor activities, you may prefer to own a single device to track everything. Whether cycling, running, hiking, paddling, walking the dog, or playing pickleball, a Garmin watch offers powerful, versatile functionality in a streamlined profile that’s always with you.

If you regularly track multiple types of workouts, while many road and gravel riders prefer cycling head units for instant access to maps, routing details, power metrics, and other data, some riders prefer smartwatches for logging ride data.

According to recent reports, not needing to learn or own multiple overlapping devices simplifies and declutters your life. And in his excellent story, “The Problem with Modern Cycling Computers Isn’t the Huge Screens,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov argues that many head units are bloated with unnecessary functions.

Mountain bikers who often ride technical trails (bike park riders and enduro racers, for example) are increasingly turning to watches to document rides. With some cycling computers costing upwards of $1,000, you don’t want it dangling off the front of your bar or attached to your top tube in the event of a crash. Additionally, a computer is sometimes an unwanted distraction when trying to concentrate on a challenging descent.

According to recent reports, triathletes and duathlon racers are another group of riders who often prefer smartwatches. Watches allow athletes to transition between segments without needing to change devices or combine files after an event. Similarly, since the discipline involves swapping out muddy bikes in the pits during a race, cyclocross racers often use smartwatches.

It has been revealed that A quick spin through Garmin’s website reveals a dizzying lineup of watches—sleek, feature-packed, and often overwhelming to sort through. While nearly all of them include the core functions you’d expect from a sports smartwatch, four series stand out as the best options for cyclists: Forerunner, Enduro, Fēnix, and Venu.

Recent findings suggest that the Forerunner series is Garmin’s core watch for cyclists and multisport athletes. It includes five models, starting with the $250 Forerunner 70, which covers the basics, and going up to the $750 Forerunner 970, which combines high-end smartwatch features with advanced training and navigation tools.

It has been revealed that the Enduro is designed for endurance athletes and offers the longest battery life of any Garmin watch. It includes the premium features of a cycling computer and smartwatch, along with extras such as solar charging and a built-in flashlight—making it a great option for long adventures.

Industry observers note that the Fēnix series shares many advanced features with the Enduro line—activity profiles, multisport tracking, and smartwatch tools—but adds specialized options for adventurers and divers. Fēnix has a slightly shorter battery life than the Enduro, and the watch faces are smaller.

Sources indicate that finally, the Venu is another option. It blends performance training, GPS, and data tracking features with fashion-forward styling. So, it looks good on and off the bike.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#114945. Tech Report: The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3954 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • According to recent reports, there are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here.
  • In a recent development, in 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, there are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here. There’s also a slew of newly introduced super shoes that made their debut this marathon cycle. We’ll update accordingly once these racers are available.

In a recent development, in 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use). Today, almost every shoe brand has a super shoe with a carbon plate and super foams, and they all make the same promise as the Vaporfly 4%: less energy expenditure while racing, or the ability to run faster with the same effort.

It has been revealed that here, we list the top performers based on wear-tester feedback and our own experiences racing in them. And if you’re in the market for other shoes to help you with your training, we have a buying guide for those too.

Your first marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)For a PR → Nike Alphafly 4 (Men’s/Women’s)But want to train in a plated shoe → Newly introduced Balance SC Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)A flat and fast course → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 (Unisex)A half marathon → Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo (Unisex)And want to try low drop → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)And need support → Saucony Endorphin Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)And have wide feet → Hoka Cielo X1 3.0 (Unisex)On a track → Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 (Men’s/Women’s)A 5K or 10K → New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 (Men’s/Women’s)On a trail → Hoka Tecton X 4 (Men’s/Women’s)An ultra → On Cloudultra Pro (Men’s/Women’s).

According to recent reports, besides our local testers, some of whom have been testing for us for the past 15 years, and staff who’ve also logged their share of road and trail time in these shoes, I have tested several of these shoes on race days. I have run 28 marathons since 2010, including 14 consecutive Boston Marathons. And I have made the split-second decision to race in new shoes marathon morning.

According to recent reports, I’ve spoken with brand shoe development teams and have kept up with the latest super shoe releases. New shoes not listed here are still undergoing the testing process and will be added once feedback is in.

All of the shoes on this list were tested by local runners and Runner’s World staff. Our local testers include 300-plus men and women of various running experience levels, paces, arch heights, and gait patterns. From enthusiasts who run for fun to several Olympic-qualifying hopefuls, our mix of testers rounds out a sample of the overall running pop.

Recent findings suggest that RW editors, including myself, have also raced in these shoes, from 5K to marathon distance (and some ultrarunners). We take into consideration fit, feel, and ride to determine the best racing shoes for almost every kind of runner hoping to PR, or just enjoy the propulsive experience of running on carbon plates sandwiched between super foams.

Industry observers note that on a plane, running a shakeout run, and anytime a marathon was weeks away or days past, I’d hear first-timers and seasoned vets say the Adizero Adios Pro 4 was their race day shoe of choice. The latest iteration is sure to have the same mentions next race cycle.

It has been revealed that I didn’t have the chance to race in the Adizero Adios Pro 5 yet, but I did try them out on my usual Central Park circuit in New York City. I was practically racing my casual loop after slurping half a can of beer (it was a long day on the job). It obviously wasn’t the kiwi-flavored Belgian White that had me clocking marathon pace (it got kinda funky after the 25th sip).

It has been revealed that the carbon rim, which replaces the 4’s energy rods, is the secret sauce that subtracts weights and encourages a powerful snap that had me run up and down Harlem Hill like a gazelle. The Lightstrike Pro foam is also slightly firmer, which helps with high rebound and stability.

My only knock is how the rim shreds the hell of my ankle if my form gets slow and sloppy. But it’s a character trait. Senior Art Director Colin McSherry, for instance, ran his first marathon and had no concerns—shoe- or first 26.2-related—during his run.

Shop Men’s at adidas.com | Shop Women’s at adidas.com.

Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 Review.

Sources indicate that the Alphafly 3 went through some major changes to become more inclusive in terms of fit, weight, and ride. How do you upgrade a shoe that was worn by the late Kelvin Kiptum, former marathon world record holder (2:00:35)? It starts with the Air units.

It has been revealed that the ones in the Alphafly 4 are lighter and softer. During his testing, Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate noted how the unit visibly squishes down when you stomp on the forefoot. The effect is a smoother, comfier ride with lots of pop.

According to recent reports, the width of the shoe is also slightly wider (Nike really wants runners to stop saying their shoes are too unstable and narrow). Dengate noted how he didn’t have to slow down when turning corners.

Sources indicate that the main critique is that loud clomping sound. But at this point—is it really an Alphafly if you can’t hear it coming up from behind you meters away?

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Industry observers note that the jury is still out on the pros and cons of solely training in super shoes, but we’re in the camp of keeping your special trainer fresh for race day. You can get a couple of runs in to troubleshoot and see if there are any challenges pre-marathon or half, but I still urge runners to save the magic. But if you can’t get enough of that super foam, carbon plate high, enter the SC Rebel.

New Balance created this shoe specifically to make your training feel easier. It has the brand’s new TPEE-based Infinion foam, tuned for power runs, just like the SuperComp Elite v6 (New Balance’s premium racing shoe). It’s also an ideal alternative for racing if you need more stability. The shoe has a broader platform and grippy outsole that kept me upright on wet mud during a long run.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Newly introduced Balance SuperComp Rebel Review.

The Endorphin Elite 3 is as squishy and bouncy as its predecessor, but Saucony made the shoe more stable by connecting the forefoot and heel. Turns are less scary, but there’s still a learning curve to master the incredible energy return running in these shoes.

I tested them at a 5K and 3K in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, which was pocked with potholes and patched with slippery gravel. The shoes cut corners, but I still felt the need to slow down—or wipe out. I think on a more controlled runner’s feet these would make her feel powerful and unbeatable.

The source of that aggressive bounce is the TPEE-based IncrediRun foam. Its ride rivals even PEBA’s energy return.

Recent findings suggest that the shoe also didn’t produce hot spots in the toe area. Saucony seems to have improved the fit with the third version. Once I wield this shoe’s power I won’t be afraid to run longer than a 10K. No friction here.

Shop Endorphin Elite 3 at saucony.com.

Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 Review.

When I ran the Tokyo Marathon last year, I laced up in the Asics Metaspeed Sky Paris because I wanted more cushioning in the forefoot area. Asics recognized there are two ways of racing: stride running or cadence running. The Sky is intended for stride running: when you have a more powerful gait with longer strides and tend to strike on the midfoot.

At the Sydney Marathon this year, I opted for the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo instead. I felt the Edge would give me the, er, competitive edge, so to speak. My steps per minute are usually more than the average runner due to my mechanics and, well, because I’m short. The shoe has a scooped plate tilted slightly downward to cater to those with shorter steps (cadence running). I ended up hitting my sub-3:10 goal, finishing in 3:05.

According to recent reports, the Edge Tokyo is updated with a softer underfoot, making the shoe more flexible. This makes the shoe have an incredible snap at toe-off. I was able to change gears at a fast clip when I latched onto a runner I was determined to pass (not always the best race strategy, but worked like a charm when I saw male runners try to overtake me).

Where competitors’ shoes have “air pods” or decoupled heels, the Metaspeeds provide runners with a simplified, choose-your-own-adventure super shoe that packs a powerful punch. One note for the wise: Because the Edge Tokyo has less firm cushioning, my heels and arches felt sore postrace. If you have heavy footfalls like me, have those recovery sandals waiting for you at bag check.

Shop Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at amazon.com.

Asics Metaspeed Tokyo Shoes Review.

In a recent development, altra started its journey into super shoes by staying true to itself. The Vanish Carbon 1 and 2 had wide toeboxes and were zero drop. But the Altra team knew there would have to be a compromise to go up against competitors’ shoes: the Vanish Carbon 3 needed a drop. The brand preserved the Altra way by adding just 4 mm (like the shoes in its Experience collection) to the heel with an aggressive rocker profile to promote propulsion.

Another Altra signature in the shoe is the roomy toebox that gives racers space to splay their toes, allowing them to engage their digits and power up during push-off.

The third iteration has pure PEBA midsole foam called FastRce. The foam provides more energy return and 2.6 percent improved running economy over the Vanish Carbon 2, which had a PEBA/EVA blend in its midsole.

The overall package presents a racer capable of racing against the other super shoes on this list.

Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

The Endorphin Pro 5 has a more stable ride than its springier sibling, the Endorphin Elite 2, which we also included on this list.

It has been revealed that its midsole is dual-layer PEBA, with one layer Pwrrun PB and the other layer Pwrrun HG. These layers provide a high-rebound ride and work with the rocker Speedroll tech to encourage fast, smooth turnover.

Testers like the shoe’s propulsive ride as well as support throughout their workouts.

It has been revealed that “What stood out most was the combination of propulsion and stability,” remarked tester Srah Pezzino. “The carbon plate paired with Saucony’s Pwrrun HG foam delivers a responsive, fast ride without feeling unstable or overly bouncy. This helped immensely during longer tempo runs when fatigue starts to creep in. I felt like the shoe encouraged good mechanics and smooth turnover rather than forcing speed.

Industry observers note that “Compared to previous carbon-plated shoes I’ve worn, the Pro 5 feels more predictable and controlled, especially when my form isn’t perfect late in a run. It’s a shoe that makes you feel fast without punishing you for not being perfectly locked in.”.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

According to recent reports, the lightest Hoka marathon racing shoe yet is the Cielo X1 3.0, with street cred at the 2025 Chicago Marathon. Hoka-sponsored pro-runner Alex Masai raced in a blacked-out prototype of the shoe, shaved nearly four minutes off his personal best time, and podiumed third with a 2:04:37 finish.

And our testers clocked the shoe’s massive updates, as well. “The 3.0 is sturdier than the 2.0,” said tester Mike Browne. “I’m referring to the sturdiness mainly on heel strikes. I wore the 2.0 during marathon training and in a marathon, and they actually underpronated a little. I think that is what caused the outside heel rubber to come off on both shoes. The 3.0 has corrected that matter and seems to strike the ground in the center, which makes for a more even wear on the shoe.”.

Recent findings suggest that besides implementing a lighter upper, the Hoka team redesigned the midsole shape, creating a long channel that runs down the center of the shoe. The rocker also isn’t as exaggerated. What you get is a more stable, smoother ride while racing with propulsion that’s comparable to Hoka’s competitors’. The fit is also broader in the midfoot, making the Cielo X1 3.0 a good choice for runners with wide feet.

Shop Hoka Cielo X1 3 at hoka.com.

Recent findings suggest that the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 is a prime pick for marathon racing, but it’s also a solid choice for everything else under 26.2 miles. The shoe is so lightweight and delivers such explosive rebound—“you feel like you’re running straight down a trampoline,” indicates a tester—that it left some of us feeling like we had brownie batter for legs after hard efforts.

The shoe was the talk of the industry prelaunch after Puma released a study (which the brand sponsored) comparing the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3’s performance to the Nike Alphafly 3, Adidas Adios Pro Evo 1, and Puma Fast-R 2. The study claimed the Elite 3 was 3.15 to 3.62 percent more economical than its competitors.

Recent findings suggest that putting those numbers aside, our testers agreed this is one powerful racing shoe. “The foam used in this shoe is very noticeable, even when simply starting with a short warmup in the shoe,” says tester Codi Januszkiewicz, who compares the ride to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4. “Accelerating from a warmup pace straight into some speedwork intervals felt smooth; somehow moving faster in this shoe felt even easier than the warmup.”.

Sources indicate that but that power is a lot to handle. “The stability is lacking,” indicates tester Sean O’Connor. “Almost felt high heelish to me, and it jacked up my calves and feet a little as well. When I ran in them it felt like I was perpetually holding onto the shoe with my feet. I think that's why it made my calves and feet sore.”.

Recent findings suggest that some can handle the shoe’s intensity over a long period of time. Others may assign the Elite 3 as their mid-distance racing shoe instead. I wore the Elite 3 at a Trackmith 5000 meters over the summer, hitting a PR at 19:12. It’s cush in the heel, but judging by my footfalls, which are heavy, I think racing them in a 26.2 would prolong my usual recovery time postrun.

When I raced the 2025 London Marathon, I had been training in the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v4 but instead opted for the FuelCell SuperComp Pacer v2. The Pacer is sleeker and lightweight, unlike the SuperComp Elite v4, which was too beefy for my small frame. The SuperComp Elite v6 is the version of the shoe I would have raced in. Unfortunately, I can’t go back to April 2025. Fortunately for you, the Elite v6 is here just in time for fall marathon season.

According to recent reports, the shoe features the brand’s Infinion foam, which was introduced in the 1080v15. The Elite v6’s version of the TPEE- and TPU-based foam is dialed-in for race-ready energy return.

I took the shoe out on a track for a 2 x 2-mile workout at 6:45 pace and the shoes handled turns and helped me hit goal pace. The ride isn’t as aggressive as the Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 or Alphafly, and the cushioning is firmer. Runners with an efficient stride and good form can get away with running marathons and halfs in these shoes, but I’d recommend these for 5Ks and 10Ks because of the firmness and less explosive rebound. The lighter weight makes it ideal for track and medium-distance road races.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Newly introduced Balance SuperComp Elite v6 Review.

Though I’ve been racing for 20 years, nothing will get me running an ultra on the trail—which is where our Senior Editor Cat Bowen comes in. Bowen conquered scrambles on steep climbs, dusty ridgelines, gnarly technical trails, and more types of terrain than I run in a year, while testing the long-awaited Tecton X 4.

Sources indicate that she gave a shoutout to the hardy Matryx upper that’s “tough as nails” and the grippy 4mm lugs that prevented her from plunging forward. The plus/minus with the shoe is that built-in gaiter collar. Bowen appreciated the extra coverage, but lamented how difficult it was to put on the shoe (we get it: a side zipper would be a good cheat but adds weight). “There is absolutely no reason why this shoe has a front pull tab and nothing in the back,” she wrote in her review.

In a recent development, still, the new cushioning, Hoka’s ProFly X, and non-winged plate make for a more energized ride that’s less rigid without losing stability. It’s a great shoe for unpredictable. but Bowen urges you to not go the no-sock route.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

For hours, days, weeks on the trail, there’s the Cloudultra Pro. Bowen has gone through three pairs of the shoe—not because they lack durability but because she likes them so much and runs that much—and appreciates how she doesn’t have to slice the sides. Feet swell during ultras, but it sounds like On prepared for that with its roomy but secure upper.

In a recent development, another plus in Bowen’s column of ultra shoe musts is the Cloudultra Pro’s lateral stability. Maneuvering over rugged, uneven terrain could spell twisted ankles and slipping and sliding, but the shoe didn’t lead Bowen astray.

Ultrarunner Pat Heine-Holmberg also wore the shoe around Germany’s Zugspitze, where he raced the 102-mile ZUT1000 and ran on “every surface imaginable.”.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com.

Recent findings suggest that brands are now beginning to release carbon shoes in men’s and women’s sizes. Still, in some cases there’s not much difference between the types of shoes except for maybe the sizing and colors. If the shoes are unisex, it may take a few try-ons to get the fit right. In my unisex racing shoe experience, I’ve found the collar can be loose while the midfoot can be tight. You may want to size up or down, and adopt the heel-lock tying method if the heel area feels too loose.

Do all carbon-fiber plates behave the same way? Sort of. An vital lesson to learn here is that the plate isn’t the secret sauce of super shoes—it doesn’t cause propulsion. Instead, the plate, sandwiched between the highly responsive foams, acts as a stabilizer to the super foam. This is why super shoes have such tall stack heights, and why World Athletics caps racing shoe stack height at 40 mm. The super foam—and amount underfoot—is a major advantage.

When choosing a carbon-plate shoe, you’ll want to consider what you’re using it for—racing on the road or trail—and, if possible, have your gait evaluated to determine the best plate angle if you’re looking at shoes specific to running type.

It has been revealed that some plates are full-length or have cutouts. In shoes like the Asics Metaspeed Edge and Metaspeed Sky, the plate’s angle differentiates running types. The Edge’s plate dips lower in the forefoot so cadence runners can roll off their toes faster. The Sky’s plate sits flat in the forefoot, allowing stride runners to leverage bounce on longer steps.

According to recent reports, the secret sauce in super shoes is the foam. PEBA (polyether block amide) was once considered the holy grail of all foams and you can still find it in most super shoes, but newer models are using TPEE (thermoplastic polyester elastomer) and A-TPU (aliphatic thermoplastic polyurethane) because they’re more resistant to bottoming out, or going flat. The ride is more durable—and can be quite aggressively bouncy and squishy.

To truly gauge which foam is best for you, trying on the shoe and giving it a run (preferably with some cornering) will help you determine if you want a firmer or squishier ride.

It has been revealed that A carbon-fiber plate shoe is an investment, costing anywhere from $240 upward of $500. There are a couple of things to take into account on a personal level before buying: Can you afford a trainer that’s less durable compared to the standard workhorse shoe, which lasts between 450 to 500 miles?

While these super shoes are more durable than the ones made eight years ago, they still have a shorter shelf life due to high-performance foams—PEBA and supercritical blends—wearing down faster. Lastly, is the return there? While brands claim these shoes can improve performance, it’s not guaranteed your running economy will improve by around 4 percent.

I spoke with Ted Fitzpatrick, Saucony’s VP of product management, about the differences. He made these key points between carbon and nylon plates:.

Industry observers note that A nylon plate is semirigid with some flexibility. A carbon plate is rigid with little or no flexibility. Popsicle analogy—Imagine the plate as the stick that holds the soft ice cream together. The fundamental use of the plates is to keep the dimensional stability of the foam. With each type of plate, each offers different levels of compliance. The plate maintains the forward rolling effect of super shoes. Carbon is the stiffest, which offers the most concentrated effect of speed roll technology. Nylon still adds stiffness, however, it offers better compliance in how the foot transitions in the gait cycle. Some individuals can respond better to different plates. It is down to what works best for the user.

Industry observers note that saucony offers the nylon-plated Endorphin Speed 6, a training shoe that complements its racer, the Endorphin Pro. The shoe can also serve as a more affordable racing shoe, at $180. (The Endorphin Elite 3 and Endorphin Pro 5 cost $290 and $240.).

Sources indicate that “The foam is what does the heavy lifting of a super shoe, however it’s the plate that guides how each foam behaves to the user,” says Fitzpatrick. “It is best to train in both to strengthen and build ‘muscle memory’ into different muscle groups.”.

According to recent reports, however, we wouldn’t recommend solely training in super shoes. For one thing, it would be extremely expensive to use these shoes as daily trainers when they have a shorter shelf life compared to standard everyday shoes. We advise going on a couple of runs before racing in the shoes, to get used to running in them and check for hot spots. While running constantly in these shoes won’t necessarily lead to injury, overuse and the desire to run faster in carbon shoes will likely lead to getting sidelined if you’re not careful.

According to recent reports, amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

These 10 Editor-Approved E-MTBs Deliver Real Trail Capability

📅 05 Jul 2019 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that autumn is our favorite season for mountain biking.
  • Sources indicate that today’s electric mountain bikes use lightweight motors and batteries, making them super capable and amazingly fun on the trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

It has been revealed that autumn is our favorite season for mountain biking. The air is crisp, the dirt is grippy, and we can’t wait to head to the singletrack after work and on weekends for great rides. And more than ever, like many other mountain bikers, we’re choosing E-MTBs for our rides. Electric mountain bikes help you maximize those rides and spend more time on your favorite trails.

Sources indicate that today’s electric mountain bikes use lightweight motors and batteries, making them super capable and amazingly fun on the trail. And while heavier than traditional mountain bikes, these pedal-assist models allow you to cover more miles, ride faster, and tackle challenging climbs.

E-MTBs are engineered for performance on singletrack trails and deep in the woods. And while their low-power motors provide a boost when pedalling, E-MTBs are not electric motorcycles. You still have to pedal an electric mountain bike; you can’t simply twist a throttle and blast down the trail.

Industry observers note that the best E-MTBs blend mountain bike components, suspension, and geometry with electronic technology in a brilliant fashion. Like non-electric mountain bikes, some E-MTBs blur the lines of XC and lightweight trail bikes, while others are burlier and take suspension and geometry cues from the top-performing enduro and downhill racing mountain bikes.

Recent findings suggest that aventon recently launched the Current, the brand’s first full-suspension E-MTB, and it is a gem! The Current ADV offers incredible value, and it’s trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, noted, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers. The Current’s motor and interface provide riders with a wide range of tuning options and lots of data.”.

Sources indicate that the Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor boasting 750 peak Watts and 110Nm torque. (The Current also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and torque to 120Nm.) Rounding out the ADV are a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

Sources indicate that in his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab especially likes the Current’s intuitive and easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data and the ability to tune the motor settings.

It has been revealed that want a carbon frame and electronic drivetrain? The Current EXP is a great package for $5,999.

It has been revealed that specialized’s Turbo motor is a benchmark for electric mountain bike performance. It has plenty of power and torque, and the Morgan Hill, California-based brand has updated, polished, and refined the motor over several years. However, the biggest downside to Specialized E-MTBs has been their very steep starting price. But that has changed.

Specialized’s newest Levo model brings the platform to a more palatable $5,000 price. The Turbo Levo 4 Alloy uses the same motor and battery as the pricier carbon-chassis Expert model but with an aluminum frame, heavier components, and mechanical shifting to save pennies. The brand bolts its 105Nm torque and 810-watt Turbo 3.1 motor to a 150mm-travel, full-suspension aluminum frame and equips the bike with value-packed parts. SRAM brakes, a mechanical drivetrain, and Marzocchi suspension highlight the alloy Levo 4’s component package.

Hardtail mountain bikes are a gateway into the sport for many riders because they’re simple, sturdy, and affordable. Plus, big, burly full-suspension mountain bikes aren’t for everyone. For some riders, they’re overkill—adding cost and complexity without delivering benefits that match their needs. Hardtail E-MTBs provide pedal assistance for about the same price as full-suspension non-electric mountain bikes.

When launched two years ago, the Ramblas impressed me with its great performance and capability for the price—and Aventon’s recent upgrades make it even better on the trail. The revised Ramblas ADV’s trail-forward components include a RockShox Psylo fork with 35mm stanchions, a 1x12 SRAM Eagle drivetrain that can handle most climbs, powerful four-piston SRAM DB6 brakes, and a useful dropper seatpost. The ADV’s tubeless rims and 2.4-inch Maxxis tires are also upgrades. These components are unmatched by any other hardtail E-MTB, especially at this price.

Superlight e-MTBs offer an intriguing compromise: In exchange for a less powerful drive unit, you get a lighter bike that feels and handles more like an analog mountain bike.

With the Turbo Levo R, Specialized asks: What if you didn’t need to compromise?

The Levo R has the same drive unit and battery as the Levo 4, but in a lighter, shorter-travel package with matched 29-inch wheels. It’s around 5 pounds lighter than a standard Levo 4 at the same price. In the top-of-the-line S-Works trim, the DU offers up to 111 Nm of torque and 850 watts of peak power with an 850 or 900Wh battery. The 41.4-pound (18.8 kg) S-Works Ultralight uses a 600Wh battery to save weight. Lower-priced models offer 105 Nm, 810 watts, and an 840Wh battery.

Recent findings suggest that after spending the better part of a year riding an S-Works Levo R (46.7 lb., size S3), senior test editor Matt Phillips calls it a winning combination for many riders. “It has all the capability and range of a big battery and full-power DU, but in a bike that’s much more flickable, lively, and, frankly, easier to ride than a heavier and bigger-travel e-MTB.” He says Specialized’s e-MTB hardware, frames, and suspension are the icing on top, and calls the Levo R one of the most entertaining mountain bikes, powered or unpowered, he’s ridden this year.

Recent findings suggest that the 29-inch-wheeled Cannondale Moterra 4 has a subdued appearance, which makes it a sleeper. Many full-suspension E-MTBs routinely cost more than $10,000. However, Cannondale keeps the Moterra 4 to a more modest $5,500 while still packing a lot of punch for its price.

At the heart of the Moterra is a trusty Bosch Performance Line CX motor mounted on a 150mm-travel aluminum full-suspension frame. And inside the bike’s stout downtube is a 600Wh Bosch battery. Cannondale’s product team made smart component choices—such as the excellent Shimano Cues drivetrain and 160mm-travel SR Suntour Xeron air-sprung fork—that save cost without sacrificing much performance. The Moterra 4 also has a long-travel dropper seatpost, tubeless wheels, and Tektro disc brakes.

Industry observers note that if you buy the Moterra 4 through rei.com, you can have it shipped to your nearest REI location for professional assembly with in-store or curbside pickup. You also get one year of free adjustments—or two years if you’re an REI Co-op member.

“I’ve never considered an e-bike a replacement for a traditional bike—until now.” That’s what Matt Phillips mentioned in his review of the excellent S-Works Turbo Levo 4. The latest version of Specialized’s flagship e-MTB is refined, quiet, fun to ride, and refreshingly free of the common annoyances that plague many e-bikes.

It has been revealed that several standout features set the latest S-Works Turbo Levo 4 apart from the crowded E-MTB segment: a powerful motor delivering 111Nm of torque, a larger 900 Wh battery, and the ability to toggle the pedal-assist cutoff between Class 2 (20mph) and Class 3 (28mph). That extra speed might sound excessive, but it’s a welcome boost when you're riding to or between trails.

Though the S-Works Levo 4 is less expensive than its predecessor, it’s still eye-wateringly pricey at $12,500. For better value—relatively speaking—we recommend the Turbo Levo 4 Expert. It offers the same carbon frame, battery, and motor as the pricier model, though with slightly less torque. A 160mm-travel Fox 38 Performance Elite GRIPX2 fork and a Fox Float X Performance Elite shock handle suspension duties, and SRAM’s GX AXS drivetrain handles gear changes.

Recent findings suggest that salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs, yet it’s packed with value. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Nm of torque) and a 430Wh battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, the Moraine has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

According to recent reports, the frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system used by Pivot), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain with four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the component selection on this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

Recent findings suggest that one advantage of an e-MTB is climbing faster and with less effort, leaving you fresher for the descent. A long-travel bike helps you make the most of that on steep, rough trails. It’s like having a personal chairlift for lapping downhill trails.

Sources indicate that cannondale’s Moterra Carbon LT 2 pairs a Bosch Performance Line CX motor and 750Wh battery with 165mm of plush, coil-sprung rear travel and a 170mm fork. Its frame combines a carbon front triangle with an alloy swingarm. Size-specific suspension kinematics tailor the suspension performance to each frame size. The mullet setup pairs a 29-inch front wheel with a 27.5-inch rear, giving you more room to move behind the saddle on steep terrain while keeping the larger front wheel’s rollover advantage. The battery is removable for off-bike charging.

For riders who prioritize steep descents and the refinement and reliability of a Bosch drive unit, the Moterra LT 2 is a strong choice.

Industry observers note that it’s no exaggeration to say Avinox reshaped the performance e-MTB market. Developed and launched by drone maker DJI before becoming an independent organization, Avinox set latest benchmarks with the M1: 105 Nm of torque and up to 1,000 watts of peak power. It also matched or exceeded established brands in features, function, and assist performance. Suddenly, longtime players were off the back, some way off the back.

Before they could catch up, Avinox followed the M1 with the more powerful, refined M2S: up to 150 Nm of torque and 1,500 watts of peak power. But power isn’t the whole story. Senior features director Louis Mazzante notes the M2S “isn’t the thunderously loud, chassis-shaking hot-rod motor that its power suggests. It is quiet. It’s smooth. It’s refined.” He also praises its feature-packed, easy-to-use app and touch-screen controls, and says the motor’s power is smooth and tractable.

That blend of power, control, and features has made the M2S highly desirable to bike brands. Ari’s Wire Peak 3.0 stands out as an affordable way to get it.

Starting at $4,999, the Wire Peak pairs the M2S with an 800Wh battery in an aluminum frame with 150mm of rear travel and a 160mm fork. This setup delivers up to 150 Nm of torque in Boost mode and 1,300 watts of peak power. The bike also has a four-bar suspension design, 29-inch or mullet wheel compatibility, and independent high/low and long/short geometry adjustments.

According to recent reports, ari delivers each bike directly to the buyer with a rider-specific setup. Buyers can customize the build through the configurator, and Ari will accommodate most off-menu parts and upgrade requests.

Recent findings suggest that after his first rides on his long-term test bike, senior test editor Matt Phillips called the chassis excellent, Ari’s buying process superb, and the drive unit best in class. He notes the Wire Peak would be his choice if he were buying an e-MTB today.

The DRT 1.1 (from REI’s in-house Co-Op Cycles brand) is a good pick if you’re looking for an electric mountain bike to explore mellower trails and ride around town. REI equips the bikes with a dependable Bosch Performance Line mid-drive motor and internal battery.

Sources indicate that this hardtail rolls on tubeless-compatible 27.5-inch wheels with 2.6-inch-wide Maxxis Rekon tires for off-road capability. The DRT’s 100mm-travel SR Suntour fork with thru axle isn’t glamorous, but it works. The only notable component missing is a dropper seatpost; it would enhance the bike’s trail capability and help riders feel more confident on challenging terrain.

It has been revealed that traditional analog mountain bikes are usually grouped by frame travel. E-MTBs, on the other hand, are categorized by their power. However, more power ≠ more better. Pick the style that suits your riding needs, budget, and local trail access.

⚡️ Full-Power E-MTBs are the most common style and are generally equipped with roughly 750-watt peak power (1 horsepower) and 85 torque, or more. Bosch, Shimano, and Specialized are three commonly used motor brands for these bikes.

In a recent development, ⚡️ Lightweight E-MTBs feature motors with less power and torque (50 to 60 Nm) and lower-capacity batteries. As a result, these bikes weigh less than other E-MTBs and ride more like an unassisted mountain bike, but with a little help on the climbs. Lightweight electric mountain bikes are less popular now than a couple of years ago, which means you can score good deals on great riding bikes.

⚡️ High-power e-MTBs are the newest category of electric mountain bikes, and they’re promptly becoming one of the year’s most talked-about cycling trends. These motors produce more than 1,000 watts of peak power and 110 Nm of torque. Category leader Avinox’s latest unit delivers an incredible 1,500 watts and 150 Nm of torque. Its power and performance have prompted Bosch and Specialized to respond with firmware updates that boost the torque and power of their premium drive units. Even so, the Avinox remains the most powerful drive unit available. But high-power motors aren’t without detractors, or potential consequences. Their use has sparked debate and hand-wringing in the mountain biking community over how much power is too much. Remember: “With great power comes great responsibility.”.

When you’re shopping for an electric mountain bike, you must factor in not only the motor’s power and features, but also the bike’s basic capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that since electronic mountain bikes are heavier than non-motorized bikes, you’ll want to consider a bike with more suspension travel than you have on your non-motorized bike. The longer your travel, the more cushion you’ll get when you encounter obstacles.

Most full suspension E-MTBs are in the 150- to 160mm travel range, which offers a nice balance of increased comfort and improved control for first-time buyers.

In a recent development, there are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding on trail systems.

Sources indicate that class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows people to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Other countries classify e-bikes differently, and many countries do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

It has been revealed that most performance-oriented electric mountain bikes are Class 1. Electric mountain bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. A mid-drive motor will almost always offer more power. Because the extra weight on a mid-mount bike is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors. Mid-mount bikes do tend to be more expensive, but all of our favorite bikes feature this type of motor.

Battery Life, Range, Maintenance, and Safety.

Industry observers note that on top of the motor, you’ll want to consider the battery size and range. More is always better for performance, but a battery with a longer range will also weigh more and cost more.

As a bike's weight increases, it requires more effort from the rider to handle. This is especially an key consideration for smaller riders; extra weight can also become a bigger challenge at faster speeds, when you need to ride the bike more aggressively.

A lighter bike will offer better handling, but if you sacrifice too much battery capacity to cut weight, you may find yourself pedaling home with no assist if you take a wrong turn.

Like all e-bikes, E-MTBs can be pedaled as a normal bike if the battery dies, so you’ll still be able to get home, but it will require extra effort and possibly more time.

While we can confidently say a larger battery provides more range, it is difficult to accurately estimate any e-bike's exact range. Many factors impact an e-bike's range: How much boost you’re using (most power systems offer three or four settings), how much you weigh, the terrain you’re riding, how much climbing you’re doing, the air temperature, rolling resistance from the tires, and even how clean and lubricated the drivetrain is.

It has been revealed that don’t take any brand's word on its range claims. Start conservatively as you test your bike’s range. The more you ride, the better you’ll understand how far your batteries can carry you in different conditions. If your bike’s main battery isn’t cutting it, some models let you add an external range booster or swap the internal battery for a fresh one. Be warned: These accessories can be expensive!

It has been revealed that like all batteries, e-bike batteries do lose capacity every time they’re charged and discharged. Unfortunately, that means that the more you ride, the sooner you’ll need to replace your battery. Even so, an e-bike battery should give you years of reliable riding.

Follow your bike's manufacturer’s recommendations for storage, but most batteries will last longer if stored with about a 40-percent charge (but don’t forget to plug your bike in about six hours before riding, to make sure you start your ride with a full charge).

Batteries should also be stored at room temperature whenever possible and not left outside or in an unheated garage in freezing temperatures. Some bike brands, including Specialized, have a setting that will prevent the battery from charging fully. This feature is designed to extend the battery’s life, but you may want to disable the feature if the rides you regularly take use your battery’s full capacity.

If, after a few years, your battery loses enough capacity that you want to replace it, be sure to contact your bike’s manufacturer or local dealer and purchase a certified replacement battery through the brand or its dealer.

Industry observers note that don’t be tempted by cheaper options available online from third-party brands. These third-party batteries are generally not certified by bike brands and may void your bike’s warranty. More importantly, third-party replacement batteries often do not have notable safety features, and, as a result, these batteries have been identified as the cause of several serious fires.

There is currently legislation pending at the state and federal level that will bar the sale of non-certified batteries in the U.S., but they are still available as of this writing.

While a handful of bicycle drivetrain manufacturers exist, almost every e-mountain bike will have either a Shimano or SRAM drivetrain. Both are reputable manufacturers that offer reliable shifting and a wide-ranging gear set. Some drivetrains feature electronic shifting. Such drivetrains offer quick and precise shifting, but they will add cost.

According to recent reports, the added power of an e-bike puts more strain on a bike’s drivetrain. You can expect to replace your chain more frequently, but you can get more life out of your components if you back off the pedals when shifting, and ease the chain between gears instead of mashing the shifter and the pedal at the same time.

Given the increased weight of an electronic mountain bike, you’ll want to make sure yours is equipped with hydraulic disc brakes, as most are. These brakes offer lots of stopping power and modulation, which ensures you’ll remain in control regardless of your bike's weight, or how fast you go.

It has been revealed that several brands offer hydraulic disc brakes, though again, Shimano and SRAM usually lead the way. For additional power, look for bikes featuring four-piston brakes.

The 9 Best Stability Shoes for Every Type of Runner
