It’s on the list because we loved the 25 so much. The 25 is currently on sale, so grab it while you can.

Sources indicate that some shoes do not have a sexy reputation. Say “stability shoe” to a certain kind of runner and they’ll look like you just suggested they run their next marathon in Crocs. Stability shoes have a reputation problem, and it’s not entirely undeserved. The stability shoes of the early 2000s were clunky, rigid bricks that treated pronation like a disease to be cured with a slab of hard plastic (looking at you, Saucony Grid Azuras). If you ran through that era, I get why you might have a negative, visceral reaction to the type.

According to recent reports, but here’s the thing: Stability shoes got better. Today’s versions are lighter, softer, and not for anything? Cuter. And they are some of the best shoes you can lace up—not just for overpronators, but for anyone whose form gets sloppy when the miles pile up. I’ve known runners who white-knuckle their way through marathon blocks in neutral racers when a little guidance would have saved their knees, their IT bands, and frankly, their sourpusses. Needing support isn’t taking an L. It’s biomechanics.

At its simplest, a stability shoe is designed to limit excess inward rolling of the foot (overpronation) after your foot strikes the ground. A little pronation is normal and even beneficial; it helps distribute the shock of the impact. But when your ankle collapses too far inward with every step, that torque travels up the chain to your shins, knees, and hips, and over hundreds of miles it can screw up not just your stride, but your long-term health.

Neutral shoes let your foot do whatever it wants. Stability shoes help guide your foot into a more correct placement, keeping your body more aligned.

Industry observers note that from pounding the pavement to scrutinizing performance in our Shoe Lab, the Runner’s World test editors and wear-testers rigorously tested all of our selections. Our process includes exhaustive market research, analysis of user feedback, and consultations with industry experts. This article was written jointly between our editors Amanda Furrer and Cat Bowen. Bowen tends to pronate, especially when she is tired or in a long training block. She has run in all the shoes on this list with the exception of the Nike Structure Plus.

It has been revealed that the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is one of the most consistent stability shoes on the market, and the silver anniversary enhancement makes a strong case for why this franchise has lasted 25 years. The big news is in the stack: Brooks added 3 mm to the forefoot and 1 mm to the heel, bringing it to 37 mm and 27 mm respectively, and dropped the heel-to-toe offset from 12 mm down to 10 mm for the first time in the shoe’s history.

Industry observers note that the new heel bevel is the smoothest the Adrenaline has ever had in the opinion of Bowen, who has put serious miles on this shoe. She also feels as though it’s the most balanced this shoe has ever been, and the most balanced on this list.

It has been revealed that “Some stability shoes can be so aggressive that the rails can begin to pinch the lateral sides of the foot during long runs,” she indicates. “The Adrenaline GTS 25 doesn’t do that, and they still have the cushion and push to power your runs.”.

Recent findings suggest that DNA Loft v3 foam carries over from the 24, but the extra volume makes the ride noticeably softer underfoot, especially at heel strike. Guide rails are still doing their thing on the medial and lateral edges—reactive, not prescriptive, engaging only when your stride asks for it. The upper is a breathable engineered mesh that has the benefit of preventing overheating and swamp foot with a stretch knit heel collar that locks down without overcrowding.

Though it should be noted that some testers, including Courtney Kazmierczak, feel as though the collar is a hair too high in the back, which requires some trial and error for sock choice.

In a recent development, at 10.6 ounces, it’s not light, but it’s not trying to be. This is a daily trainer for runners who want structure and protection. It’s a shoe that simply does not pinch or bite.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

According to recent reports, this is not a rebuild or huge design change. This is a fine-tuning. The basics are the same; the Adrenaline GTS 26 still uses guide rails as the support system, it has the same stack height, the same drop, the profile hasn’t changed, and the core of the midsole is still the DNA Loft v3 foam.

According to recent reports, what did change is that they made it a little bit more breathable by using an engineered mesh upper. The tongue is a bit flatter for a more tuned-in fit, and the heel collar is more refined with a generous pull-tab, which is great for runners with accessibility or limb differences.

The trade-off here is that it is a teensy bit heavier. We’re talking a few tenths of an ounce difference. And, if I’m being the picky and petty editor that I am? I think the colors and design for this model aren’t as cute. I know, I know, lame thing to bring up, but I really just want a stability shoe in a fun neon. Just because I run like a duck doesn’t mean I don’t deserve fun.

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

These may be our best value pick, but they’re also some of the most durable daily stability trainers on this list. “I like the durability and stability of these shoes and the fact that they are lighter than previous models,” said shoe tester Lauren Woodall. “I am able to put more miles on these shoes before they need to be replaced than other running shoes.”.

The thing is, even though it’s heavier, and the durability is noticeable, they’re not bricks. They are your easy run shoes, your throw-on-and-go trainers. They’re not the fastest, but they’re not meant to be. When your body is tired, and you need the assistance of that wave plate and the heft of the Enerzy NXT foam, it’s there for you like an old friend holding out a hand. The guardrails on this shoe aren’t superpowered corrections like they were on earlier models, but the gentle effectiveness of them cannot be overstated. Simply put, these shoes just feel really good on your run.

In a recent development, one note about fit: a few of our testers found that you can get a bit of heel slippage in these. However, Mizuno gives you that extra eyelet for a heel lock, and that can absolutely change the fit of the shoe once you lace up. It’s a point worth remembering.

Shop Men’s at usa.mizuno.com | Shop Women’s at usa.mizuno.com.

In a recent development, the Arahi 9 is Hoka-soft, but not max-cush beefy. It’s a versatile model that does double duty as an everyday trainer or tempo shoe. The brand made small tweaks to the upper for a better fit, and made them a little bit less expensive as well. It’s not a huge redesign as much as it’s a refinement.

You forget the Arahi 9 is a stability shoe because of how streamlined the design looks: it’s sleek and a compliment magnet. Hoka modified the upper to dial in the fit a bit more, make it a little more breathable, and adjust some of the hot points felt in the 8.

Recent findings suggest that invisible to the eye is the H-Frame system that keeps you stable. The H-Frame is a dense piece of foam in the midsole that’s H-shaped. The result is surprising; you’d think the H-Frame would make the Arahi rigid and heavy, but instead the shoe is lightweight and the ride is smooth. Running in it, Furrer felt like she was gliding.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

There’s something about the Nike Structure Plus that demands attention. In the words of Furrer, “I have a soft spot for this shoe, it’s just so good on long runs.” And that right there is spot on. For the days when you know you have a long run on the calendar, but that long run is full of mixed tempos, hill climbs, potential obstacles, and rough surfaces that you’ll start to feel underfoot after six miles, this is going to be the shoe you reach for. That’s what Nike designed it to handle when it combined the ReactX and ZoomX foams with a dual-zone rubber outsole. It gives you cushion where you need it, flexibility where it matters most, and a nimble feel when you’re dodging pavement cracks.

Arguably the most stylish shoe on this list, Nike really leveled up its stability line with the Structure. It’s also very orthotic-friendly. The collar and the lacing system can handle a lot of pulling, allowing you to get those insoles in correctly. Beyond that, it’s remarkably comfortable as a shoe just to take out and live in. It’s a solid walking shoe, and we love it as a versatile, more cushioned alternative to wear with dressier outfits.

That’s not to say it’s flawless. It’s a bit on the heavier side, and if you’re someone who prefers a shoe that has a lot of responsiveness or bounce, you won’t find it in this shoe. It’s also just a hair on the “runs smaller” side front to back. But other than those small quibbles, it’s a great pair.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

The differences between the Gel-Kayano 32 and the 33 are crucial, but not massive. They retooled the design of the support system, employing their FluidSupport tech, which is a bit more malleable than previous iterations, working more with the body’s movements and mechanics. They’ve also softened the foam, updated the fit throughout, and for many runners, it should feel and ride more comfortably.

In a recent development, that being remarked, it still has all the Asics features you expect and love: a breathable upper, geometry that works to move you forward, and a grippy sole that keeps you upright on wet pavement. It is on the heavier side, but nothing out of the ordinary for a stability shoe, and the collar could have a hair more cushion. However, we love the well-placed heel tab, especially when our hands are sweaty.

Industry observers note that the cushion is going to be the biggest win on long-run days. You may not get a ton of energy return, but what you are getting is that added comfort with the guidance that will help you maintain your form and keep you from hating yourself after the run when you’re inevitably lying on the floor propped up on your hands.

Shop Men’s at asics.com |Shop Women’s at asics.com.

The Saucony Guide 19 is a stability shoe that actually earns the word “versatile,” which stability shoes rarely do. Most of them feel like you’re being guided rather than running, but the Guide 19 threads the needle between structured support and genuine responsiveness.

It has been revealed that the foundation is Pwrrun foam, which delivers a cushioned but not marshmallow-soft ride. It’s lively enough to handle tempo work without feeling like you’re fighting the shoe, and cushioned enough that you’re not destroyed after 18 miles. The medial TPU guidance frame offers mild overpronation correction without the brick-like rigidity you get from old-school posts. It’s more a gentle steer rather than having the shoe take the reins and navigate your feet for you.

For long runs, the 8 mm drop and 32 mm stack height in the heel keep things comfortable for time-on-feet without creating that spongy instability that kills your form late in a run. For daily training, it’s durable and consistent and a shoe you can lace up without thinking too hard about what’s on your schedule.

Industry observers note that and it’s just plain comfortable. At least according to our wear-tester Dave Block, who “can’t remember a shoe that’s felt this great.” And even for tempo days on the track, the fit on this shoe just gets it right. It fits snugly enough that at faster paces it doesn’t feel sloppy.It won’t replace a racing flat, but for runners who want one shoe that handles most of their weekly mileage without drama, the Guide 19 makes a strong case.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com |Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

Industry observers note that what separates the Hoka Rocket X 3 from other super shoes is its broader base and accommodating fit. The shoe has a winged carbon plate to help with propulsion and a dual-density PEBA midsole to provide high energy return and supportive cushioning. An important update: a sticky rubber outsole to prevent slipping and sliding when the race forecast predicts rain or snow.

Recent findings suggest that “These shoes were very stable, which is different for a racing shoe,” states tester Shane Houghton, an overpronator. “Most super shoes feel kind wobbly but I felt lower to the ground and never felt in danger of rolling an ankle. When I stand in the shoes I feel flat on my feet and I don’t feel any lateral-rocking. I had no anxiety wearing these during loopy intervals or running around curves. The lacing is tight and like the texture of the ribbed laces. It keeps them from coming undone or loosening while running.”.

In a recent development, sometimes, shoes that are very much stabilizing or stability-adjacent shirk that term for optics. I can’t prove it, but I believe the Nike ACG Zegamas fit that description.

In a recent development, I’ve spent months running in these, and as someone who pronates frequently, I can tell you they deliver the structure and support of a true stability shoe wrapped in the rugged outsole of a trail runner. It comes down to that revised last. The Zegama cups the outer rim of your foot so thoroughly that it holds you locked in place, correcting the roll before it starts.

The support straps built into the upper wrap all the way around your foot, the padded tongue and lacing lock your midfoot down, and the heel keeps you planted without any slip. It doesn’t feel neutral, but it doesn’t steer you, either. Instead, it almost feels like it’s anticipatory rather than corrective.

Pair that underfoot security with a grippy Vibram outsole and aggressive lugs that bite into mud and wet rock, and you get the best of both worlds—the stable, planted feel of a stability shoe with the traction to handle whatever the trail throws at you.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

With any piece of running equipment, comfort should be your foremost deciding factor. Here are a few thing to consider before your next shoe fitting:.

1) The shoe should have enough room for your toes to splay in the toebox, about a thumbnail’s width from the front of the shoe to the tip of your longest toe.

Sources indicate that 2) The shoe shouldn’t feel too tight or loose around the midfoot area. There are lacing techniques to help modify your shoe’s width, but you should also consider different widths instead of the standard D (men) or B (women) width.

It has been revealed that 3) A secure heel is also paramount, as slippage can cause blisters. The heel-lock lacing method—threading each lace in the etra eyelet next to it to create a loop, then crisscrossing the opposite laces through the loop to create a “lock”—can give you a more secure fit.

4) Give the shoes a run at the store or check website’s return/exchange policies. Besides trying on the shoe, the best way to know if it’s comfy is if you run in it, too.

Some runners want maximum cushioning underfoot while others want less padding to experience more ground feel. Latest foam technology has given us the best of both worlds with plush, high-stacked cushioning that’s lightweight, too. Because of these high stack heights, stability tech is added to help runners run course tangents—and not twist their ankles while doing so.

Still, shoes with thicker cushioning and a high stack (36mm or more) tend to be squishier, making them less stable. Shoes with lower stack heights (32mm or less in the heel) provide a closer-to-the-ground feel and better feedback.

It has been revealed that you don’t have to give up max-cushioning if you’re an overpronator, however. Besides looking for shoes with built-in stability features, like guide rails and stability planes, consider shoes with wide, exaggerated soles, particularly under the heel, and a wider midfoot. Raised sidewalls (the interior padded sides of the shoe) create a snugger fit that will also enhance support, ensuring optimal stability and comfort.

Besides looking for shoes with stability features, you should also consider the type of workouts you’ll be performing in these shoes.

Recent findings suggest that for speedwork, like tempos and track workouts, lightweight trainers (less than 9 ounces for men or 8 ounces for women) with a curved “rocker” midsole help you surge forward. For everyday runs and longer runs, slightly heavier shoes with more padding provide the comfort and durability that you want on a daily training run. Or if you’re interested in venturing off-road, it’s key to have a trail shoe made for rough, undulating terrain.

Do I actually need a stability shoe?

It has been revealed that stability shoes are specifically designed for overpronation, a type of gait pattern when your foot rolls too far inward upon landing. Flat-foot, low arch runners can also benefit from this extra padding in shoes.

In a recent development, not every flat-foot runner or overpronator may need the extra support, however, especially if their feet only have a slight roll. We strongly advise having your gait evaluated by a professional, such as a podiatrist, physical therapist, or movement specialist. They can confirm if you need motion-specific shoes or an orthotic insert.

The best stability shoes focus on enhancing comfort and promoting a natural gait rather than imposing a harsh, corrective feel. While extra padding may sound like a plus, it can be too prescriptive for some runners. Worst-case scenario: Overcorrecting a neutral stride could increase your chance of injury, rather than make you more comfortable.

If you’re a fresh runner unsure of your gait pattern, we recommend running in a neutral shoe, like the Hoka Clifton 11s, first.

When should neutral runners consider wearing a stability shoe?

Some shoes with stability tech lend support to late-onset overpronators, i.e., neutral runners whose form becomes erratic midrun due to fatigue. Brands like Brooks and Altra, for instance, use denser foam on the medial and lateral sides of the midsole to help control excessive movement and promote knee and foot alignment, resulting in a more efficient stride.

Is there an adjustment to running in stability shoes?

Industry observers note that as with any running shoe transition, like trying zero-drop trainers for the first time, you’ll want to gradually make the switch if you usually wear neutral shoes. Start with shorter runs and then slowly ramp up mileage or runtime as your body adjusts to the new shoes. Read your body for cues; if you feel some discomfort you may need a slower process before fully committing to stability shoes. Muscle fatigue and pain can also be non-shoe-related and be attributed to overuse. If this is not the concern and it is the shoes, discontinue running in them and talk to a specialist for further evaluation.

Do stability shoes “fix” overpronation?

According to recent reports, no. Instead, they support your existing gait pattern. Your shoes can make you feel more comfortable and stable, but it doesn’t change that pattern.

According to recent reports, in the words of Test Editor Morgan Petruny: “Keep in mind that a stability shoe is not a cure-all or magic pill. Rather, it is a tool.”.

According to recent reports, overpronation can be due to various factors, including biomechanics, muscle strength, and flexibility, so stability shoes are just one component of a comprehensive approach to managing its negative effects. Strengthening exercises, gait analysis, and proper running form can also play important roles in that effort.

(Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete).

It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.

Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the plan is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.

We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day strategy complete with sets and reps.

Day one covered the lower body and core: squats or goblet squats, Romanian deadlifts, reverse lunges, standing calf raises, dead bugs, and side planks.

Day two went after the upper body and posterior chain: dumbbell bench press or push-ups, rows, lat pulldowns or assisted pull-ups, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, glute bridges or hip thrusts, and Pallof presses. The prescription included three sets of 8-10 reps, for 40 to 50 minutes per session, to be followed for 8-12 weeks.

It all looked perfectly sensible and not too dissimilar to what many triathletes do in most strength workouts. But for a triathlete who’s already squeezing three sports into one week, strength workouts should really be periodized and designed to augment what’s happening in the triathlete’s sport-specific training life (and the off-season is the one time of year when it’s great to do more in the gym, not less).

So with this in mind, we handed the plan to strength coach Sam Hengehold, who works with triathletes of all ages and abilities at Kinesis Integrated Performance in Boulder, Colorado. “I’d argue it is not right, but it’s also not wrong,” she says. “The plan is general, but it is not beneficial.”.

Here’s the surprise: Hengehold wouldn’t strike a single exercise from the list.

“All exercises listed are actually great and could very well be integrated into a triathlete strength routine,” she says. “The limiter here is the lack of periodization and volume/load variables.”.

Two of ChatGPT’s picks earn special praise:.

In a recent development, calf raises: “Many triathletes miss this integral exercise in their strength routine,” Hengehold says. “Lower leg injuries are extremely common with triathletes.” As a general rule, Hengehold wants athletes working toward calf raises at 1.5 times their body weight to build resiliency against injury in the calf, ankle, and foot.

Sources indicate that glute bridges: “A safe way to build power for beginners in strength training,” Hengehold notes. They mostly train the glutes and core, the muscle groups that underpin all three disciplines.

Recent findings suggest that so if the exercises are fine, where does the wasted time come in? It’s in how the proposal asks you to do them.

To its credit, ChatGPT suggests lifting less often as race day approaches and adding a little load once the sets feel solid. But the exercises, sets, and reps never change. Your swim, bike, and run training is built in cycles around your races, and Hengehold advises that your lifting should be too.

In the off-season, strength work can take priority and endurance training becomes the base. In race season, that flips: Lifting is there to support your swim, bike, and run, and to keep your body resilient. A blueprint that looks identical in January and July does neither job well.

“Over time, it will just be an energy suck of a session, causing more fatigue in the athlete with minimal benefit,” Hengehold warns.

ChatGPT’s warm-up gets one line: 5-10 minutes of easy cardio, mobility, and lighter practice sets. Hengehold wants something more deliberate, with activation work chosen to prepare you for the main lift of the day.

Sources indicate that “Warm-up and activation encourages proper form and oils the muscles,” Hengehold states. “Typically, that would include some sort of dynamic stretching, mobility, or preparation exercise that will aid in the main lift goals of the session. Before squats, for example, that might mean 90/90 hip rotations for hip mobility and banded clamshells to wake up the gluteus medius.” This matters if you want to avoid injury and get the most from every rep.

Recent findings suggest that the substantial, complex lifts belong at the start of the session, when you’re fresh and can control your form. They also work better when paired with an athletic movement, Hengehold notes, so the brain learns what the strength is for.

It has been revealed that follow loaded squats with box jumps, for instance, and you reinforce the power you need at toe-off on the run or when pushing watts on the bike. ChatGPT’s plan has no jumps and no explosive work at all.

Industry observers note that “Neuromuscular understanding and adaptation is absolutely necessary for triathletes to maximize the benefit of strength training,” Hengehold says. Without it, you get some injury prevention and extra muscle mass, but not much else.

Hengehold named three categories of strength work that matter most for triathletes:.

Recent findings suggest that core work: Think isometric holds and slow, controlled movements, with deep breathing throughout, to work the transverse abdominal muscles. Hengehold’s picks: planks with alternating shoulder taps, dead bugs, and bird dogs.

Unilateral movements: Single-leg Romanian deadlifts, Bulgarian split squats, front-foot elevated reverse lunges, and single-leg calf raises all make each side do its own share of the work. Swimming, biking, and running give a stronger side plenty of chances to cover for a weaker one, and these exercises help break those overcompensation patterns.

Squat variations: Isometric squats (holding the position) and eccentric squats (slowing the lowering phase) are a safe way to build resilience in the lower body and core. The squat is also endlessly adjustable, so it can be tweaked to target whatever you need most.

What you lift, and how, should depend on how far you are from your next race.

According to recent reports, far from race day: This is the time for heavy strength training alongside base swim, bike, and run work. Make complex lifts the centerpiece. Hengehold likes the trap bar deadlift. Get the form and technique down first, then spend a block (typically four to six weeks) building a base with high reps and low weight. Take a deload week, then switch to low reps and heavy weight to build real strength and durability.

In race season: Triathlon training takes over, and strength work drops to maintenance. Unilateral exercises move to the front, scheduled closely around your key sessions and races. Reps and load should go mostly on perceived effort and how you’re feeling, physically and emotionally. Hengehold also stresses mobility work, foam rolling, and stretching during this period.

Industry observers note that one last thing no chatbot can do is look at your form. If you’re upcoming to the weight room, Hengehold recommends having a gym friend or personal trainer check your technique early on: “Bad habits are hard to break and cause damage over time, and the same is true with your swimming, biking, and running.”.

Yet technique is only part of what a generic plan misses.

In a recent development, “Triathletes are some of the most hardworking individuals on the planet and managing training, fatigue, and recovery requires extreme attention to detail,” Hengehold states. “The time, energy, and hard work need to be maximized to be worth it, which means a generalized strength initiative will not meet the standard. Each athlete is a unique individual with individual needs that require an individualized plan.”.

None of this is an argument against strength training — far from it. Hengehold calls it “absolutely essential to longevity in sport and health” and recommends it for every athlete. The argument is against spending your limited time and energy on a blueprint that wasn’t written with you in mind.

15-Minute Evening Yoga to Unwind (That You Can Practice in Bed)

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This short evening yoga routine is designed to help you release stress when you’re ready to wind down for the evening or let go of the day.
  • According to recent reports, the stretches are essentially yin yoga poses, except we’re staying in the shapes for less time than the usual 3 to 5 minutes that we expect from yin yoga.
  • Because you’re trying to calm the body and mind, these stretches are not about chasing sensation or pushing yourself into an extreme shape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This short evening yoga routine is designed to help you release stress when you’re ready to wind down for the evening or let go of the day. It brings you a full-body stretch and a lot of relaxation. The poses are all either seated or lying down, so there’s very little effort required. You can even practice the yoga for better sleep routine in bed.

According to recent reports, the stretches are essentially yin yoga poses, except we’re staying in the shapes for less time than the usual 3 to 5 minutes that we expect from yin yoga. But these are all poses that you would find in a yin yoga class, so you could stay in any or all of the poses a little longer. The exact 15-minute sequence could be a 75-minute yin yoga class if you have the time or wake up in the middle of the night and are trying to go back to sleep.

Because you’re trying to calm the body and mind, these stretches are not about chasing sensation or pushing yourself into an extreme shape. Try to find a little more ease in each pose as you invite a slower, deeper rhythm to your breath, which signals your nervous system that it’s time to unwind and release. Every time you exhale, see if you can relax a different part of your body and let go of whatever is on your mind from your day.

Recent findings suggest that these stretches are suitable for any experience level. No props are required. Let yourself linger and release into each shape and stay there for 5 to 10 breaths.

Start sitting and then straighten your right leg in front of you. Option one, you can either do your Head to Knee Pose, which we call Half Butterfly in yin yoga, with your left foot to the inside of your thigh.

In a recent development, option two, you can stretch a little more through the hip and inner thigh if you take your left knee out to the side and your foot behind you with your heel tucked in toward your glutes. If you try option two and you experience any pain or sensitivity in the knee, come back to the first option.

Sources indicate that then start to walk your hands in front of in a forward bend. Let it be a passive stretch, which means you want to let your back round and your head hang. Let gravity do the work for you. Stay here for about 5 breaths or so. While you are in the pose, can you let go of any tension in your arms, jaw, and neck?

Press your hands against the mat and slowly lift yourself back up to sitting.

In a recent development, if it’s not already, bend your left knee out to the side so it’s in line with your left hip. You want to create about a 90-degree bend in your leg and bring your ankle in line with your knee. Then align your right knee so it’s also at a 90-degree angle.

Press your left hip back toward the wall behind you and start to walk your hands back on a diagonal behind you. As soon as you start to feel that sensation through your left hip, pause and breathe into it a little. You can stay propped up on your palms, lower onto your forearms, or lie all the way flat on your back. I’m going to stay propped up on my hands. I find I get the best stretch this way. Breathe here.

Walk your hands in, slowly lifting yourself upright.

Sources indicate that bring your left leg straight in front of you. Cross your left foot over your right thigh, bringing your left foot to the mat outside your right leg. Wrap your right arm around your left and bring your left fingertips to the mat behind you and let them support you. Lift tall through the spine, pressing your shoulders down and away from your ears, then twist toward the left in a Seated Twist. Press into your left substantial toe and keep both sit bones on the mat. Breathe here.

Then take your Head to Knee or Half Butterfly on the other side, followed by Deer Pose or 90/90 and Seated Twist.

In a recent development, lower all the way down onto your back. Pull your knees toward your chest. Then initiate a little pumping motion. So place your hands on the tops of your knees.

As you inhale, straighten your arms and push your thighs away.

As you exhale, draw your thighs back toward you. Try to relax your legs fully so your arms are controlling the motion. As you do this simple motion, you’re trying to release your lower back muscles as much as possible. You almost want to feel like your legs are moving in water. Take a few more like this.

In a recent development, the next time you bring your knees toward you, widen them toward your shoulders. Either hold here or come into Happy Baby by grabbing hold of your substantial toes with your two peace fingers, taking your elbows to the insides of your knees, and using your arms to push your legs open a little more. Think of pressing your lower back into the mat, keeping your head and shoulders down on the ground. Sometimes rocking a little side to side can feel really good.

From Happy Baby, keep your right knee close to your chest and extend your left leg straight on the mat to stretch the hip flexors along the front of your left hip. You can take a few ankle rolls with your right foot by making circles, flexing and pointing through your toes, and making any motion through the ankles. Reverse the direction of those circles.

Recent findings suggest that come into your twist from here, crossing your right leg over your body to the left with the help of your left hand. Stretch your right arm straight out to the side. Think of relaxing your right shoulder down and trying to stack your right hip on top of your left hip.

If you notice yourself obsessing over anything or going over and over a particular thought, just observe what’s happening. Notice that tendency in that pattern, and maybe instead focus on something else that’s a bit more tangible, like the physical sensations in your body from the poses or just the flow of your breath.

Come all the way back to center.

According to recent reports, straighten your right leg any amount, stretching the hamstrings. You can flex and point your foot a couple times.

Recent findings suggest that then come into Reclined Pigeon Pose by sliding your left foot in, crossing your right ankle over the top of your left knee in a figure-four shape, and reaching your arms along either side of your left leg as you pull your left thigh toward you. Only using a little arm strength. Try to relax your shoulders and keep your head on the  mat. Breathe here.

Keep your left knee drawn toward your chest as you release the pose and extend your right leg straight on the mat. Repeat your ankle rolls, Reclined Twist, and Reclined Pigeon on your left side.

Then you’ll set yourself up for Savasana, your final resting pose. Take up some space with your arms and your legs and then close your eyes. You might do a body scan, bringing your awareness to the crown of your head and slowly working your way down to your fingers and your toes, asking each muscle to relax, to let go, almost as if you could sink into the mat or mattress.

In a recent development, allow yourself about two minutes here or more if you have the time. Just enjoy the silence and stillness. If you’re already in bed, maybe you stay here.

It has been revealed that start to deepen your breath. Maybe you move your fingers and toes a little. Nice and slow, roll to one side and come to take a seat. Find some length in your spine as you release your shoulders down.

Just pause here. Notice how you feel after just a few minutes of stretching and silence.

It has been revealed that thank you so much, everyone, for doing this short bedtime practice. I hope you feel ready to ease into the rest of your night.

‘One of a Million’: She’s 3-Foot-9, Just Ran a 3:42 Marathon, and Is Chasing a Boston Qualifier

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

💡 Key Takeaways

  • During a marathon, Juli Windsor admits she doesn’t always get to take in the scenery.
  • “Most runners can see what's coming ahead, and they can see beyond the shoulders and all the heads,” she said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

During a marathon, Juli Windsor admits she doesn’t always get to take in the scenery.

“Most runners can see what's coming ahead, and they can see beyond the shoulders and all the heads,” she said. “For me, my view is hundreds of butts. It’s not the most inspirational view.”.

According to recent reports, it’s one difference that Windsor, who is 3-foot-9, has learned to navigate as a runner with dwarfism. But that hasn't stopped her from beating many of those butts in races.

At the Indianapolis Marathon on November 7, Windsor, 39, ran 3:42:00 to finish in the top third of her 35–39 age group, averaging an 8:28 mile pace. The time was a PR by seven minutes and is provisionally a newly introduced American record for the T40 para category (a division for athletes with short stature).

Industry observers note that windsor was born with an extremely rare form of dwarfism called acromesomelic dysplasia. “Last I heard, I’m one of a million,” said Windsor, who works as a physician assistant in developmental pediatrics.

According to recent reports, windsor’s run in Indianapolis is more impressive considering that this is part two of her marathoning career. After taking a decade off to raise her two kids in 2014, Windsor has come back even stronger, knocking off more than an hour from her pre-hiatus personal best.

It has been revealed that “I just think the human body is just such an amazing thing,” she remarked. “And that when asked something difficult of it, what you’re capable of doing can sometimes be really surprising.”.

As a middle schooler, Windsor joined the track team to hang out with her friends and went in with low expectations. But that changed when she beat another runner in an 800-meter race. It was motivating, and Windsor eventually realized that although she couldn’t dust her peers in a sprint, she had exceptional grit and endurance. “I might not be able to outrun them, but I could outlast them,” she remembers.

It has been revealed that in her twenties, Windsor set her sights on the marathon—and one marathon in particular. She wanted to become the first person with dwarfism to run the prestigious Boston Marathon. In 2013, her dream almost came true, but as she neared the finish line on Boylston Street, she was forced to stop. Terrorists had detonated bombs at the finish. Windsor was unharmed, but her dream would have to wait.

Recent findings suggest that the next year, Windsor became the first person with dwarfism to complete the historic race, running 4:43:26. That would be her last marathon for a decade, as Windsor raised two kids and focused on her family.

It has been revealed that in 2025, she felt pulled back to the distance. She signed up for the Spinx Marathon in Greenville, South Carolina, where she ran 4:09:51—more than 30 minutes faster than her personal best from Boston.

Recent findings suggest that not long after, Windsor started working with coach Esther Atkins, a former professional marathoner who coaches with McKirdy Trained. Atkins saw potential in Windsor and had a hunch she could run a lot faster. While unsure at first, Windsor was assuaged when she nabbed another massive personal best, running 3:49:42 at the 2026 Boston Marathon in April.

Recent findings suggest that atkins, who works with about 40 athletes, is impressed by how coachable Windsor is. “She’s always open to trying something different, and very eager to push the boundaries of what she has done before or what she has believed she was capable of,” Atkins mentioned.

“I’m not used to people expecting more of me than I expect of myself; usually it’s the other way around,” Windsor remarked. “And that’s how I know I have an exceptional coach. She sees the possibilities and isn’t stumped by my unique challenges.”.

Industry observers note that as a runner with dwarfism, Windsor is presented with obstacles that most runners don’t face. Her cadence, for example, is much higher than the average runner. While 180 steps per minute is a commonly cited target among runners, Windsor averaged 207 steps per minute at Indianapolis, and because her stride length is much shorter, she covers less ground per step. (For reference, Windsor is about the height of an average 6-year-old.).

It has been revealed that windsor also has to navigate crowds carefully—she doesn’t always show up in the peripheral vision of competitors. She generally runs on the right side of the road to improve her visibility and avoid getting tripped up or surprising people as she passes. At larger races, like Boston or Indy, she is able to start a few minutes ahead of the masses to let the race string out.

Recent findings suggest that and then there are shoes. Windsor wears a kids’ size 13, but it’s hard to find athletic shoes in her size that aren’t Velcro or light-up. She generally sizes up to a size 1 for running shoes and uses custom orthotics. But such small sizes don’t have the bells and whistles of normal running shoes. And super shoes that small don’t exist.

In a recent development, so far, Windsor has liked Asics the best. “I don’t think I fully appreciated the difference of having a good quality shoe until I tried [an Asics shoe] on,” she noted. “And even just having a gel cushion was like, ‘Is this how everybody else feels? This is what I've been missing out on.’”.

Windsor ran Indianapolis in the GT-2000, although they’re still a little pared down compared to a mass-market adult shoe. “I really wish there were better options and better technology, because I've had to just work with what my options are,” she said.

Until recently, Windsor wasn’t able to find a GPS watch that fit her wrists. Last summer, she discovered that Garmin made a 42mm watch, which finally allowed her to run without a phone and gave her insights like cadence and stride length. She partially credits the data for her recent improvement.

Looking ahead, Windsor has two goals. The first is to qualify for Boston in her age group. Windsor has already nabbed a BQ in the adaptive athlete field, but she’s targeting the able-bodied BQ. She turns 40 next spring, which will bump her to the 40–44 age group. She’ll need to run under 3:35:00—about 7 minutes faster than her personal best—to achieve the standard.

Sources indicate that her other goal is to create more opportunities for runners in her Paralympic category. At the moment, World ParaAthletics doesn’t sanction running events in the short stature division. USATF recently began to include the marathon in the T40 category, a record which Windsor owns. But the record book isn’t what drives her.

“It's less about competition, more about just setting some sort of a standard, and that records are meant to be broken …” she said. “I would love for to open up opportunities for people to at least be curious and give it a try.”.

In a recent development, next up for Windsor? The Tokyo Marathon on March 7—one week before her 40th birthday.

Theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. He’s a former all-conference collegiate runner at Winthrop University, and he received his master’s degree in liberal arts studies from Wake Forest University, where he was a member of one of the top distance-running teams in the NCAA. Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, New York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. (Look for colorful ovals around football fields.).

#114937. After 50 Years of Running, I’m Facing My Toughest Challenge: Having to Let Go of the Runner I Used to Be

After 50 Years of Running, I’m Facing My Toughest Challenge: Having to Let Go of the Runner I Used to Be

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Some runs are shouts, and some runs are whispers,” I wrote a few decades back in Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running, an attempt to capture the many moods—the many functions—that running served in my life.
  • Sources indicate that I chuckled a little upon seeing it.
  • In a recent development, this upcoming reality that came with illness and settled in for the long haul wasn’t easy to accept.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Some runs are shouts, and some runs are whispers,” I wrote a few decades back in Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running, an attempt to capture the many moods—the many functions—that running served in my life. I scrolled past the phrase recently on social media: Somebody had designed it with colors and typography and posted it, apparently finding resonance in the sentiment.

Sources indicate that I chuckled a little upon seeing it. If I wrote that today, I’d add something else: “Some runs are walks.”.

In a recent development, this upcoming reality that came with illness and settled in for the long haul wasn’t easy to accept. I’ve been running on and off for more than 50 years, some 85 percent of my life. I jogged along with my older brother when I was a girl, competed in high school as a teen, trained for a sub-3 marathon as a working professional in my 30s, plodded with a baby jogger in my 40s. Now, past 60, running has shape-shifted again. The transformation is different this time, the lessons deeper and, frankly, a little harder to grasp. But after a period of struggle, I’ve made peace with it. Because as usual, if you dare to listen, running will speak to you.

Most of us who run spend years or even decades seeking to improve, from a 5K to 10K, from breaking 4 hours in a marathon to then trying for 3:45. For a long time, wherever you are, improvement is possible, and change generally trends in one direction. Not every run, of course. The body has good days and challenging ones; that variability is a given, and progress is not a straight line. But we can expect a trajectory that provides a satisfactory feedback loop, one of betterment.

Inevitably, aging will bend the line of progression into an arc. We can know that and still have trouble seeing it at first, because the heavy legs or knee catching feels like just another hard day. Nothing a little rest or cross-training can’t solve.

Recent findings suggest that if seeing it is difficult, accepting it can be even harder. The forward march has been the natural state of things for so long. The battle waged for incremental increases in mileage or decreases in time was never easy. Shouldn’t I be pushing past this? Isn’t it what runners do?

Running taught me to be tough. For years, that served me even beyond the sport. In work, the tug of fatigue from long nights at the ad agency felt familiar and manageable as a long run. Giving birth called back the discipline of breathing through pain; the years of motherhood to come called in the lessons of patience, of quietly putting in the hours without immediate affirmation or result. I loved being a badass in the endurance sport of life. The ability to override tiredness felt powerful. I enjoyed telling myself I was fine when evidence pointed to the contrary. I relished pushing against edges and limits.

According to recent reports, until the day I woke, swung my feet over the side of the bed to stand, and felt the world spin wildly out of control. The floor rushed up to my face, and I curled in a ball seeking safety and stillness. Confusion mingled with nausea. I could feel the whirling even with eyes closed. The fetal position proved fitting. I’d spend years relearning how to be in this upcoming world, where vertigo could strike at any time.

My first reaction was “I’ll fight!” Though for months that thought came while I was sprawled on the couch, unable to focus my eyes or lift my arms. A year of doctor visits, scans, and tests eventually ruled out physical problems and delivered a neurological diagnosis: vestibular migraine. As with other forms of migraine, the condition is underdiagnosed, women suffer more than men, and precious little is understood about what is actually happening in the brain to produce the symptoms. Some connection has been made to hormonal fluctuations, and, for some, a genetic link seems to exist; stress, I learned, is a reliable exacerbator of triggers.

My own onset remains a mystery.

The impulse to fight landed ineffectually in space against the judo of forced rest. Any struggle against this opponent would only feed it. Somewhere along the way, a newly introduced understanding dawned: Vertigo was my body saying, “Stop.”.

Tough got me here, but it wasn’t going to get me through this next chapter. The fighting stance I’d adopted so long ago was not going to serve me well with the changes happening now. Some things about the body are not in our control, despite our best efforts. With precious few alternatives, I did something I never had before: I paused, I listened to what my body was saying, and I opened to the possibility of unlearning some things that running and life had drilled into me so very long ago. This time the lesson wasn’t about pushing through. It’s also not a sob story about slowing down. It is about acceptance.

According to recent reports, now, three years since my first vertigo attack, something akin to gratitude has set in. The softening and adapting are treasured new tools. Essential new tools. Because the fact is: you don’t “overcome” aging.

Nowadays, when I’m feeling good enough to put on my shorts and running shoes, I might have an idea of what I’d like to do. But it’s just that, an idea. I start slowly, so as not to tweak a knee or an ankle. Eventually, my body will tell me what this day has in store. If I’m lightheaded and the sun feels too bright, triggering aural distortion, I walk and think, yes, it is a fine day for a walk. If I feel strong, I push to the degree I can and think, how wonderful, to feel good. Neither situation really surprises me anymore. None of it is bad. I feel lucky to be out here.

It has been revealed that the point is this: It is all like this now. And if I can’t accept that in my running, I’m going to be in for an exhausting battle with every other part of aging. Don’t mistake this for giving up. I am working harder to stay fit than I have in a very long time. Pushing the pace all those years? It came pretty easy. It felt damned good. What I’m doing now takes more effort: Spin classes that give my knees a break... and where 80-year-olds are dusting me. Full-body lifting that leaves every hidden muscle protesting. Yoga classes that make it clear balance has never been a prerequisite for anything before in my life. The objective now isn’t performance—it’s simply to age as well as possible.

In a recent development, there is no fairness in this, no way that this “should” go. Aging comes differently for us all, as an entire generation who grew up during the first running boom is now learning. Our running will change in its own way, a reflection of everything we have done before, plus the ineffable element of luck.

My son-in-law’s mother is one of those seemingly defying the years. Pushing 60, she’s also pushing into upcoming territory with a string of 50K trail races. Her streak of runs is proudly documented on Strava, which cheerily alerts me every time she becomes the “Local Legend” of some new stretch.

She’s excited, posting every day, a wide smile spread across her face. She exudes the joy of progress. I’m a bit envious, sure. I’m also glad for her. Both things can be true.

Recent findings suggest that I have other friends who do not run anymore. In one way or another, their bodies—joints that didn’t respond to surgery, chronic illness that has sapped their energy—have let them know those days are done. The ones doing the best move on, find newly introduced challenges.

It has been revealed that my joy comes from somewhere else now. It’s not so much the running per se; rather, everything around it. The feeling of autumn’s first cool air on my shoulders. The smell of spring’s thawing mud. The sheer pleasure of moving through space outdoors one more day. In fact, these things are more present than before, without the distraction of pace and goals.

In a recent development, if my running taught me everything about how to persist, why wouldn’t it be the thing to teach me about how to let go? Our running is always “becoming.” Just as we are ourselves. We have an opportunity to learn from it, because the fact is that running isn’t the only thing that is changing.

As with everything else, it might not be the lesson you want, but it’s always the lesson you need.

According to recent reports, dagny Scott is the author of Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running. She is currently working on a book that explores the beauty in finding authenticity and acceptance in an aging body. Scott lives, writes, runs, and walks in Boulder, Colorado.

#114935. Are Your Recovery Runs Too Long? Experts Explain the Line Between Productive Recovery and Added Fatigue

Are Your Recovery Runs Too Long? Experts Explain the Line Between Productive Recovery and Added Fatigue

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that getting faster isn’t just about training harder.
  • While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that getting faster isn’t just about training harder. It also requires smarter recovery.

While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.

Big picture, recovery runs should help you stay consistent between harder sessions; they shouldn’t leave you carrying extra fatigue into your next workout. However, simply running at an easy pace doesn’t guarantee an easy training load because the longer you run, the more energy you use and the more repetitive impact you take on.

So how long should your recovery runs last to maintain the volume-building, bloodflow-boosting benefits? And what signs mean it’s time to cut the run short?

We asked run coaches and exercise physiologists to explain how to find the right recovery run duration to ensure you’re not dragging for your next workout and when calling it a (rest) day might work best.

It has been revealed that recovery runs allow runners to increase their overall aerobic training volume without taking a complete rest day after every hard session, says run coach, author, and founder of 80/20 Endurance, Matt Fitzgerald. For instance, if the sole objective were to recover from quality runs as quickly as possible, total rest (a.k.a. not running at all) is more effective.

But receiving the benefits of recovery runs without elevating fatigue or injury risk depends on keeping duration within a certain range.

“As a run extends, we’re also continuing to consume energy and introduce mechanical load,” explains Pamela Geisel, CSCS, RRCA-certified run coach, exercise physiologist, and director of Performance and Wellness Services at the Hospital for Special Surgery in Upcoming York City. In other words, your muscles are still contracting, your body is still using fuel, and your bones, tendons, and joints are absorbing the repetitive impact of every stride.

If you extend a recovery run too long, the stress caused by this additional workload begins to outweigh the aerobic benefits of the run and can lead to the aforementioned heightened fatigue and injury risk, especially if you’re recovering from a particularly demanding training session.

Sources indicate that this logic is exactly why experts all agree that recovery runs absolutely can go on for too long. The tricky part is finding the line.

“There’s no established duration or mileage at which an easy run becomes detrimental to recovery,” says Michael Landram, an exercise physiologist and assistant professor at the University of Scranton.

Instead, each person’s ideal duration depends on a variety of factors, including training history, current fatigue, nutrition, sleep, and the demands of any upcoming workouts, Landram explains.

Here’s a three-step checklist for making sure yours fall in the right range.

Usually, Geisel recommends keeping recovery runs between 20 and 40 minutes in length, but that window should shift depending on how much you’re accustomed to running.

In a recent development, for example, if you’re averaging around 20 miles per week, Geisel suggests aiming for approximately 15 to 25 minutes. If you’re regularly logging up to 60 miles per week, you can pencil in 25- to 45-minute recovery sessions.

Recent findings suggest that and remember, these recommendations are starting points, not strict limits. Danny Mackey, head coach of the Brooks Beasts Track Club, says he might prescribe a recovery run of just 20 minutes for an 800-meter specialist, while long-distance runners accustomed to running 75 to 80 miles per week can comfortably handle a 60-minute recovery run.

Additionally, it’s vital to take into consideration how long you’ve maintained your current weekly mileage.

Industry observers note that landram explains that a runner who’s consistently logged 50-mile weeks for several years may tolerate longer recovery runs than someone who’s only recently built up to that level. Even if both runners in this example have similar cardiovascular fitness, their muscles may not be equally adapted to the repetitive demands of 50-mile weeks.

So, if you’ve recently increased your weekly mileage, stick to shorter recovery runs and gradually extend their duration as your body adjusts.

If you’re relatively new to running, are only running a few days per week, or have only easy runs on your schedule as you build endurance and consistency, you may not need a dedicated recovery run at all. Rest days allow for proper rejuvenation between workouts.

Fitzgerald recommends using your typical easy-run duration as a reference point and making recovery runs shorter and slower (zone 1, anyone?). If your scheduled easy runs are usually 60 minutes long, for instance, a recovery run—particularly one scheduled after hard, quality workouts—might last 40 minutes or less, at an even lower intensity.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve just completed a particularly demanding interval session, long run, or race, consider keeping your recovery run at the shorter end of your usual range. The same applies if you have another hard workout scheduled within the next 24 to 48 hours.

Heat, hills, and uneven terrain can also make an otherwise easy session more taxing, so it’s worth considering an even shorter duration in those circumstances.

Overall, your recovery-run duration should reflect what your body is accustomed to handling, rather than a mileage target you’re trying to reach.

Even if you’ve planned your recovery run carefully, it’s crucial to pay attention to how your body responds once you start moving.

One of the first warning signs is a change in perceived exertion. If your usual recovery pace suddenly feels harder than it should or your legs feel unusually heavy, you may need to reconsider how long you’re running.

Geisel also recommends paying attention to changes in your stride, including heavier foot strikes and other form issues getting worse as the run progresses.

In a recent development, the metrics available on your watch can also indicate a recovery run has gone too long. For example, an unusually elevated heart rate at your normal easy pace may signal you’re carrying too much fatigue, Landram explains. Though remember heat, dehydration, sleep, and stress can also affect heart rate, so pair it with how you feel to determine if you’re going too long.

If you’re feeling unusually tired during a recovery run, Shannon Hugard, a biomechanics researcher at the University of Oregon, recommends a simple midrun check-in. “If you’re feeling more fatigued or sore than usual, run that first mile,” she advises. “See how you’re feeling. If you’re still sore or fatigued, cut that easy run duration by about 25 to 50 percent.” If you’re experiencing pain that affects your stride, however, it’s better to stop immediately rather than push through.

It’s also worth paying attention to how you feel after your recovery run.

Industry observers note that for Mackey, the biggest giveaway that an athlete isn’t recovering adequately is often what happens during their next hard workout. “If they’re struggling to hit their usual paces, feeling unusually fatigued, or showing a noticeable drop in motivation, I know it’s time to reassess their recovery sessions,” he says.

In a recent development, if these warning signs persist, the best option might just be skipping your next recovery run altogether. A rest day, walk, or low-impact cross-training session can give your body a break from the repetitive loading of running, particularly when you’re dealing with lingering fatigue.

And if you think cutting a run short feels like a missed training opportunity, take a cue from the pros: “This is one of the biggest differences I see in elite runners,” claims Fitzgerald. “They take pride in their restraint and ability to hold back, because they know it’s part of a more intentional plan.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that glute bridge post-run.
  • For this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a new study on anti-movement vs.
  • “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).

For this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a new study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

“Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.).

Industry observers note that when we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

Why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly notable for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

When running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

It has been revealed that while running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

According to recent reports, while some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Industry observers note that even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

Sources indicate that enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an key role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

In a recent development, runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global).

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes.

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles.

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators.

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

There are breakthroughs, large and small, awaiting you on the full Moon in Gemini. Insights that have the power to change everything can arrive in an instant. A sentence you have repeated to yourself for years might suddenly sound false. A thought that once felt like a fact might reveal itself as a fear. You might hear yourself say something about your life and realize, in the middle of saying it, that you no longer believe it. It’s a powerful supermoon, one designed to help you release what no longer belongs to you.

The Moon reaches its fullest light on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, at 6:54 am PT.

According to recent reports, gemini is the sign of the twins, ruled by the planet Mercury and the element of air. It moves quickly, influencing our intellect and communication and touching our minds, our nervous systems, our voices, and the way we take in and share information. Gemini is the part of us that asks questions, makes connections, strikes up a conversation with a stranger, and wants to know a little about everything. It is curiosity in motion.

The twins also represent duality. Gemini reminds us that we are complex, that we can hold two feelings at once, and that life is rarely black or white. There are shades of gray everywhere, and within that uncertainty exists endless possibility.

Gemini is the voice in your head that narrates your day. It names what is happening to you, decides what it means, and tells you what to expect next. This voice speaks to you more than any other person in your life. It is there when you wake up and when you fall asleep. It comments on your work, your relationships, and your decisions. It is the stories you live by. Most of the time, you do not even notice it is speaking. It feels less like a voice and more like the truth.

Recent findings suggest that but it is a voice. And a voice can change.

It has been revealed that think about where your inner voice came from. Some of it is yours, formed through your own experience and your own knowing. Some of it was inherited. A parent’s worry. A teacher’s doubt. A sentence someone said to you once, at the wrong moment, that you have been repeating to yourself ever since. Some of it came from society, from every message that told you who you were supposed to be and how much you were allowed to want. Over the years, all of these voices blended into one, and you started to call it you.

The words you use about yourself become the life you live. If your inner voice tells you something is not possible, you stop reaching for it. You do not apply, you do not ask, you do not try, and the life that follows proves the voice right. But when the voice changes, the reaching changes. And when the reaching changes, the life changes. A latest inner voice is how you begin to believe what is possible.

In a recent development, there is science behind this. Research on moments of insight, those sudden aha experiences, reveals that they tend to arrive when we’re in a less-anxious state of mind rather than straining for an answer. The brain makes surprising connections when we stop gripping the problem. This full Moon asks you to slow down, breathe, and loosen your hold on the old voice before reaching for the new one. The breakthrough comes more easily when you make space for it.

Gemini is also one of the most social signs of the zodiac, and that is part of the medicine. Sometimes the new voice arrives through someone else. A friend reflects you back to yourself in a way you never considered. A stranger claims the exact sentence you needed. A line in a book or a song lands differently than it ever has before. Be open to these messages. Stay curious. Talk to people. Listen more than usual. The universe often delivers our breakthroughs through the voices of others.

On the full Moon in Gemini, let yourself be curious about your own mind. Listen to the voice in your head as if you were hearing it for the first time. Notice what it states. Notice whose voice it sounds like. And then notice the quieter voice underneath, the one that has always believed in you. That is the voice that is ready to rise.

#114932. Research Highlights This Is the Best Way to Balance Strength Training and Running
