#114925. Tech Report: Triathlon as the Latest Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2963 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Triathlon as the Latest Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities.
  • According to recent reports, what do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon?
  • From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities. (Photo: Courtesy Alexa and Branden Scheel, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson, Hannah Bradbury, Hilary Topper, and Kyla Lupo).

According to recent reports, what do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon? You could throw up your hands in defeat and frustration over the bro culture and inclusion challenges, vowing to train in solitude like a spandex-clad, multisport monk. Or … you could start your own tri club, team, group ride, or clinic.

From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.

When Altitude Multisport Club, a tri club in Denver, Colorado, was founded in 2010, the board consisted of all men.

Industry observers note that “While friendly, it had a very ‘bro’ vibe and club events were rarely organized by leadership and club meetings were salesy,” says Erin Trail, Altitude Multisport Club’s former president and current volunteer. “What did it for me was a no-drop group ride that the current president and coaching director were on. I had done three Ironman races, and they dropped ME. I knew the route and was fine, but I thought: ‘What if I was a fresh person? What kind of experience would this be?’”.

Since the president was term-limited, Trail was able to step up as president in 2016 to change the atmosphere to a friendlier, more inclusive one.

“That first year was very hard. I decided to make the club more inclusive and friendly to beginners and women, eliminating sales or conflict of interest problems and improving communications,” Trail indicates. “I lost a LOT of club friends because I wanted to make things different. Half my board quit because they didn’t want to be held accountable. But in my first year as president, membership grew from 50 to 150 members!”.

Today, Altitude Multisport Club features winter Sunday pool swims with a coach and travel camps to Moab and a local state park in addition to regular training and racing activities.

“My second term as president was much better, with a diverse board that I handpicked. We added a family membership so households, including kids, could join at a group rate,” Trail notes. “And we made it clear that the environment is welcoming, organized, and a safe space to learn for everyone.”.

“A LOT of skinny white men. That’s what I saw in triathlon. I didn’t see enough women, and I really didn’t see anyone who was bigger. I realized that if I wanted to see more folks that looked like me, I had to be the coach that made triathlon a place for all folks, regardless of size, shape, color, or anything else,” claims Kyla Lupo, who took things into her own hands, getting certified as a coach, learning everything she could, and starting her team, Go Major!, with just one athlete and “a bunch of friends pretending to be my team.” Since then, Go Big! has grown to 22 athletes.

“Our team makes a point to let folks know that they are already loved, exactly as they are. Team Go Big! stands for a radical level of body inclusivity, both in sport and the world,” Kyla notes. “On Team Go Big!, we work to overcome our fear and doubts while getting fit and ready for the start line. Anyone can tri in the body they have right now.”.

Social connection is crucial to the Go Big! community and takes the form of weekly team meetings where members from around the country learn, share their goals, ask for support, and expect accountability.

“We are from all over the country, but there’s a Tuesday morning virtual trainer ride to further connect us. And of course we get to party together at races,” Lupo states.

Disruptors: Alexa and Branden Scheel.

People often join tri clubs to find community, only to discover that they are a small fish in a big sea. When you’re one of hundreds of athletes, you and your journey can get lost in the mix.

Industry observers note that “My husband, Branden, and I were part of two different teams like that. We felt like ‘just another membership,’” Alexa Scheel says.

So she and Branden pursued certifications from USA Triathlon and began building the kind of team they actually wanted to be part of. In 2023, the Scheels debuted Branden Scheel Racing, which focuses on athlete relationships and connection. Despite being a team with athletes around the world, the Scheels strive to make their team feel like family and make each athlete feel seen.

According to recent reports, “If we don’t personally know something about each of the team members, we’ve grown too significant, which is why we sit between 100 to 150 members. We are committed to keeping this team on the smaller side,” Scheel indicates. The beating heart of the team is its Facebook group, where athletes connect through monthly games and seminars, get answers to their most pressing questions, and find encouragement.

In a recent development, “On our team, every athlete stays until the last athlete completes their event because EVERYONE deserves to have someone cheering them on at the finish line. We’ve even had 15 people stay at the finish line for the midnight finish of Ironman Arizona for one of our athletes,” Scheel states. “Having a tri family on and off course to cheer for you and celebrate one of the best days of your life is a huge part of our team culture.”.

Disruptors: Jaclyn Fahey, Tara Hofmayer, and Sami Saad.

In a recent development, fifteen years ago, Jaclyn Fahey started a tri team through a bike store. As it evolved, Fahey recognized the need for a more affordable Long Island-based team, and Landshark Endurance was born.

“It began as a pizza-and-beer team with a triathlon problem, but Tara and Sami have helped take the lead. Because both are speech therapists and have the gift of gab, they’ve attracted a lot more members,” Fahey states. The open-level, co-ed multisport team supports members of all backgrounds with educational clinics and workshops, group workouts, and of course, social events that revolve around pizza and beer.

“By sharing our passion and experiences, we hope to show young athletes that success isn’t always measured by winning, but by perseverance, sportsmanship, and the courage to try,” Fahey notes. “You don’t have to be the fastest or the strongest. You just have to show up for yourself, put in the effort, and enjoy the journey. At the end of the day, the greatest part isn’t always crossing the finish line – it’s the people who help you get there.”.

“I’m non-binary, and when I visit online triathlon groups and ask if there are any fellow non-binary athletes, it’s not uncommon that transphobes will flood the comments. I can only speak for myself, but the fear of discrimination, or being attacked verbally or worse, can be the most intimidating thing for non-binary and trans triathletes about tri clubs,” indicates Ruth Carter, a lawyer and triathlete. “There’s so much misinformation out there about trans women and non-binary athletes, as well as assumptions that are not supported by research.”.

When Carter couldn’t find a triclub that promoted equal participation and respect, they created Mutants & Masochists, a tri club that believes in equal participation, recognition, and respect for all triathletes, and advocates for non-binary and trans triathletes.

“We’re just getting started, but I hope the club is a place where trans people can connect, both online and in real life,” Carter says.

In 2023, Hannah Bradbury was training to break an open-water swim record when she was rushed to the ER for an emergency surgery to remove her gallbladder.

It has been revealed that “My first thought when I woke up was, ‘When can I get back in the water?’ The answer was six weeks at least,” notes Bradbury, who had already lost half of her thyroid to cancer in 2017. In an attempt to be part of sport in a way that cancer or a freak surgery couldn’t disrupt, Bradbury created Chicago’s North Avenue Swim and Triathlon Yo (NASTY) Instagram account to post about swimming until she could get back in the water. She also debuted book clubs and threw happy hours to create space for people to be more than just athletes, from cancer survivors to diabetic athletes striving to stay in sport on their own terms.

“Tri and swim clubs are great at training people. They’re not always great at holding onto people when they’re injured, sick, slow, starting over, or just burned out. I wanted to build a club that could hold everyone, from those winning the Chicago Triathlon to anyone rebuilding from injuries, or battling setbacks and the identity crises nobody warns you about when you’re sidelined,” claims Bradbury, who faced another cancer scare in 2023. “While I waited on the biopsy, my friends kept me distracted by doing a 100-mile ride with me, covered in glitter, that we called the ride Centuslay.”.

Fortunately, the biopsy came back negative, and the women’s century became an official NASTY tradition every fall.

In a recent development, “Before NASTY I had a hard time making real friends with people who don’t just ask, ‘How was your swim?’ Through NASTY, I met friends who ask how they can show up for me,” Bradbury says. “NASTY has grown to over 340 members, and through this community, people have found jobs through a swim or a random happy hour, and even fallen in love. Sport has become an accessory to our friendships, not the glue.”.

According to recent reports, “When I first got into triathlon in 2010, I was fortunate to have a warm, welcoming entry point into the sport. My goal with the T2 community is to pay it forward so others can also ease into the sport, learn to love it, and stay connected for the long haul,” claims Bryan Mewes, who opened T2 Triathlon & Cycling, a triathlon-focused bike shop in Long Beach, California, in 2023. “The biggest hurdle for beginners is usually being overwhelmed by gear. That and the open-water swim. Once they realize that the shop is a space where they can comfortably ask questions and our group is built on encouragement rather than competition, that anxiety disappears fast.”.

Mewes explains that while it’s easy to say “everyone is welcome,” making sure someone is paired up with a partner at their pace or ensuring no one gets left behind takes actual effort that T2’s committed to making. Beyond the group rides, weekly runs, and bay swims, T2 brings people together off the course and keeps the vibe low-key and welcoming by hosting family dinners at local restaurants, beach days after races, and even a movie club.

In a recent development, “Some people only do our social events, while others only join our rides. What matters is that they participate in their way and see themselves as part of the community. That’s the core of T2. Training is just the anchor,” Mewes indicates.

Disruptors: Ruth Marie Oliver and Team Rocket’s Race Directors and Officers.

Team Rocket Tri Club (TRTC) is on a mission to promote a fit and healthy lifestyle. Every month, the club organizes a themed, post-brick social, and throughout the year, it hosts various races, from a beginner-friendly pool swim to a duathlon and sprint triathlons.

Recent findings suggest that during the summer months, TRTC hosts Tuesday night bricks featuring a multitude of pace groups, ensuring no rider is left behind and everyone has buddies to ride with. And in the winter, the focus is on swim clinics and winter trail running.

“Our club president, Ruth Marie Oliver, has done amazing things, including growing our membership to over 300 people,” says Cynthia Mitchell, race director of TRTC’s Heel and Crank Duathlon.

Recent findings suggest that to up the fun factor, TRTC has its own well-traveled bike box that members can borrow, adding their own sticker to its travel history and essentially bringing the whole team along for that athlete’s adventure. There’s also a TRTC hat that is at the moment “on tour.” It’s been spotted everywhere from Leeds, Alabama, to the head of Bob Babbit in Kona during the Ironman World Championship this year.

Disruptors: Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson.

In 2019, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson relaunched TriBabes WI, a women’s-only, USAT-certified team, to provide a community for women of all abilities and ages to train together.

According to recent reports, “Some women join us purely to have the chance to work out with others for one, two, or all three sports. No matter what the sport or goal, we support each other without all the egos,” Merten notes. TriBabesWI makes aspects of triathlon like climbing hills, changing tires, nutrition, and making a race plan less daunting through the clinics it offers. For TriBabe’s annual team triathlon, athletes can ride with a buddy for the bike portion.

Recent findings suggest that team offerings aren’t limited to the swim-bike-run. There are team hikes, skiing and snowshoeing in the winter, and opportunities to volunteer and shake a cowbell for others.

“We’ve donated our time and efforts to Breakthrough T1D, USAT triathlon events in Milwaukee, Ironman Wisconsin, and naturally Girls on the Run,” Merten indicates.

“When I was new to this sport, I went for a bike ride with a triathlon group and got dropped within moments,” says Topper, an author and coach who started WeREndurance in 2017. “If you’re just starting out, don’t look like everyone else, or just feel different from everyone, many clubs can feel elitist, especially when you get dropped. WeREndurance is nothing like that. It’s inclusive and diverse.”.

As the group’s triathletes grew older and more injury-prone, however, WeREndurance membership began to drop, so Topper proposed transitioning from a strictly triathlon group to a lifestyle group. Now, WeREndurance members who live locally in Long Beach, Latest York, can participate in monthly hikes and quarterly races, as well as pool parties, holiday parties, diner breakfasts, and even a psychic night. Members who live out of state can stay connected through monthly meditation sessions, a book club, and monthly/bi-monthly educational webinars.

“These types of activities welcome everyone, including those who are injured or on the sidelines. This builds bonds and social connections,” Topper explains. “As you get older, you realize that sport is not only about being on the podium. It’s about community and having fun with your peers. The social aspect becomes just as vital as training and racing.”.

Disruptors: Brian Masayon, David Bahia, and Kristoffer Crisostomo.

In 2017, Masayon, Crisostomo, Bahia, and six of their friends formed a “silly” club to make training fun, and in doing so, others began taking notice.

Recent findings suggest that “People started reaching out, asking how to join the team. I replied that there was no team. After the 20th inquiry or so, the nine of us decided to open 3P TRI to the public as a fun, drama-free group. That was in October 2017. By the end of the year, we had over 120 members join,” Masayon states. As word spread, the nonprofit tri club’s inclusive vibe attracted members from Canada, Australia, the Philippines, and Mexico.

While Ironman race entries cost athletes between $900 and $1,200, 3P TRI has removed the financial barrier entirely, offering clinics and free 140.6-mile races that are fully supported by the team.

“There is no timing chip, so members are not pressured to prove how fast or slow they are. Instead, they train and then enjoy race day with their teammates,” Masayon says. For 3P’s 140.6 triathlon, members come from different states to volunteer and help their teammates finish.

Sources indicate that “People are intimidated by tri clubs because they have this impression of triathletes as being fast, quick, and strong. Our members, however, come in all shapes and sizes, and this becomes an inspiration to many people,” Masayon adds. “Nobody talks about speed and ability. We don’t play the comparison game.”.

It has been revealed that five years ago, a group of New Jersey moms tried a mud run. They had so much fun that one run turned into a road race, followed by group bike rides, and finally dipping their nail-less toes into triathlons, despite the level of intimidation.

“At a 5K, you’ll see everyone from Boston qualifiers to families participating together, sometimes with little kids in tow. Triathlons can seem like a different world from road or obstacle races. They require training and preparation across three disciplines, and the level of athleticism on display can be intimidating. Sometimes it feels like there are no actual beginners, just really accomplished athletes with super fancy bikes,” says Merino, adding that if someone demonstrates up to ride with a mountain bike, they probably know it’s not the fastest option and don’t necessarily need unsolicited advice about upgrading. The same goes for swim form, running technique, or anything else. “If someone asks for pointers, we absolutely help them! Otherwise, the most encouraging thing we can do may be simply making them feel like they belong.”.

In a recent development, “That’s what Team Thunderclap is all about. We might not have the fanciest gear or be the fastest people, but we show up, give it everything we’ve got, and probably laugh a whole lot along the way,” Merino says. “At the end of the day, most of us aren’t competing for Olympic medals. We’re ordinary people doing extraordinary things in our spare time.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Practicing stretches for energy can be a simple way to feel more awake and alert throughout the day. This practice was created by yoga instructor Laia Bové, who has taught students of all levels for more than a decade.

Maybe you’ve heard that yoga can help improve your energy level, or you’ve already felt that fresh-out-of-yoga-class and ready-to-take-on-the-world feeling while walking out of a gym or studio. If only you could bottle that feeling and use it anytime you’re slumped at your desk, feeling exhausted from the week and more than a little bleh. The truth is, you sorta can.

Industry observers note that this yoga practice is designed to help connect you with how you feel—physically, mentally, and energetically—so you can walk away ready to re-engage with the world as a refreshed version of you. And it only takes 14 minutes.

Perhaps the most energizing benefits of yoga result from a consistent practice. And it doesn’t need to take long. Doing this yoga sequence for a few days or weeks in a row can also help you build a more sustainable habit thanks to its manageable length and simple postures.

Whether you want to practice first thing in the morning, take a break midday, or relax at night, give this yoga class a try.

According to recent reports, sit cross-legged or in another comfortable position. Reach your arms toward the sky. Exhale as you lean toward the left, keeping your arms overhead, and feeling a stretch along your right side. Inhale and return to center with your arms overhead. Exhale as you bend toward the right, feeling a stretch along your left side. Inhale and return to center.

Sources indicate that from your seated position, reach your arms out to the sides in a T shape. Inhale as you reach your chest forward, lift your gaze toward the sky, bend your elbows, and draw your arms slightly behind you in seated Cow Pose. Exhale as you draw your navel toward your spine, round your back, and wrap your arms around yourself in a seated Cat Pose variation. Repeat a few times at your own pace.

Sources indicate that reach your arms straight out to the sides. Exhale as you turn your palms toward the sky and your elbows to face the floor. Reach your thumbs toward the wall behind you and your pinkies toward the sky. Take a few breaths here.

Exhale as you rotate your arms forward almost 360 degrees so your elbows and palms face the sky again. Reach your thumbs toward the wall behind you and your pinkies forward. Take a few breaths here.

Exhale and twist your chest toward the right. Place your left hand on your right knee and your right fingertips on the mat behind you. Take a few breaths here.

Inhale and return to center. Reach both arms overhead, then twist your chest toward the left. Place your right hand on your left knee and your left fingertips on the mat behind you. Take a few breaths here, then return to center.

Sit with your legs bent, feet on the mat, and your hands behind your hips with your fingertips pointing toward your body. Exhale and press your hands and feet into the mat as you lift your hips into Reverse Tabletop. Gaze forward or at the sky. Breathe here. As you exhale, lower your hips back to the mat.

It has been revealed that place your hands on the mat a few inches behind your hips with your fingertips facing forward. Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the mat in front of you. Lean back slightly, placing some weight into your hands. Lift your right foot off the mat. Then lift your left leg to meet it as you grasp behind your thighs in a Boat Pose variation. Breathe here. Lower your right toes to the mat, then the left.

Sources indicate that sit on the mat and draw the soles of your feet together, as close or as far from your hips as feels comfortable. Inhale and lift your chest. Exhale and fold forward, gently resting your hands on your ankles or feet in Bound Angle Pose. Stay here for a few breaths or you can instead make it a dynamic stretch if you lean forward, roll to an upright position, and then reach your chest forward over your legs again, repeating that motion a few times. Roll up to seated.

Come to your hands and knees. Spread your fingers wide and make sure your shoulders are stacked over your wrists and your hips over your knees. Make circles with your hips so your shoulders move ahead of your wrists, and then move your hips toward your heels. Repeat in the other direction.

Industry observers note that from your hands and knees, tuck your toes, sink your hips toward your heels, and walk your hands back until you’re sitting on your heels in Toe Squat. If the stretch along the bottoms of your feet is too intense, you can keep your hands on the mat and your chest leaning forward to help minimize the stretch. Take a few breaths here.

Return to your hands and knees.

Lower your knees, chest, and chin to the mat. Press your hands and the tops of your feet into the mat as you lift your chest any amount in Cobra Pose.

Return to your hands and knees. Tuck your toes and shift your hips up and back into Downward-Facing Dog. Take a few deep breaths here.

From Down Dog, lower to your knees. Inhale and straighten your right leg straight behind you. Press the ball of your foot into the mat or lift your foot hip height. Take a few breaths here.

From Bird Dog variation, step your right foot forward between your hands. Lift your chest, draw your navel toward your spine, and place your hands on your hips or reach your arms overhead in Low Lunge. Take a few breaths here.

Sources indicate that as you exhale, lower both hands to the mat to frame your right foot and step back into Down Dog. From Down Dog, step your left foot forward between your hands, lower your back knee to the mat, and repeat Low Lunge on this side.

Sources indicate that from Low Lunge, step your back foot forward to meet your front foot. Place your hands on your shins or thighs and inhale as you lift your chest slightly and lengthen your spine in Standing Half Forward Bend.

Sources indicate that from Standing Half Forward Bend, exhale and lower your chest toward your thighs. Place your hands on the mat or on blocks in Standing Forward Bend. Relax your head and neck.

Sources indicate that from Standing Forward Bend, slowly roll up and reach your arms overhead. Lift your gaze toward the sky in Upward Salute. Lower your arms in Mountain Pose.

Reach your arms overhead again, then lower back into Standing Forward Bend.

From Standing Forward Bend, bend your knees as much as you need to plant your hands on the mat and step one foot behind you, then the other, into Plank. Take a couple breaths here.

Lower your knees, chest, and chin to the mat.

Industry observers note that sink your hips toward your heels and reach your arms forward with your palms planted on the mat or you can bend your elbows and stack your forearms. Lower your forehead to the mat, a block, or your stacked arms in Child’s Pose. Breathe here.

Recent findings suggest that sit cross-legged on the mat in Easy Pose or come into another comfortable position. Take a few deep, slow breaths before returning to your day.

Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Our usual go-to shoe recommendation for new runners has always been the Brooks Ghost. It’s the ideal trainer to choose when you’re overwhelmed with all the offerings out there, unsure where to start or which shoe is right for you. The Ghost was a part of the quintessential runner starter pack:.

Industry observers note that but this year was different. When we covered the Ghost 18’s release in May, our staff had already logged a few weeks of mileage in the shoe. And the verdict was... mixed.

Sources indicate that it’s been six months since that initial testing, and during that time, the brand’s cushier model, the Brooks Glycerin 23, surpassed the Ghost in terms of popularity and positive feedback. What it all came down to was fit.

Sources indicate that when we evaluate running shoes, we rate key attributes like weight, flexibility, and durability. Predictably, the Glycerin 23 scored a lower overall average score in weight compared to the Ghost 18 (the former is tenths of an ounce heavier than the Ghost). Other features between the shoes were relatively similar, except when it came to comfort. The Glycerin 23 received high scores, whereas the Ghost 18’s comfort was rated high by men and very low by women. The keyword here was “crammed.”.

“I had no cramming of my toes,” noted Glycerin 23 tester Maura Dalek. “My feet had plenty of room to move around in and kept my feet dry and cool.”.

Juxtapose this with Ghost 18 tester and Deputy Editor Mallory Creveling’s comment: “The length was great; the width not so much...[My] forefoot area [felt] crammed the more I ran.”.

In a recent development, it wasn’t just women testers who felt this version of the Ghost ran narrower than previous iterations. Art Director John Hamilton remarked he would have felt comfier in a wider fit. Despite his discomfort, he still gave the Ghost 18 a high rating.

Industry observers note that like eating mushrooms or drinking a martini neat, sometimes running in a shoe is an acquired taste. While it’s not the advice I’d give to runners shopping for running shoes (“You’ll eventually love it. Really!”), it’s a pickle we sometimes allow ourselves to fall into: a model you’ve always liked and the newest one doesn’t feel the same, but you’re going to stick it out anyway.

So I asked testers what they thought of the Ghost 18 months later. Creveling remarked she gave the shoe several chances, and had maybe two pain-free runs in them.

According to recent reports, but here’s where our testing is limited: The Ghost 18 is available in several widths, including narrow, wide, and extra wide. Our samples come in the standard width (B for women, D for men), and our testing pool includes runners of various foot shapes. Fit varies across brands, and yes, even from model to model.

Here’s one piece of gear advice I can’t emphasize enough (people in the back, do you hear me?): It’s vital to try on a shoe and go for a test run in it first before making a commitment. Another underrated piece of advice is getting your foot measured to see if you need a narrower or wider width. Your feet change over time due to aging, life events, and gravity.

One tester who had no issue with the shoe’s fit had this to say: “High [score] overall for the latest edition of the Ghost. As an owner of previous Ghost models, this one is a worthy successor. Everything that makes the Ghost great as a daily trainer is present here—stability, durability, great on wet roads or loose gravel.” And on the fit? “Plenty of room in the toebox...Super comfortable.”.

It has been revealed that runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate was also satisfied with the Ghost 18’s comfort. “Brooks continues to nail the fit,” he remarked. “It’s one of the reasons I love their shoes—no matter how a model evolves, I know I’m going to get a good wrap. Even in the Ghost, which is a little more spartan for padding and luxury, it still wraps the foot well and feels good no matter how far I run.”.

He is referring to the familiar touch points we know and love about Brooks shoes: a plush heel collar that fits securely around your ankle, a flat ribbed tongue that looks like the cuffs on a cozy knit sweater.

Though the shoe doesn’t pack as powerful a punch with DNA Loft v3 foam (nitrogen-infused EVA) compared to shoes with TPEE or PEBA, it’s a reliable mile muncher, making it worthy for logging those everyday workouts when you’re building toward a race or just getting started with running.

Recent findings suggest that at $150, the Ghost 18 is comparable to the $145 Latest Balance Ellipse. If you want a slightly heavier, cushier daily trainer that costs $175, go with the Glycerin 23. If you want a true Goldilocks shoe that’s slightly lighter with a generous amount of cushioning, go with the Ghost 18. Just consider your width options before buying!

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

It has been revealed that amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#114922. 6 Myths About Max Heart Rate Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1473 w)

6 Myths About Max Heart Rate Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that to dial in your training, it’s vital to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides.
  • The formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr.
  • Sources indicate that over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that to dial in your training, it’s vital to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides. The catch? The most common formula for calculating max heart rate is not very accurate.

The formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr. William Haskell and Dr. Samuel Fox in 1970, and it wasn’t necessarily validated by research and involved data from a wide mix of people, including those with heart disease and smokers. As a result, the formula tends to overestimate max heart rate for younger people and underestimate it for older adults.

Sources indicate that over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age). However, it’s still a rudimentary system—like, “might as well use an abacus as a bike computer” rudimentary, indicates Cherie Miner, M.D., a sports medicine specialist in Birmingham, Alabama. “It’s been the standard for years, but there are a lot of variables that can throw off your max heart rate.” Some of those variables: how fit you are, how hot it is, and how much stress you’re under.

Because of these variables, there are also a lot of myths surrounding max heart rate. Here, we debunk some of the most common ones so you can get to know your heart, and use your metrics to train efficiently.

You’ve got to admit: This is equally horrifying and comical. But you can rest easy because it won’t actually happen.

According to recent reports, “Most people have one to two minutes at their max heart rate—highly-trained athletes may have more,” Miner claims. Expect to see your performance suffer very quickly if you try and maintain your max heart rate for more than just a short burst. Fortunately, years of evolving to survive prevents us from actually killing ourselves.

The old-school formulas assume that it is the same, but Golich says it’s much more nuanced than that. Max heart rate is largely untrainable and determined by genetics—some of us have hearts tuned like humming birds’ while others have the slow-and-steady type.

It has been revealed that although not perfectly accurate, age-based formulas give athletes an easy and accessible way to find a rough baseline of their max without undergoing rigorous (or sometimes dangerous, in the case of a sedentary person) testing. That mentioned, The American College of Sports Medicine suggests age-based formulas with a lower standard deviation, for example, the Gelish equation: 207 minus (0.7 x age) or Tanaka: 208 minus (0.7 x age).

In a recent development, no matter which way you calculate it, your max heart rate is not an indication of performance, Golich says. “If your max is 200, and someone else’s is 190, it doesn’t mean one of you is the better athlete.” In fact, Golich has worked with numerous talented athletes at both ends of the spectrum.

According to recent reports, it’s good to remember that everyone’s max heart rate does drop as they age—but again, that doesn’t mean you’re losing fitness. Regular training and good nutrition will affect performance more than the fact that your max heart rate is now slightly lower than it was three years ago.

Industry observers note that in reality, it’s not your max heart rate that determines your fitness level. Being able to hold your max heart rate for longer and longer sessions is what’s key.

Heart rate is a reaction to work being done, not a measurement of actual work. For example, Golich indicates that if you ratchet yourself up to 200 watts (wattage measures your cycling power) for three minutes, for the first minute, your heart may tick along at 170 beats per minute (bpm). By minute two it may be at 180 bpm, and by minute three you could be pushing 189. But you’re doing the same amount of work the whole time: 200 watts.

If you were to ride for three minutes with the intention of maintaining the same heart rate, things would look different. Say you ramped up to 180 bpm to start—you might ride at 200 watts for the first minute, but you’d likely have to drop your watts to sustain that heart rate for minutes two and three.

Golich says he prefers to have his clients train with power meters or using rate of perceived exertion (RPE)—a personal appraisal of how hard you feel you’re working—rather than heart rate.

“There are a lot of grey areas with heart rate,” he claims, adding that being overheated, under-fueled, or even just hopped up on caffeine will throw your heart rate numbers off for the day.

In a recent development, furthermore, the number displayed by your heart rate monitor or the screen on a gym treadmill may not be accurate. Sure, using a computer is certainly more accurate than the 220-minus-age formula, but Golich adds that because these devices take measurements every few seconds, they’re probably not dead-on.

If you really want to know your true max heart rate, an EKG is one way to go or a cardiopulmonary exercise test for even more accurate measurements, both of which require a visit to your doc or a lab.

Also, if you think that unless you’re hitting your max heart rate on every ride, you’re not working hard enough, here’s your license to chill. Max heart rate workouts should be done sparingly, Miner notes, since the ultra-high intensity can lead to injuries, extreme fatigue, and other symptoms of overtraining.

According to recent reports, plus, there’s merit to working in many different heart rate zones—from increasing your base fitness with low-intensity sessions to pushing the boundaries at your lactate threshold, and even tipping into some anaerobic work. If you only have two speeds—hard and harder—you’re doing yourself a disservice.

Sources indicate that heart attacks, while rare, happen to athletes at all different workloads. Even so, cardiologist James Beckerman, M.D., says you’re slightly more at risk when working at very high intensities.

“This is likely related to a combination of high heart rate, higher blood pressure with exercise (which is normal), and higher levels of catecholamines (hormones produced by the adrenal glands),” he states. “For people without heart disease, exercising at higher intensity is generally safe.”.

If you’re someone with heart disease or who has exhibited risk factors, however, it’s a good idea to talk to your doctor about safe heart rate ranges for exercise and even get a stress test, he claims.

You’re not mistaken—your max heart rate for cycling really may be different than your max for another sport. Again, this is indicative of how variable heart rate is, Golich says.

Activities that are load bearing—like running—will generally push your heart rate higher, because you have to do more work to overcome gravity. Cycling, because it has the mechanical assistance of the bike, will generally produce a lower max heart rate. And swimming, which happens in a pool with zero-impact, may be lower still—since the water is keeping you cool, Golich indicates, heat will be less of a factor in raising your heart rate.

What exactly is heart rate reserve? According to Miner, heart rate reserve is the difference between maximum heart rate and resting heart rate.

Your heart rate reserve can actually be a good measurement of how fit you are overall. “A higher heart rate reserve indicates better physical fitness,” she states. That’s because, unlike maximum heart rate, a lower resting heart rate is associated with better fitness. “If your resting heart rate is lower, then your heart rate reserve will be higher,” Miner says.

According to recent reports, tamanna K. Singh, M.D., is a board-certified adult clinical and sports cardiologist and RRCA-certified run coach. She earned her medical degree from Boston University School of Medicine and completed her Internal Medicine Residency at Boston Medical Center. She completed her Cardiovascular Medicine fellowship at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Fresh York, New York and her specialty training in Sports Cardiology at Massachusetts General Hospital. She is right now the codirector of the Sports Cardiology Center at Cleveland Clinic in Cleveland, Ohio and assistant professor of medicine at the Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine of Case Western Reserve University. To date, she has held several council roles with the American College of Cardiology (ACC). As a sports cardiologist, Dr. Singh provides cardiovascular care for professional, competitive, and recreational athletes and describes herself as an advocate for safe participation in sports. Media and print contributions include the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Time Magazine, and others. Outside of her profession, she enjoys running marathons, hitting the weights in the gym, playing sous-chef to her wonderful husband while cooking plant-based meals, and playing with her four beautiful dogs.

It has been revealed that in 1977, the Vantage was the first Brooks shoe to top our charts. The running renaissance began several years prior, when Frank Shorter won the 1972 Olympic marathon in Munich. Two years later, the shoe industry would be changed forever with the introduction of ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) foam, which was lighter, softer, and had more rebound than the rubbers used in midsoles around that time. Our editors knew Brooks had a winner when we tested the Vantage.

Almost half a century later, the brand is still dazzling us with its innovations and earning prizes in the 2026 Runner’s World Shoe Awards. And to think the firm started out more than a hundred years ago manufacturing ballet slippers and bath shoes.

It has been revealed that since the 1970s, Brooks has solely focused on upping the ante in shoe tech. The Vantage also introduced the varus wedge, which was basically a medial post used to help with instability caused by overpronation. Now the varus wedge is dated and has been replaced with Brooks’s “GuideRails” system. EVA is also being phased out with improved foams that are bouncier and even softer.

In a recent development, our team vets hundreds of shoes a year and distributes models to more than 250 local testers for evaluation. Shoe testers of different levels, ages, arch heights, and gait patterns log at least a hundred miles before submitting feedback on a shoe’s fit, feel, and ride. It has been revealed that brooks has categorized its shoes to help runners choose the best pair that fits their running style and preferred experience. I’ve been a Brooks die-hard since my high school days. For the past 20 years, I’ve been keeping tabs on product updates and saying goodbye to discontinued lineups (taps for the PureProject minimalist list). Here’s a breakdown of everything you need to know—foams, stability tech—about Brooks’s footwear.

One helpful way to choose Brooks shoes is by knowing Brooks’s foams. The kind of foam determines the type of running experience the shoe is meant for.

Through the decades, Brooks revved up its EVA foam, developing MoGo foam in 2006, and then DNA foam in 2013. Known for its adaptive midsole cushioning, DNA has undergone an evolution of its own, breaking into its own subcategories in types of shoes.

Runners looking for a more cushioned shoe will want to try trainers with DNA Loft midsoles. DNA Loft v3, for example, which is featured in the Ghost 18 and the Adrenaline GTS 25, is nitrogen-infused EVA and rubber. It has large cells of air to pack in cushioning without adding extra weight.

At the beginning of 2025, Brooks released the Glycerin Max which showcased DNA Tuned. In developing DNA Tuned, the brand’s team found they could manipulate the cells creating larger cells in the heel and smaller cells in the forefoot. In an interview with Runner’s World, Brooks Chief Product Officer Carson Caprara explained how this dual-cell cushioning softens landings and becomes a springboard for responsive toe-off.

Industry observers note that for runners looking for shoes for speedwork or racing, they should look for shoes with DNA Flash or DNA Gold; the latter is a pure PEBA midsole. DNA Hype is a combination of EVA and PEBA. We found in our testing its good for speedwork.

Before the Adrenaline GTS rolled out in 1999, Brooks had set out to build off of the success of the Addiction. Runners wanted a more flexible version of the stability shoe, and so, the Adrenaline GTS—Go-to-Shoe—was born.

In 2018, Brooks adapted a more holistic approach with stability, implementing a guide rails system into its shoes. The guide rails system has two dense foam pieces in the midsole, one on the medial side and one on the lateral side. These foam pieces reduce your foot from rolling outward and inward when your form becomes erratic due to overpronation or late onset overpronation.

Now redefined as Go-to-Support, GTS Brooks shoes are the stability counterpart of their neutral models. In this way, you can easily find your favorite Brooks trainer with just a little extra support in the midsole and not much else changed with the shoe.

Guide rails offer unobtrusive support for both overpronators and neutral runners.

Our lab tests show that DNA Loft remains Brooks’s softest midsole material.

Screen-printed mesh provides lightweight structure with more airflow and flexibility.

This sticky outsole compound aids grip and wet-surface traction on trail shoes.

The most responsive expression of Brooks’s DNA foam debuted on the Hyperion Tempo.

What’s the best Brooks shoe for beginning runners?

It has been revealed that we always recommend the Ghost because it provides plenty of supportive cushioning without being too bulky. It’s an ideal daily trainer for beginners to start with as an offshoot.

How does the Hyperion Elite 6 compare to other carbon shoes?

According to recent reports, according to testers, the Hyperion Elite 6 feels less softer and more accommodating compared to other super shoes they’ve tested. The new DNA Gold midsole adds more edge compared to the Hyperion Elite’s DNA Flash foams, with testers saying the rebound is comparable to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4 or Saucony Endorphin Pro 5.

Does Brooks have bargain-priced shoes and how do they stack up to more expensive models?

The Launch 12, included on this list, has a fit and feel almost on par with more expensive models. It’s not as responsive compared to $140 to $160 trainers due to its EVA cushioning, but it delivers a smooth ride.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant. The two bottles bounced loosely against my chest, with water leaking down my shirt throughout the run. It was not a flattering look. Every step came with its own sloshing soundtrack. I spent so much time adjusting the thing (despite an across-the-chest strap) that I barely enjoyed my run.

Recent findings suggest that so when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from. During a Reddit AMA hosted by BBC Sport, the Scottish middle-distance star, who casually broke the mile world record in July with a 3:42.66 finish, shared his thoughts on the growing popularity of running vests.

"I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr said, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.

For context, we're talking about a world-record holder, Olympic medalist, and world champion in the 1500 meters. He knows a thing or two about logging miles. And while 12 miles might look quite different on his watch than mine, I don't think his suggestion was particularly outrageous.

And because everything is contested on the internet, plenty of people disagree.

Runner @natalie.the.capn shared Kerr's comments on Threads and explained that she wears a hydration belt on every outing so she has somewhere to keep her phone, particularly in case of an emergency. "Funny how men rarely think of that," she wrote.

Industry observers note that I do understand her concern. I'm a guy, so I'm definitely not going to pretend I have the same safety considerations that women often face while exercising alone. I also bring my phone everywhere, usually carrying it in my hand because iPhones only get bigger and the pockets on most of my running shorts haven't kept up.

She also pointed out that some of her routes take her six miles or more between places where she can get water, which is an entirely different experience from mine.

In a recent development, I live in New York City, where Central Park has plenty of water fountains (that work ... most of the time) and there's usually a deli within walking distance to snag a Gatorade. I can see why Kerr's approach makes sense here, especially for shorter runs. I've also tried handheld bottles and waist straps, and neither has been particularly enjoyable. Between the bouncing, adjusting, and occasional hand cramps, I'd love to carry as little as possible in my hands.

That changes a lot during marathon training, something I've put myself through four times now, when I'm out for considerably longer and need water to wash down those pasty gels. Aside from the hydration aspect, stopping to buy something, pausing my watch, and interrupting my stride halfway through a long run is a vibe killer.

It has been revealed that and I'm certainly not arguing against being prepared. I learned the hard way that sunscreen deserved a permanent spot in my prerun routine after years of neglecting it ended with some casual skin cancer surgery.

The Threads debate, naturally, has brought out some pretty different opinions. One commenter, siding with Kerr, wrote, "Yeah im gonna listen to the guy who runs for a living but thanks." Others pointed out that beginners, slower runners, and people training in hot weather could have very different hydration needs.

According to recent reports, they're definitely right about that. Twelve miles is a long way for plenty of runners, no matter what their experience level, and access to water, weather, pace, and individual needs all change the equation. Kerr even acknowledged that people have different reasons for carrying gear, something that seems to have gotten a little lost as his comments made their way around social media.

According to recent reports, I still think he has a fair point about how much equipment we sometimes convince ourselves we need on a run. That stated, if your vest makes your runs more comfortable or gives you peace of mind, by all means wear it. For me, I'll be keeping my phone close and bringing an appropriate amount of water when I need it.

As for my hydration vest, it's been collecting dust ever since that first outing, and I haven't missed it one bit.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

The Air Canada Aeroplan stopover rule is genuinely one of the last great loopholes in loyalty travel. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop: a business class flight from Toronto to Singapore — routed through Tokyo with a multi-day stopover — retails for **$8,000 to $10,000 in cash**. You can book that same itinerary for **70,000 Aeroplan points** (plus 5,000 for the stopover, so 75,000 total). At a conservative cash value of $8,000, you're extracting **10.7 cents per point** — more than double what most programs offer, and squarely within Aeroplan's documented range of **5.7 to 14.3 cents per point**. What makes this feel different from other premium redemptions is the *shape* of the trip itself. You're not just flying business class — you're building a mini round-the-world itinerary. Tokyo and Singapore in the same award ticket. Two of the world's great cities. Two business class flights. One redemption. The inefficiency here isn't accidental — it's baked into how Aeroplan prices stopovers at a flat 5,000 miles, regardless of where you stop. Recent findings suggest that the core insight is this: Air Canada Aeroplan uses a fixed partner award chart for Star Alliance flights, and it prices stopovers at a flat 5,000-mile premium regardless of routing complexity. That single policy decision transforms a standard business class award into a multi-destination adventure at a fraction of the combined retail cost.

According to recent reports, here's the mechanism. When Aeroplan relaunched in 2020, it did something most programs had abandoned years earlier: it kept a fixed-rate award chart for partner airlines. While programs like United MileagePlus moved to fully dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate with demand — Aeroplan locked in predictable rates for Star Alliance partners. The YYZ to SIN corridor in business class sits at a rate that reflects the geography, not the current demand spike or revenue management algorithm. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community can systematically exploit.

Industry observers note that layer on top of that the stopover rule: Aeroplan allows one free stopover on one-way partner awards for just 5,000 additional miles. A stopover is defined as a connection of more than 24 hours. So your Toronto → Tokyo → Singapore routing becomes a Toronto → Tokyo (stopover 3 days) → Singapore itinerary, all on one award ticket, for 75,000 points total. Montreal-based running apparel brand Ciele certainly knows a thing or two about running in the cold, and the brand just released its second-ever Woolmark-certified collection of merino wool running apparel and accessories.

Industry observers note that the collection highlights Ciele’s two merino-based fabrics: Sorino WS, a merino-silk blend used in base layers, and Sorino W, a 100% merino fabric used in headwear. The collection includes several hats, two facemasks, and base layers for men and women. Woolmark, an independent wool authority, certifies all gear to ensure wool textiles meet industry standards for fiber content, colorfastness, and durability.

Check out some highlights from the collection below, and shop the full lineup at Ciele.com.

According to recent reports, the beauty of this hat is its simplicity: a straightforward cap that lets merino wool's natural performance shine. Made from pure merino, it fits snugly, so it won’t shift while running, and the knit fabric naturally traps heat, vents excess moisture, and resists odors. Added bonus: This hat is machine washable (on the cold setting), and the “speedway” pattern gives it a snazzy look, too.

Industry observers note that prefer a more classic “watch cap” style beanie? Check out the VNTBeanie, also made from 100 percent merino fabric. You’ll get all the performance benefits of merino, plus the hat’s ribbed structure boosts its breathability (and looks great, too).

According to recent reports, the FRDMask will help you power through icy winds and single-digit temperatures. It’s way more than a face mask: Made from a plush merino-cashmere blend, it keeps your entire head, neck, and face warm. The key is its all-encompassing design, which layers neatly under a jacket and seals cold spots that outerwear and a hat would normally leave exposed.

The HLSLongsleeve really shows the value of merino as a performance fabric. Made from a comfy merino-silk blend, it regulates your temperature, breathes well, resists odors, and feels great (Ciele says the silk gives it a smooth texture and boosts its strength). The snug fit and thumbholes make it easy to layer under a jacket and gloves, but it’s also great in warmer weather—the fabric is rated UPF 30, so it protects you from sunburn when worn on its own.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone. At the opposite end of the spectrum, swimming in very warm water can also crater your comfort and results. That’s why we were psyched to test the EZ Hydro-Glide Cap, a one-of-a-kind attempt to boost swimming performance and safety using wearable technology designed to enhance thermoregulation.

In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.

Before we dive into the science, an important clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap. More on that below.

In a recent development, but first, kudos to EZ Gains, a popular outside-the-box triathlon retailer, for attacking a problem that numerous triathletes experience – significant discomfort when swimming in very cold and very warm water. We’ve learned a lot in recent years about thermoregulation, and any improvements in this area could help many athletes, including friends of mine who’ve quit the sport after repeated unpleasant swims.

EZ Gains’ approach is based on credible science. The company notes that your head plays an outsized role in your body’s response to ambient temperatures, given the extensive network of blood vessels and nerves just beneath your scalp. This rings true, as does the contention that regulating the temperature difference between the water and your head – both the initial gap and the ongoing variance – can mitigate the downsides of extreme heat and cold.

According to recent reports, we use insulated neoprene caps for chilly swims, after all. What if a single, more sophisticated solution helped us thrive in both polar and equatorial waters?

It has been revealed that EZ Gains’ answer is a honeycombed high-tech foam and hard plastic wedge that sits at the top of your forehead under an (included) standard swim cap. Before putting it on, you can place one or two small thermal packs (also included) inside the hollow center of the wedge. These packs – and an additional thin heating strip – provide a cooling or warming effect as needed. In warm water, you can use a frozen pack or two to cool your forehead, which is meant to keep your core temp down and reduce heat fatigue.

You’re also supposed to use frozen packs when swimming in frigid water – say 60 degrees F or less – according to EZ Gains. The idea is to pre-condition your head to the chilly temps you’re about to encounter. This may sound counterintuitive, but EZ Gains states the pre-cooling technique can prevent cold shock, a serious autonomic response that elevates your heart rate and can cause panic and even cardiac arrest. The packs can also be heated for a touch of warmth when facing cool-but-not-arctic conditions.

For more preparation for swimming in cold water, read: How to Acclimate and Prepare for Cold-Water Triathlons.

To evaluate the system, I tested it in various bodies of water over the course of five months, from midsummer to late autumn. My primary locations were indoor and outdoor pools in Boulder, Colorado, and our local reservoir. Water temperatures ranged from 84 degrees F all the way down to 50 degrees F. All of my swims were 45-90 minutes long, more than enough to mimic race conditions and assess how well the device limits heat and cold stress.

Recent findings suggest that the TLDR from my testing: Some new technologies sound great on paper but don’t pan out in real life. Sadly, this device is one of those. On two of its three core value propositions, the Hydro-Glide fell short. I’ll tackle them one by one.

First, EZ Gains says the cap will reduce heat fatigue and related complications – anxiety, increased heart rate, dehydration, and confusion – when using the frozen packs. I did notice a cooling sensation in the early parts of my summer swims, typically lasting 10-15 minutes. But while I appreciated the initial cooling, I didn’t discern a material difference in fatigue, judgment, or heart rate after an hour, even during my most intense workouts.

According to recent reports, second, the cap is supposed to prevent the instant discomfort and cold shock that many people experience when diving into frigid water. Perhaps I’m less sensitive than other athletes (my long-suffering wife might have an opinion on this), but using slightly thawed ice packs to pre-cool my head (as instructed) didn’t eliminate the ice cream headaches.

In my experience, this kind of pain starts in my face and forehead, neither of which are protected by the device. It’s possible that the Hydro-Glide would help other swimmers, since physiological reactions vary widely, but I’d speculate that too much of your face, forehead, and neck remain exposed for the cold to be significantly neutralized.

In a recent development, third, EZ Gains indicates the cap will protect your head when another swimmer clobbers you, which seems legit in the case of head-on impacts. A friend in my Masters group sustained a concussion last year when another swimmer swerved into her during a backstroke set. While I didn’t do any head-banging to test this claim, it’s reasonable to believe the Hydro-Glide’s foam would’ve absorbed that blow. Since the wedge doesn’t cover the sides or back of your head, though, it wouldn’t deflect all-too-common errant elbows or kicks to those areas during a race start.

It has been revealed that there are two additional downsides to consider. If you have an XL melon like mine, you may experience discomfort from the pressure of the cone against your head. I did, typically after about 30 minutes. And if you’re even the slightest bit fashion-conscious, you will probably draw the line at looking like a Corythosaurus from Jurassic Park. The first time I demonstrated up at the pool wearing the Hydro-Glide, several of my masters teammates burst out laughing. Someone compared me to a Conehead.

Industry observers note that which I could possibly live with if the results had been stellar. However, the Hydro-Glide didn’t deliver a meaningful upside for me versus a standard swim cap. While EZ Gains deserves praise for its waaay-out-of-the-box effort to improve swim safety and comfort, this product’s current execution doesn’t justify a $270 investment.

#114913. Tech Report: This Coach’s Fartlek Workout Is One of the Best for Learning a Crucial Running Skill

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1481 w)

Tech Report: This Coach’s Fartlek Workout Is One of the Best for Learning a Crucial Running Skill

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1481 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success.
  • Learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World.
  • Moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success. Go out too hard and you may struggle to hold on. Run too conservatively and you might miss your goal finish.

Learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World. One workout he recommends for building this skill is a fartlek he learned from fellow run coach Brad Hudson, his coauthor on the book, Run Faster from the 5K to the Marathon: How to Be Your Own Best Coach.

Moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them. The goal? Building both aerobic fitness and a greater sense of pace control.

This workout helps improve your ability to settle into the right effort earlier, as well as enhance your capacity to hold those paces for longer—a perfect session for both optimizing your weekly speed run and helping you run your fastest race.

After an easy running warmup, you’ll run five faster segments, separated by an easy jog of the same duration.

It has been revealed that the base workout uses three target paces: 5K pace for the one-minute segments, 10K pace for the two-minute segments, and half-marathon pace for the three-minute segment. If you don’t know your race paces, you can also go off of rate of perceived exertion (RPE), with 10 equaling all-out effort. You should still be able to have a conversation around 4 RPE.

Fitzgerald indicates the workout should feel “fun hard,” meaning the faster running should feel challenging, but you shouldn’t finish the workout feeling like you just went all out in a race. Each surge is relatively short, so focus on hitting your intended effort rather than pushing as hard as you can.

More experienced, higher-volume runners can extend the pyramid to 1-2-3-2-1-2-3-2-1, again jogging for the same duration after each faster segment. This version includes 17 minutes of faster running and 17 minutes of recovery jogging, compared to just nine minutes of each in the original version.

In Fitzgerald’s experience, many runners tend to think of their effort in two broad categories: slow and fast, but this workout challenges that by demanding more care in differentiating between faster paces.

In a recent development, the one-minute 5K pace efforts should be faster than the two-minute 10K pace efforts, which should be faster than the three-minute half-marathon effort, explains Fitzgerald. The differences between these three paces are small—often just a few seconds per mile—so learning to recognize what each one feels like can help you become a more efficient and more confident runner.

Recent findings suggest that before each segment, think about the effort you’re trying to find. For the first one-minute interval, Fitzgerald suggests literally imagining that you’re starting a 5K race. You wouldn’t want to sprint the opening minute of that race and flame out, so resist that urge here, too.

Recent findings suggest that try to settle into the right pace by feel, then use your watch to check and adjust. Over time, you’ll grow more attuned to the connection between how you feel and how fast you’re moving. “Your watch can’t [run the workout] for you,” Fitzgerald indicates. “It can tell you how fast you’re going. It can’t tell you how fast you should go.”.

In a recent development, learning to run by feel translates to race day, when you want to hit your goal pace. Your body’s response to the conditions and the effort helps you decide how to proceed through each mile, slowing down or speeding up.

This workout doesn’t ask you to spend a long time at any single pace. Instead, it gives you short exposures to several intensities within one session.

Hudson, who’s coached multiple Olympians and world-class athletes, tells Runner’s World that moving through a range of paces during a single workout helps with not only pace control, but also running economy or the energy required to run at a given speed.

It has been revealed that additionally, Hudson explains the continuous nature of the fartlek session gives it an aerobic emphasis because you never actually stop running throughout the entirety of the workout. “The faster portions [of the workout] increase oxygen demand, but as you go longer in a workout, the more it becomes aerobic, no matter what,” he says. “If you’re keeping the running continuous, the aerobic energy systems just keep going up and up and up.”.

Fitzgerald agrees, although he also notes athletes get some anaerobic stress during the shorter, faster efforts. Think of it as a way to work on several aspects of your fitness at once, rather than a session designed to train just one. Plus, switching between paces can make the workout more mentally engaging than returning to the same effort over and over again.

It has been revealed that the first time you try the workout, you might overshoot a target pace or find it difficult to feel the difference between efforts. That’s okay. Fitzgerald says trial and error is an notable part of developing the skill.

Sources indicate that when you repeat the session, look for signs that your pacing is becoming more controlled: You start each segment closer to your intended effort, settle into a steadier rhythm, and maintain a clear difference between your 5K, 10K, and half marathon paces. You may also find it easier to keep your recovery jogs consistent.

The point is, you don’t need to nail every second of this workout. Learn from your mistakes, adjust when necessary, and remember Fitzgerald’s advice: “Progress over perfection.”.

In a recent development, it may be tempting to think of the easy jogs simply as passing time between hard segments. But both coaches emphasize the value of continuous running and implore runners not to lose focus during the recovery intervals.

It has been revealed that fitzgerald states teaching your body to recover from a faster effort while still moving presents a unique challenge. Your muscles must learn how to continue producing the energy needed to keep you running efficiently while your body works to recover from the harder interval at the same time. This adaptation translates directly to race day when you have to settle back into race pace after surging to pass another runner or gliding a little too fast down a hill.

The key is paying attention to how your recovery intervals feel. If you have to slow them down more and more to prepare for the next segment, Fitzgerald says that may be a sign you’re pushing the faster portions too hard.

According to recent reports, the beauty of this workout is if you realize you’ve gone out too promptly, you can easily adjust so you can still complete the workout. If you overcooked one of your speedier segments, Fitzgerald suggests tacking on another minute or so to the easy jog until you breathe easier and lower your heart rate—then adjust your effort level on the next interval.

Because the workout touches several intensity levels, Fitzgerald recommends it during base training or in the off-season. It can help runners maintain well-rounded fitness before they begin building toward a more specific goal.

It can also work as the de facto speed workout during a lighter training week or serve as a secondary quality workout during half-marathon or marathon training. In this case, the session offers a chance to maintain some faster running while the biggest emphasis remains on your long runs and race-specific efforts.

Hudson uses the workout as a key tool in returning to training post-marathon. After a week off, he generally has his athletes begin with easy running. Then, he adds this workout as a way to reintroduce different intensity levels and prepare his athletes for more demanding work ahead.

Whenever you use it, keep its purpose in mind: It’s designed to help you practice changing gears and build general fitness, and using it to support key workouts specifically tailored to your next race makes it even more effective.

Zwift’s Dedicated Indoor Bike Makes Your Winter Riding Better—and Protects Your Road Bike

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future.
  • Sources indicate that when I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sources indicate that I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future. It’s easy to use and reliable. It did exactly what I needed it to do—turn my bike into a trainer for offseason training.

Sources indicate that when I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use. More than that, every shop team I’ve worked with would use the Wahoo Kickr Core as their trainer of choice. Then I was introduced to the Zwift Ride and realized I was not done buying trainers just yet.

It has been revealed that as the shop’s service manager, I got firsthand experience assessing bikes after a season of sitting on the trainer; let alone season after season, year after year. The level of maintenance needed for those bikes was initially shocking to me as well as to the customer. Most of us are aware we need to do maintenance on our bikes that we ride outside, but it’s easy to forget about our unsung hero—our trainer bike sitting in the basement constantly covered in sweat, spilled drink mix, and getting the watts cranked into it day in and day out.

There’s a better way than just throwing your bike on the trainer for your offseason. The Zwift Ride V2 with the Wahoo Kickr Core is now my top recommended way to use a bike trainer. It’s easy to see why.

For those who have multiple riders in one house, this may be one of the biggest benefits. When I had my bike set up on the Kickr Core it was harder for my wife to just hop on the trainer. Since my old trainer bike was carbon, even a simple saddle adjustment required a torque wrench. I’ve even gone so far as to change out stems to change the reach too—not the hardest thing to do, but by no means convenient. On the Zwift Ride, most fit adjustments are super easy and take just seconds.

Recent findings suggest that the Zwift Ride 2 I’ve been on even has multiple crank length options set up in the cranks, so you just swap the pedals to a different hole in the crank to change the effective crank length. Taking out one more friction point between me and being able to start my trainer ride means I’m even more likely to get my winter trainer miles in.

In a recent development, the other day I was a few minutes into my warmup and I needed to adjust my reach a bit. I pulled the integrated 6mm Allen key out from its place under the top tube, easily adjusted the reach at the handlebars, tightened everything down, and reinstalled the tool all without interrupting my cadence. Having the tool I need to adjust just about anything on the bike is a upcoming level of convenience I was not used to.

As Matt Phillips pointed out in his Zwift Ride 2 review, “Mechanically, the Ride is almost primitive.” For clarity, this is by no means a negative—when it comes to a trainer bike, mechanically primitive but extremely functional is a best-case scenario. This bike has a chain that goes from the chainring, through a chain tensioner, around the Zwift Cog attached to the Wahoo Kickr, and back up to the chainring. There’s no derailleur, no front tire that needs air, no brakes to knock out of alignment. The handlebars don’t even turn, so there’s no headset to replace in the spring because it was sitting in a pool with sweat all winter.

It has been revealed that on the other side, you’re saving your daily driver from a lot of unseen mechanical damage. As the snow thaws out on the roads, road riders are ready to get back in the saddle under the sun, but if you use your bike on the trainer all winter, it may need A LOT of love before it’s road-worthy.

A bike that sits on the trainer all winter collects significant corrosion in headset and bottom bracket bearings. The sweat that comes off your head drops straight onto your headset and sweat from your body (and any of those sticky drink mixes) drop straight down toward the bottom bracket. Then we get to the drivetrain. I’ve had bikes come in around March that need full drivetrain replacement: chainrings, cassette, and chain after a good season of indoor miles. Finally, we get to the handlebar—at a minimum you should replace that bar tape after a season riding on the trainer. This also gives you a chance to get the handlebar looked at to make sure all that corrosion (sweat) hasn’t eaten into the them.

Sources indicate that I’ve seen service tickets range anywhere from $100 to almost a thousand dollars just to get a bike off the trainer and ready to ride outside. For some people one season of trainer riding on the Zwift Ride 2 could be more cost-effective than using your road bike on a trainer.

Before an activity becomes a habit people are good at finding reasons not to do something. It doesn’t take long to setup a bike on the Wahoo Kickr Core, but even that little bit of set up time to pop your bike on the trainer is one more hurdle for you not to ride today. If you have to swap your cassette over from your bike to the trainer—you can almost forget about it.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn’t just go for getting your bike on the trainer. This week in Pennsylvania we’re having a stretch of perfect riding weather—relatively low humidity, sunny, and temperatures between 55 degrees and 60 degrees. Next week’s forecast calls for colder temperatures and rain, also known as great indoor-riding weather. But this week, if I have a window of time to ride, I want to be able to just hop on my bike and go; I don’t want to have to take the bike off the trainer and reinstall my cassette before I can even start pedaling outside. With a dedicated trainer setup, I can just take my bike off the hook on the wall and roll away. Next week, when the weather goes south, I can just hop back on the trainer.

Sources indicate that the Zwift Ride makes it easier to do things like use power-ups, steer the avatar, and toggle through screens, but those features are just an added bonus compared to the other reasons to pick one up. It is a burly, simple, near-flawless machine for riding on the trainer. It’s stable when putting out your max watts. The built-in tool makes it easy to accommodate different riders—including adjusting the reach. Even the bottle cages are designed to fit almost any bottle. The bike’s handlebar tray fits an iPad or other tablet well, but I pair it with a rolling trainer table if I’m using my laptop. You can buy the Zwift Ride itself, or as a package deal with Wahoo’s excellent Kickr Core 2, which gives you everything you need for a stress-free indoor riding season.

Industry observers note that jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.
