💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics.
  • Research indicates just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine.
  • The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics. But your torso muscles—which include your abs, back, glutes, and hip flexors—play a crucial role in cycling that goes way beyond looks.

Research indicates just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine. One 2019 study, published in PLoS One, found that an eight-week core training program improved balance and core endurance (which you need to maintain posture through long miles) in the 21 college athletes who participated. Another research review, published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2022, says core training should have a place in all athletes’ training programs.

The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability. The authors also write that these core strength benefits help prevent “energy leaks,” therefore leading to better performance.

In a recent development, to help you gain these benefits of a strong midsection, you need a solid workout to add to your routine. Thankfully, Noam Tamir, C.S.C.S., founder and CEO of TS Fitness in Latest York City, created this dumbbell core-strengthening workout.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to the research that proves the benefits of core strength for athletes, the moves Tamir chose for this workout make an ideal mix for those looking to improve performance. Not only will the moves improve your stability in an upright posture, allowing you to ride and breathe more efficiently, but they also target the core from multiple angles, hitting every muscle of the torso.

Even better: While these moves resemble familiar core exercises, each one has a creative spin. This means they not only challenge your body in fun new ways, but also engage your brain.

Recent findings suggest that how to use this list: Do each exercise below, in order, for the reps listed. Repeat for 3-4 rounds. Rest as needed between exercises and rounds.

It has been revealed that tamir demonstrates the exercises in the video above so you can learn proper form. You will need one light to medium dumbbell for this workout. An exercise mat is optional.

Industry observers note that why it works: The half-kneeling halo exercise focuses on trunk stability. “It works the core at 360 degrees because the dumbbell is moving around the body while you’re maintaining an upright position,” Tamir says. You do the same thing on a ride—hold a strong posture and upright body position while your arms and legs move.

According to recent reports, how to do it: Start kneeling, right knee on ground, and left foot planted in front, both knees bent 90 degrees. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chin. Keeping torso and lower body steady, circle dumbbell clockwise around head. Elbows stay close to head. Return to chin. Repeat in other direction. Do 8-10 reps in each direction. Switch leg stance each round.

It has been revealed that why it works: Target the obliques with this rotational move. You’ll also hit the rectus abdominis (those six-pack looking abs) and work on coordination of the upper and lower body, Tamir explains.

It has been revealed that how to do it: Start seated on floor. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chest. Lean back slightly, and lift legs off floor, hips and knees bent about 45 degrees. Bring dumbbell to outside of left hip by rotating torso to right and extend left leg straight out, foot lowering close to floor. Keep shoulders down and back. Next, bend left knee and extend right leg out, lowering foot close to floor and lift dumbbell up and over to the right, rotating torso to the right. Bring weight back down to outside of left hip, as you extend right leg out and pull left knee back in. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: This explosive movement focuses on the hips. “The core is not limited to just the abdominal muscles,” Tamir notes. “You also need the whole body to create power, strength, and endurance.” This exercise gets more muscles in on the action, while the hinge motion helps to improve riding, especially during acceleration, he adds.

Industry observers note that how to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbell in right hand down by side. Hinge at hips, by sending butt straight back, dumbbell reaching behind you. Keep back flat and core engaged. Using glutes, drive feet into floor and extend hips. Let the power of your glutes send dumbbell forward and up to shoulder height. Engage core, like you’re hitting a standing plank position at the top. Let the momentum of the dumbbell guide you back into a hinge position. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps.

Recent findings suggest that why it works: This anti-rotation exercise works the deep core muscles, including the transverse abdominis that wraps around your midsection, and the multifidus, the posterior core muscles that protect your spine, Tamir explains. “It also helps to stabilize the pelvis to reduce risk of injury,” he adds, and aids in strong posture by working the back.

How to do it: Start in a plank position, left hand on a dumbbell, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be slightly wider than hips. Pull left elbow straight up, dumbbell reaching to ribcage. Lower back down. Repeat. Keep hips as steady as possible. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: The pullover crunch focuses mainly on the rectus abdominus (the muscles on the front of the torso) which helps to stabilize the spine and, in turn, maintain good form, Tamir states.

How to do it: Lie faceup, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands overhead, dumbbell behind you, arms extended. Bend knees, feet planted on floor. Pull dumbbell overhead and crunch up, lifting head, neck, and shoulders off floor. At the same time, lift feet off floor, driving knees toward arms. Slowly lower back down, dumbbell hovering off floor behind you, and feet hovering off floor in front of you. Repeat. Do 12-15 reps.

Why it works: This is a great move for stabilizing the spine, while teaching abdominal bracing, Tamir claims. The weight on one side also forces the core to resist rotation, which you need for efficiency on the road.

It has been revealed that how to do it: Lie face up. Hold dumbbell in right hand over shoulder, arm straight. Extend left arm overhead, biceps by ear. Lift head, neck, shoulders, and legs a few inches off floor. Use legs to rock back and floor, maintaining the hollow body position. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat with dumbbell in left hand.

The collegiate fall racing calendar isn't quite finished, with the 2026 NCAA Cross Country National Championships bringing together teams and individual athletes looking to end their seasons with a title.

Sources indicate that division I gets underway Saturday, November 21, in Terre Haute, Indiana, where 32 men's teams and 32 women's teams will compete. Alongside them will be 38 individual qualifiers whose schools didn't make the team field.

If you've been keeping a close eye on college cross country this season, there's plenty to be excited about this weekend. Oklahoma State returns as the defending men's team champion and winners of two of the past three titles, while NC State's women will look to add another trophy to a particularly successful stretch of their own, having collected four championships since 2021.

According to recent reports, fortunately, you don't have to make the trip to Indiana to catch the action. Here's when everything starts, where the races are being held, and how to watch from home.

The Division I and Division III championships will both take place on Saturday, November 21, although the two competitions will be held in different states.

Division II runners will have to wait a little longer, with their national championship scheduled for Friday, December 4.

According to the NCAA's championship schedule, here's where each division will compete:.

For Division I, ESPNU and the ESPN app will carry the national championships live on Saturday, November 21, with coverage beginning at 10 a.m. ET.

The women's 6K starts at 10:20 a.m., followed by the men's 10K at 11:10 a.m., and the trophy presentation scheduled for around noon.

Fans following Divisions II and III can watch their respective competitions through the NCAA.com's live streaming schedule.

Industry observers note that oklahoma State has been tough to beat in recent years, finishing near the top of the men’s standings more often than not. The Cowboys have claimed two of the last five national titles, winning the national title in 2025, with 57 points, 25 points ahead of runner-up New Mexico.

In a recent development, NC State’s women have enjoyed a similarly strong run, having won three straight titles from 2021 to 2023, before BYU took the 2024 championship. NC State reclaimed the top spot last year, with 114 points.

Division I's national field includes 32 teams per gender, with 18 earning automatic spots through the nine regional championships and another 14 receiving bids through an at-large selection process.

According to recent reports, there are also 38 individual qualifiers in each race, representing schools that didn't advance as teams, so the competition for the individual titles extends well beyond the athletes wearing jerseys from the leading programs. With both individual and team titles on the line, there's plenty to follow once the starting gun goes off.

Tech Report: U.S. Women Could Be Upgraded to World Half Marathon Gold After Kenyan Runner’s EPO Ban

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emma Grace Hurley, Weini Kelati, and Jess McClain already had plenty to celebrate after earning the United States its first women's team medal at September's World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.
  • Sources indicate that on Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) revealed that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance.
  • The Kenyan women originally led with a combined 3:17:33, ahead of the Americans' 3:19:51.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emma Grace Hurley, Weini Kelati, and Jess McClain already had plenty to celebrate after earning the United States its first women's team medal at September's World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen. But nearly two months after finishing with silver, the American trio could soon have gold added to their résumés.

Sources indicate that on Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) revealed that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance. The decision officially disqualifies her second-place finish at the September 20 event, where her silver medal helped Kenya secure the women's team title. But with Loleo's result now thrown out, Kenya's team score has to be recalculated. Countries are ranked by the combined finishing times of their three fastest athletes, and Loleo’s removal means Kenya must now count Lilian Kasait Rengeruk, who finished 34th in 1:10:36, potentially lifting the U.S. to first place in the team standings.

The Kenyan women originally led with a combined 3:17:33, ahead of the Americans' 3:19:51. But removing Loleo's 1:06:05 pushes Kenya's total to 3:22:04, leaving the U.S. in first place by two minutes and 13 seconds. Kenya would drop to second and Ethiopia would remain third, although World Athletics has yet to officially confirm the updated results.

Sources indicate that hurley recently acknowledged the uncertainty in a comment on Citius Mag's Instagram, noting that nobody can know exactly how the race would've unfolded without Loleo. Still, she admitted, "it would've been so cool to celebrate gold 🥹.".

In a recent development, loleo's sample was collected during an out-of-competition test on September 6 ahead of the championships, two weeks prior to the competition. She initially told investigators she couldn't explain the positive result, mentioning an injection she'd received for an injury, but later admitted to the violation on October 30, which earned her a one-year reduction from the standard four-year suspension.

Loleo wasn't the only major Kenyan distance runner to receive a final decision Thursday. Peres Jepchirchir, the reigning world marathon champion and 2021 Olympic gold medalist, was also handed a three-year ban following an EPO finding.

“The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go,” AIU chief executive Brett Clothier remarked in a statement.

“The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.”.

Jepchirchir, who had been provisionally suspended in October, has accepted the disqualification of her results dating back to July 17, including her August victory at the Sydney Marathon. Fellow Kenyan Irine Cheptai is expected to inherit that title.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This time of year, it is easy to start to look ahead to 2027—more than a few riders I know are starting to trade their outdoor rides for more Zwift and gym time. If you’re thinking about winterizing your bike for the season, then it’s the perfect time to start looking at your strength training plan for the offseason.

According to recent reports, for a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside. For others it takes form as time on fat bikes, skis, or even a pair of running shoes. Regardless of how your winter activities take shape, be sure to add some strength training to make sure you can hit your 2027 goals.

Recent findings suggest that the workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training. Each exercise targets a different part of the body to dial in the strength you need when you are trying to power up climbs next year. The workout can be done as a stand-alone set of exercises or it can be added on to your current strength training initiative.

Industry observers note that so many cyclists want to just spend time in the saddle for training—that’s great up to a point. Eventually we all need to get off the bike and spend some time strength training to help break through those frustrating plateaus. These three overlooked exercises can help you elevate your climbs for 2027.

Today I had my first hill-focused ride after a few weeks focusing on running and trainer rides. The first steep pitch swiftly reminded me how much I use my upper body while getting up a hill on the bike. As I climbed, I felt myself pulling on the handlebar with each pedal stroke while gravity was trying to pull me back. Developing the pull muscles is something that will benefit the whole kinetic chain while climbing. Bent-over rows in particular are a great upper-body exercise for this because they engage multiple muscle groups for one movement pattern. Rows can be done with so many different types of equipment: dumbbells, kettlebells, TRX Suspension Systems, elastic bands, and more. Here’s how I recommend doing them with dumbbells.

One of the reasons I love deadlifts for cyclists is because they are exercises that works almost all the muscles through the kinetic chain in one simple move. As we climb, we are pulling energy through our upper body, driving through the hips, and pushing the power through our legs into the pedals. This exercise trains the muscles through your arms, back, and core, while simultaneously working the muscles throughout your legs. Another reason deadlifts are one of my go-to exercises is that they can be done with several different types of equipment. My favorite equipment for this exercise is a barbell, but deadlifts can be done with dumbbells and kettlebells too.

Recovery Tip: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is very real, and depending on the person, your muscle burn can last for a few days after your training session. Proposal accordingly for your rides following a heavy weight day. Listen to your body and add a recovery ride or off-bike activity if that's what you need.

Your core is what ties everything in your body together, so it is integral to grow your stability and power here. While riding today, I was trying to really be in tune with how I was using my core when climbing. When I was in the saddle I felt like the focus from my core was on stability, allowing for a sound upper body while pushing power through my legs and out of the pedals. My simple go-to core exercise to improve climbing is a plank with cross-body knee taps. This works stability through your core while working the internal obliques through the cross-body motion of the knee tuck. This exercise will really show its gains when you get out of the saddle as the climb pitches up.

Recent findings suggest that A quick note on consistency: strength training will give you the best results when you incorporate it in your blueprint week after week. It will offer significantly diminished results if you are sprinkling it in sporadically. If you are able to, try to commit to adding strength training consistently for a four- to six-week block and see how that impacts your rides.

Our strength training program can help get you started with a more in-depth workout strategy. It’s important to remember it does not matter where you are in your cycling journey, there are gains to be found from adding some level of strength training to your calendar.

Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#114900. This Mileage Target Can Help You Determine Whether You Built a Strong Enough Base to Start Race Training

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (729 w)

This Mileage Target Can Help You Determine Whether You Built a Strong Enough Base to Start Race Training

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that base training involves spending a few weeks running at an easy pace and slowly increasing your mileage over time.
  • Building a sufficient aerobic base helps you avoid the aches and pains that come with ramping up mileage too rapidly, especially if you’ve been running sporadically or took some time off.
  • The hard part of this foundational phase?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that base training involves spending a few weeks running at an easy pace and slowly increasing your mileage over time. It’s a crucial first step in any running journey, designed to help you ease into race-specific training.

Building a sufficient aerobic base helps you avoid the aches and pains that come with ramping up mileage too rapidly, especially if you’ve been running sporadically or took some time off. It also makes running feel more doable, as it bridges the gap between your current routine and your goal training strategy.

The hard part of this foundational phase? Figuring out if you’re ready to tackle the first few weeks of a plan and start race-specific workouts. Thankfully, coaches offer a helpful benchmark to hit, plus they explain how to smoothly transition your base routine to race training, without shocking your system.

Building a strong base before racing any distance helps prevent injuries and improves long-term performance, including improved aerobic capacity, endurance, faster recovery, mental conditioning, and weight and stress management, Jill Becker, a personal trainer and run coach at Life Time in Westminster, CO, previously told Runner’s World. That’s why the phase is necessary for all runners, whether you’re fresh to the sport or have a Boston qualifying time on the list of goals.

“Even a 5K race relies heavily on aerobic systems for energy production—so the better the aerobic base you have, the faster you can race,” Laura Norris, owner and coach at Laura Norris Running in Boulder, CO, previously told Runner’s World.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, Norris says doing these easy miles weeks before your goal training block allows your body to adapt to the mileage first, so you can then add in speedwork leading up to race day with lower risk of injury and burnout. Taking this approach helps you avoid increasing volume and intensity at the same time, which can often lead to overtraining.

Finally, tackling a base phase means you’ll feel more confident heading into, say, a four-miler with faster-paced efforts (like tempo or race pace miles), as you’ll have already run four miles at an easy pace consistently for several weeks.

Sources indicate that building a strong base requires covering a certain number of miles consistently over the course of several weeks. Beginners should aim to spend at least 10 weeks on this training block, while intermediate runners can follow a six-week plan, and more advanced runners typically need about four weeks to set that aerobic foundation, Becker notes.

According to recent reports, if you’ve already picked out your training plan, Norris recommends working up to at least 80 percent of the weekly mileage prescribed in the first week of that plan. For example, our 20-week beginner marathon plan prescribes 12 miles in the first week. That means you’ll want to work up to about 10 miles per week before diving into the plan. If you’re looking to break two hours in the half marathon, which requires running at least 18 miles in the first week of the Runner’s World plan, then you’ll want to work up to about 15 miles.

Industry observers note that if you haven’t identified your training strategy yet, Becker recommends adding at least 10 miles to your current weekly volume. (If you’re right now running 10 miles a week, work up to 20.).

Look for a blueprint that builds up to that mileage goal slowly, following the 10 percent rule, which means increasing your mileage by no more than 10 percent each week.

Keep in mind, base training is about setting the foundation for your next training block, and a part of that process should include recovery time. This means making time for rest days and down weeks (in which you reduce your volume to allow for recovery and better performance), as well as staying on top of your nutrition, sleep habits, and cross-training.

#114899. Industry News: Think Your Saddle Is Too High? The Signs Every Cyclist Should Know Before Their Next Ride

Industry News: Think Your Saddle Is Too High? The Signs Every Cyclist Should Know Before Their Next Ride

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours.
  • And because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix.
  • Industry observers note that to get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours. It can show up as pain behind the knee, pressure in the saddle, numbness, or that familiar feeling that you’re reaching for the pedal instead of driving through it.

And because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix. Riders often blame the saddle itself, their bib shorts, or even their flexibility when the issue is simply that the seat is a little too high.

Industry observers note that to get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change. Check out Bicycling’s Guide to the Perfect Bike Fit.

Industry observers note that that stated, saddle height is also where fit advice gets messy. There isn’t one perfect number that works for everyone, and the usual rules of thumb are only starting points. Your ideal height depends on your body, your mobility, your injury history, your cleat setup, and more.

Quick Signs Your Saddle May Be Too High• Pain behind the knee • Saddle sores or numbness • Discomfort where your hamstrings meet your glutes • Rocking hips while pedaling • Reaching for the pedal at the bottom of the stroke Quick Fix• Lower the saddle a few millimeters, do a real ride, and reassess.

Here’s how to tell whether your saddle may be too high and a simple at-home check you can do before your next ride.

In a recent development, saddle height is one of the first things riders adjust, and for good reason. When it’s close, you feel smoother and more comfortable. When it’s off, the problems can spread everywhere.

But this is where people get tripped up: saddle height is important, but it is only one element in an interconnected system. If your cleats are in the wrong place, your saddle is too far forward or back, or your crankarms don’t suit you, changing saddle height alone may not solve much. It’s the beginning of fit, not the whole thing.

A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel. Two riders with the same height and inseam may still end up at different saddle heights because bodies aren’t identical and neither are pedaling styles.

Pain is the clearest warning that something in your position needs attention. Riding is hard. Suffering through an interval is one thing. Pain caused by pressure, strain, or repeated irritation from a bad setup is another.

A saddle that’s too high often indicates up in a few predictable ways:.

This is the classic one. If you feel pain at the back of the knee, especially after longer rides or harder efforts, a too-high saddle is one possible cause.

But not the only one. Fit problems tend to overlap. So treat this as a clue, not a verdict.

If the back of your pedal stroke feels strained, tight, or tuggy, especially when you’re trying to make power, your saddle may be a little high.+.

It has been revealed that A high saddle can make you unstable on the bike. Instead of sitting planted, you start shifting and searching. That extra motion can increase friction and pressure, which can mean hot spots, sores, and numbness.

If your hips are dropping side to side at the bottom of the pedal stroke, there’s a decent chance you’re compensating for too much saddle height.

Sources indicate that some riders point their toes naturally. But if you’re really reaching at the bottom of the stroke and compensating by going toes-down, that can be another sign the saddle is too high.

Rocking hips can also happen with a saddle that’s too low. So can a toes-down pedaling style. Tight hamstrings, limited mobility, weak core stability, and other fit concerns can all muddy the picture. Back-of-knee pain can come from saddle height, but it can also come from saddle fore-aft, cleat setup, or a combination of things.

Sources indicate that that doesn’t make the signs worthless. It just means you should think in patterns, not absolutes.

If you have knee pain plus hip rocking plus pressure and instability in the saddle, now the case gets stronger.

Todd Carver, Specialized’s human performance manager, shared a simple check that can help flag a saddle that may be too high.

If the distance from heel to pedal is more than about one centimeter, your saddle could be too high.

The result is a prompt to look closer, not a green light to make significant changes without further investigation.

Don’t make a giant change. That’s how you turn one problem into several problems.

According to recent reports, start small. Lower the saddle a few millimeters at a time, then ride it long enough to notice whether the change actually helps. One short spin around the block is not enough. You want enough ride time to see whether the pain eases, whether your pedaling feels smoother, and whether you stop shifting around on the saddle.

If you’re dealing with persistent pain, don’t keep self-diagnosing forever.

A good fit pro can sort out whether saddle height is the actual problem or just the most obvious symptom.

Recent findings suggest that riders fixate on saddle height because it feels fundamental. And it is. But it’s also just one part of a system.

A high saddle can absolutely cause trouble. So can cleat position. So can saddle setback. So can crank length. So can your mobility. The goal is not to chase some magic formula you found online. It’s to get to a position that lets you pedal smoothly, make power comfortably, and finish rides feeling worked, not damaged.

That’s why the best takeaway is a modest one: use the common signs, do a quick check, make small changes, and listen to what your body tells you.

#114898. For Years, Doctors Blamed My Mysterious Symptoms on Running. A Simple Blood Test Proved Them Wrong.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (928 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

For Years, Doctors Blamed My Mysterious Symptoms on Running. A Simple Blood Test Proved Them Wrong.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 concern of Runner’s World.
  • Sources indicate that running and menstruation entered my life around the same time, at age 13.
  • Throughout my years on the high school cross-country team, this irregular pattern stuck: I only got about four periods a year and never knew when they would arrive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 concern of Runner’s World.

Sources indicate that running and menstruation entered my life around the same time, at age 13. I got hooked on running the mile, and, swayed by a persistent and impactful track coach, I eventually left soccer behind to join the cross-country team. My first period arrived right before my first track season; however, while the training cycles progressed, my menstrual cycle didn’t—my second period wouldn’t come until five months later.

Throughout my years on the high school cross-country team, this irregular pattern stuck: I only got about four periods a year and never knew when they would arrive. I felt confused and left out whenever my teammates asked me for a menstrual pad I had no use for, like my body couldn’t do what it was supposed to do.

When it came to running, though, my body felt strong, capable of carrying me through interval workouts and lifting heavy weights during weight room sessions. On the track, I felt more equal to my teammates. The training cycle was one I could control.

Sources indicate that at my yearly physical exams, I expressed concern that my periods weren’t occurring monthly, and the feedback was the same every time: I was still young, and sometimes it takes time to become regular. That I accepted. What didn’t sit well with me was what followed: “You’re missing periods because you run a lot. Try eating more.”.

In a recent development, neither felt like an answer to the problem. My 20-something-mile weeks kept me physically fit and helped me deal with anxiety, especially when my dysfunctional home life felt out of control. Not only did the exam show I kept a healthy weight, I had been putting on muscle mass from deadlifting 200 pounds. But hoping the doctor was right, I took a year off from distance training.

Still, no regular cycle in sight.

At 19, I started seeing a new primary care physician. My doctor was surprised when I recounted my prior experiences. “So you’ve never had any blood tests done?” they asked. I underwent the test and a pelvic ultrasound, and it didn’t take very long to get an answer: The likely culprit was polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in people assigned female at birth of reproductive age, yet so much about the condition is still unknown, including the cause of PCOS, according to the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. The National Institutes of Health requires only two of the following symptoms for PCOS diagnosis (all of which I’ve experienced): ovulatory dysfunction (irregular, heavy, or missed periods), high androgen levels (often manifesting as excessive body hair or acne), and/or one or more cysts on the ovaries. Besides irregular menstruation, PCOS can cause, for example, infertility and weight gain. Although there isn’t a permanent cure, some patients are able to treat their symptoms by managing their lifestyle: eating well, exercising regularly, and getting enough sleep.

Industry observers note that the diagnosis came at a turbulent time in my life. I was swept up in another cycle: emotional abuse stemming from controlling relationships. I escaped this abuse through schoolwork and decided to take extra classes over the summer so I could graduate from college a year early and find my own place.

But I also got back to running, which has always helped me build a sense of agency and played a substantial role in my postgrad transition—I spent that summer running across the empty campus and habitually relying on a few miles to calm me when faced with chaos. I started taking an herbal supplement that others with PCOS raved about. I moved in with roommates. I found a therapist to help me unpack the trauma I’ve experienced.

And at 21, I finally started to get a regular monthly period.

Every menstruation since has felt like Christmas morning…followed by some gnawing cramps.

What I am only now starting to understand is just how much my environment affected my mental health and how that in turn impacted my physical health. I recently read research studies linking PCOS and emotional abuse, and that’s when I found what felt like the last missing link.

According to recent reports, I still mourn for the runner I was in high school, who felt lost and frustrated without any answers, dealing with conflicting feelings around her body image. I remember lying on cold, uncomfortable tables, intimidated by informational pamphlets—none of which covered hormonal health—all while doctors were delivering confusing medical advice or dismissing my concerns with oversimplified notions. A 2022 health survey found that 29 percent of women and 21 percent of men felt doctors disregarded their worries during visits. I was told my problem existed “because I ran.” In reality, it’s far more complex than what many people are told, and I am just one example.

It has been revealed that I’ve since run two half marathons while maintaining regular periods throughout each training cycle. Running was never the problem. On the contrary, the very thing doctors blamed my symptoms on brought me relief all along—and I will never give it up again.

Recent findings suggest that kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and right now competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

Recent findings suggest that you won’t catch me heading out for a run without a hat. Unlike headbands, which tend to slip over my eyes or off my head, caps stay put and have a long list of features that optimize your run. The whole point of a hat is to make my runs easier.

When I’m shopping for the perfect hat, it has to check off several boxes:.

Sources indicate that the hat completes my race outfit when I’m running any distance from a mile to a marathon. It keeps my hair from getting into my eyes, and sometimes has extra features, like UPF or even a pocket. And with brands making hats with cool patterns, it can also be a vessel for self-expression. They know that wearing a favorite accessory, one that puts the fun in functionality, can get you into the right headspace when you run.

Recent findings suggest that I started wearing running hats seven years ago. I’m so used to wearing a hat on a run that I feel naked running without one. As I accumulated hats, I started to see some fits and features trumped others. The hats on this list were evaluated with years of experience, research, and hat testing.

On top of my own research, I also had some of our RW staffers test caps and provide feedback.

The caps below all have features that cater to different needs and types of runs. From logging a run on a blistering hot day, going for a workout in the evening, or having a penchant for snacking on pickles during training, know this: there’s a hat for that.

I’ve also added some beanies for the colder months. When testing beanies, I paid attention to fit, comfort, and warmth. It’s not true that you’ll catch cold if your head isn’t covered, but that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t wear a hat to keep your cool.

The Ciele FSTCap wins Best Overall as a cap-wearing runner because of its no-fuss, flexible design. The brim isn’t rigid, allowing it to sit comfortably on your head, and it doesn’t flop out of shape. It’s lightweight and breathable, with fast-drying, anti-odor mesh panels.

In a recent development, but its best feature is the adjustable bungee cord closure. I’ve worn several iterations of Ciele FSTCap at races, and the simplicity of the hat gives me peace of mind before racing because the toggle doesn’t require much dexterity when my arms feel like Jell-O during a marathon when I have to loosen or tighten the cord. It’s machine-washable, too.

This hat is Best Budget, but it’s also Best Visibility. The entire rim of this Headsweats’s Hat has reflective trim for visibility in low light, making a car’s lights heighten your bobbing cap’s outline when you’re running on the shoulder at dusk or dawn, or even nighttime. This feature is fantastic if you feel the neon colors are a little too loud to your liking. The black version isn’t a bad choice, thanks to the reflective rim.

It has been revealed that the hat is a great tool when you’re an early riser or night owl, and the knit shell is soft and breathable. I do have one main critique: it looks cheaply made. I can get over the knit material wearing fast—proper care, like machine washing and air-drying only, should add to the cap’s longevity. Maybe it’s the lack of patterns or even mesh panels or overlays besides the logo on the side. While this hat doesn’t win fashion contests, it definitely fulfills its purpose for running safely by staying visible.

The Ponyflo Alex Active was tested by me and editor Monique LeBrun, who mentioned we should add this hat to our guide for runners who specifically wear high hairstyles. The positioning of the pony opening allows you to run without your visor comically almost covering your eyes if your hair is half-braided high. Runners like me will appreciate how the positioning makes my hair stop just above my back so it’s not whipping my back when I run.

Sources indicate that the hat comes in a variety of colors and there’s even an edition with a longer, wider brim for more sun coverage; though both LeBrun and I felt like we were about to spend a day out gardening wearing them. We felt the brim on the Alex Active sufficed, but the option is there.

Even though the Ciele FSTCap is my racing hat of choice, we’re giving the best racing hat accolade to the Rnnr Pacer Hat. Our testers loved how feather-light the Pacer is and how its perforated panels provide ultimate ventilation.

My one knock would be the buckle, but we didn’t find ourselves struggling to adjust the closure.

“I suppose the best thing I can say about this hat is that never once did I have to adjust it midrun,” remarked RW News Director Andrew Daniels, who tested the whimsically graphic Jungalow version.

Our other Pacer tester, News Editor Theo Kahler, chose to wear the less loud, mostly black Bolt iteration. He appreciated how the hat wasn’t bulky or stiff. “It didn’t give me headaches like some hats do,” he said. But he had one complaint: “On the inside, it indicates ‘Party pace wins the race.’ I don’t really know what that means and could personally do without that.” And as Scroogy as the comment may have sounded, I got a kick out of that.

A pocket in a hat is hard to find, so I was glad to stumble across Nathan’s Run Cool Stash. The hidden pocket can doubly serve as storage space for ice, a key, or even an ID card. The pocket is drop-in below and above; I can tuck in my ID card in both flaps, or clip on a running light. It’s a close stretch against your head so items won’t bounce in the compartment as you run. It’s perfect for my key fob when I park my car by a trail, and can’t store it in my pocket-free shorts.

One caveat: you can only stash on one side of the hat, so if you’re feeling the heat on your right side, I guess you’ll have to wear the cap backwards to cool that side down.

All hail the hard-brimmed trucker hat—only Oiselle does theirs with a twist. The firm brim folds in half down the center, making it easy to downsize into a little triangle and stash into your pocket if you want the sun to hit your face (or maybe have that hat rim forehead imprint fade before you head to work in the morning).

Industry observers note that this was the only hat I packed when I stayed in Sydney for a week leading up to the marathon. The interior sweatband’s mantra “Go fast, take chances” was the positive energy I needed running a race on the opposite side of the world. The wide-holed mesh back also kept my head cool as the race went on and the day got warmer.

A small drawback is how funky the hat can get after a couple wears. The hat is hand-wash only, which explains why an old Runner Trucker’s toggle broke after a machine wash. The hat is mighty on the run, but delicate during a wash cycle.

It has been revealed that I’m going on five years running in my Pickle Peeps hat and have had several compliments over the years whenever I wore it. The all-over print of smiling, shades-wearing dills, gherkins, and cornichons helps me take my races not too seriously. And I’ll absolutely use this hat as an unvoiced request to have the pickle that comes with your sandwich during a postrun brunch.

According to recent reports, I loved this hat so much, I called a Barnes & Noble in Dallas, Texas, to find it and please mail it back when I realized I returned home without my Pickle Peeps in tow. But it’s not just this hat: bananas, ice cream, flying pigs, pizza slices—I have a Sprints hat for every craving and every mood.

Sources indicate that my only critique is the Velcro closure. It’s ruined running shirts, scarves, and whatever else is in my laundry basket or accessories pile. Sprints has snapbacks, but they don’t come in an extensive pattern collection. Sometimes I have to safety-pin the closure when the humidity puffs out my hair.

The Varsity Runner’s Hat brings to mind snowy winters on campus when I went to college in New England. The hat stays put when I head out on windy winter runs, and functions as an out-and-about beanie when I’m not running. The 100-percent merino wool material helps with thermoregulation and sweat-wicking.

The Creek Run Beanie’s waffle knit texture screams cozy, but you can also wear it when you’re actually running (as its name suggests), or skiing if that’s also your thing during the winter. This hat is stretchy but it does run small.

The Skida Alpine is a stretchy, toasty hat that doesn’t overheat your head. Senior Editor Cat Bowen appreciated how the hat was sensory-friendly; its material feels super smooth, and it requires no tugging or micro-adjusting.

Fit can sometimes be tricky when the hat you’re interested in is unisex, or the over-confidently phrased “one size fits all.” You want the hat to be secure around your head so it doesn’t fly off on windy runs, but not too tight that you get a headache.

If the hat comes in multiple sizes, peruse the site’s fit instructions to match. If it’s the dreaded OSFA, check the type of adjustability and material to make sure it stretches and it can expand—or tighten—around your crown.

Concerning caps, you have plenty of options to consider in terms of adjustability and closures. Velcro allows you to easily adjust without fumbling with toggles or buckles and straps, but the material isn’t stretchy and can lose its adhesiveness. Buckles/snaps stay put but can be a pain to troubleshoot and aren’t always easy to adjust midrun.

My personal favorite is the bungee toggle, but they don’t always lock in place and the cord can overstretch over time.

I’m the owner of several hats and no matter how much I rotate or wash them, they eventually get funky. Besides retiring old hats or soaking them in vinegar and baking soda, one thing that doesn’t draw flies to my head postrun is perforated panels or mesh on my cap.

It has been revealed that material is also key, especially when it comes to beanies. Instead of the inevitable sauna your head would be subjected to running in a rigid, cotton-canvas trucker hat, technical running caps are made of nylon and polyester, and beanies are made of polyester and merino wool, which evaporate moisture by drying fast.

Any ol’ running hat, IMHO, is better than none, but there are hats with extra features to look for if you want a hat more tailored to your needs. Some hats come with UPF to block UVB and UVA rays. Reflective detail is something to consider if your runs are mostly in low light. Pockets are great for storing small items, like a key or even a photo ID if you’re okay with running with a noticeable rectangle on the side of your head. I sure am.

How do I measure my head to get my hat size?

Recent findings suggest that the circumference around your head, above your eyebrows and ears is the measurement you seek. You can use a tape measure, or string and ruler if you don’t have measuring tape, to find your circumference. Then, check the brand’s sizing, if provided, to find your fit.

Does running in a cap make you warmer?

It has been revealed that this depends on the thinness of the material and the breathability features—is it mesh, perforated? Some caps like the Nathan Cool Stash Hat can store cold packs or ice in a pocket. An easy way to keep your head cool is to dunk your hat in cold water before heading out on a run. And to keep your head warm? Go with a hat made of merino wool, which naturally insulates.

For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that there are plenty of reasons to start riding inside. Questionable weather, overly packed schedules, and less daylight can cause outdoor riders to head inside for some indoor saddle time. It’s also possible you’re someone who doesn’t ride outside and you just want a good low-impact workout in the comfort of your own home—without breaking the bank.

Recently we did extensive testing in the office on different exercise bikes. I found that some people who don’t ride bikes outside may actually prefer some of the less expensive exercise bike options. Some of the higher-end exercise bikes we tested feel like a real bike outside—and pair with specific apps like Zwift for when you want to get some group rides or racing in. If you aren’t used to a bike outside, then getting comfortable in that position can be a hard transition. More narrow saddles, a more aggressive position, and controls that simulate the shifters on a bike may not be what you want. Largely, these more inexpensive exercise bikes have more upright positions, wider and more padded saddles, and controls that would resemble the exercise bike you might see on the floor of a fitness center.

According to recent reports, keep in mind that inexpensive is relative—the bikes we have on this list range from about $200 up to $700. If you’re looking to boost your mood, stay consistent, or supplement your training with an affordable indoor cycling bike, these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best mix of value, performance, and reliability.

If you're further along in your indoor training journey and none of the bikes on this list feel like the right fit, take a look at our reviews of the Peloton, Zwift Ride V2, and other premium models.

It has been revealed that this budget-priced, belt-driven bike operates a 35-pound flywheel that provides a smooth and quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable via a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately, if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches, and allows riders to adjust the handlebar height as well as the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

In a recent development, using the single-button monitor, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned as you exercise. Just below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame is designed to provide stability and durability, but it's easy to move if you tip it up onto the small wheels on the front edge.

It has been revealed that besides being designed to look like an entry-level Peloton, the Yesoul S3’s biggest selling point is its Bluetooth connectivity, which pairs with the Yesoul Sports App (on both iOS and Android) and works with Zwift and other interactive training apps. All your workout data, including distance, time, calories burned, speed, heart rate, odometer, and cadence, is tracked and easy to access.

In a recent development, the bike has a quiet belt drive and magnetic resistance, with 100 levels that are easy to adjust with a knob. With a height- and distance-adjustable seat and handlebar, the S3 is built to fit riders from 4-feet-9-inches to 6-feet-2-inches—though riders at the higher end of that range and those with disproportionately longer legs might find the riding position to feel a bit “off.” The bike is easy to move on two small transport wheels, and it comes in both white and black models for a sleek, Peloton-like aesthetic.

Sources indicate that this is a fantastic price for a budget bike that delivers a Peloton-like experience. It has the same sleek silhouette, with a saddle that adjusts both up/down and fore/aft, plus an adjustable handlebar height—just like the real thing. The belt-drive system is another massive plus, keeping noise to a minimum so the only sounds you hear are your own effort (and hopefully some music to cover it up).

To keep costs down, this bike skips the large built-in display, instead offering a tablet holder and Bluetooth connectivity. That means you can ride with any third-party app you prefer—including Peloton classes—using your own device. At this price, it’s a fair trade-off. But if you want a built-in screen, Merach offers a similar model with that feature for about $450 more.

According to recent reports, merach’s newest bike, the A26 Aura, is one of the best Peloton competitors I’ve seen. It follows the familiar design cues of premium exercise bikes — a sturdy frame, heavy flywheel, and whisper-quiet belt-drive system. The seat adjusts up and down as well as fore and aft, and the handlebar also moves vertically for a comfortable fit.

At its current sale price, the Merach A26 Aura makes a compelling case as one of the best values on this list.

The Echelon Connect Sport 2 delivers a Peloton-like experience at a more affordable price. It connects via Bluetooth to the Echelon Fit app, allowing you to track speed, distance, and calories. If you’re taking a live class, you can also view your ranking on the leaderboard. The app offers over 40 live classes daily and a library of more than 15,000 on-demand sessions. While the bike doesn’t have a built-in screen, its device holder accommodates tablets up to 8 inches wide.

That remarked, you don’t need the connected features to get a great workout. At its core, this is a solid, well-built exercise bike with a heavy flywheel and 32 resistance levels, manually adjusted with a knob behind the handlebar. The bike features a “one size fits most” design, with adjustable saddle and handlebar positions to suit most adults. However, some shorter riders have reported difficulty positioning the saddle close enough to the handlebars for a comfortable fit.

With Bluetooth and USB connectivity to the Schwinn ConnectTM, Zwift, and MyFitnessPal apps, this stationary bike is a great option for interactive workouts—particularly if you want to work through pre-programmed sessions and track your progress over time. The bike has the standard DualTrack console shared by similar-level Schwinn and Nautilus products, which has two sharp, backlit LCD screens loaded with 29 workouts.

Unlike many of the bikes we've selected that adjust gradually in difficulty at the turn of a knob, this model has 25 preset levels of magnetic resistance, which provides a nice range in difficulty. The seat and handlebar adjust by height and angle to fit consumers from 4-feet-6-inches to 6-feet-6-inches; however, as always, those at the far ends of the range might have more difficulty getting a comfortable fit. Ultimately, the bike is a solid package for the price—especially if you can catch one on sale for around $400.

Looking for a cheap home exercise bike that will neither take over your space nor break the bank? When not in use, this compact device folds down to half its size and can be easily rolled into a closet or tucked under a bed.

While it may have a minimalist design, it still has the basic functionality needed for a workout. It touts 12 levels of magnetic resistance, adjusted via a knob below the handlebar, that allows you to adjust the intensity as needed. The built-in LCD screen, although very basic, keeps track of key workout stats, including distance, time, speed, calories burned, and heart rate.

Recent findings suggest that users love how quiet this bike is, making it perfect for multitasking or watching TV while riding. Though it may not provide the high resistance some hardcore riders seek, many praise it as a “sturdy, well-built machine” with a “comfortable seat and great height adjustability.”.

Recent findings suggest that just like with a regular bicycle, if you want the best experience on your indoor bike, it’s notable to get the proper fit. Josh Taylor, a global brand ambassador for the online fitness site Spinning, recommends finding an indoor cycling bike that puts you in the same position as the bike you’re accustomed to riding outside.

For example, if your daily rider is a road bike, look for an indoor cycling bike with a handlebar option that incorporates a traditional bullhorn bar and mimics the hand-position options of drops and brake hoods. However, if you’re already used to taking studio classes, an indoor cycling bike with just the traditional bullhorn-style bar will work great, says Ben Sharp, three-time Order of Ikkos medal recipient and founder of Sharp Coaching.

Recent findings suggest that if you don’t ride at all outside or in a spin class yet, then it will take a bit more playing around with the exercise bike to figure out sizing and position. Start with getting saddle height set up correctly, then if you can adjust reach to the handlebars that’s step two. For the reach shoot to have a slight bend in the elbows and remember to keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. Matt Phillips, Senior Test Editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on dialing in saddle height. What applies to saddle height on an outdoor bike largely applies to exercise bikes as well. “A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel,” says Phillips.

Join Bicycling All Access for more in-depth gear reviews.

When you’re riding an outdoor bike, you’re mostly working against inertia as you pedal. In order to recreate that sensation and effort on a stationary bike, manufacturers have to simulate that resistance in some way. Most choose to use a fan or a flywheel (a weighted disc that spins as you pedal).

Flywheels work by storing inertia as they spin, and smoothing out the pedal stroke to eliminate that choppy up and down motion you’d otherwise experience. For most budget spin bikes, a heavier flywheel means a smoother ride, though some bikes opt for a light (8-pound) flywheel that maintains its inertia by spinning four times as fast instead.

Industry observers note that since the pedals on spin bikes are fixed to the flywheel (no coasting), the smooth-moving mechanism helps keep your pedaling consistent. These bikes will usually have a knob or lever that allows you to adjust the resistance, making it harder or easier to pedal, independent of your cadence (how fast you’re spinning the pedals). If you’re used to riding a bike outside, then think about it like riding a fixed-gear bike or fixie.

Fan-operated resistance bikes are a bit simpler: As you pedal, the fan blades push against the air around the machine. Your cadence is directly related to the amount of effort required to push the pedals, meaning these bikes don’t allow you to spin at a fast cadence with low resistance, which can be nice for warming up or cooling down.
